OSM Finding:
OSM has determined that these minor, editorial revisions do not affect the meaning or effectiveness of Ohio's regulations, which continue to be no less effective than the Federal regulations at meeting the requirements of SMCRA, and OSM therefore approves them.
D. Revisions to Ohio's Rules That Are No Less Effective Than the Corresponding Provisions of the Federal Regulations
OAC 1501:13-1-10 Availability of Records
In 2009, Ohio deleted language from subsection (B)(2) that required certain county offices in counties where mining is occurring or proposed to occur, but in which DMRM does not maintain its own office, to either make copies of certain records available for public inspection or make available a description of information available for copying and mailing to requestors. Ohio's revision would have put the sole responsibility for making those records available on the DMRM district office responsible for inspection of the operation, in whichever county that office happens to be located. In 2016, as part of this current program amendment, Ohio restored the language it had deleted in 2009. Additionally, Ohio revised subsection (B)(2)(b) and added subparagraphs (b)(i) and (b)(ii), to make a distinction between requestors who are residents of the area where the mining is occurring and those who are not. Subparagraph (b)(i) provides that if the requestor is a resident of the area where the mining is occurring, DMRM will provide copies of the requested documents at no charge, and subparagraph (b)(ii) provides that for other individuals requesting copies of the records, DMRM will comply with ODNR's policy in charging a fee for copies.
OSM Finding:
Ohio submitted its 2009 revisions as part of a program amendment that OSM docketed at SATS No. OH-252-FOR. Subsequent to that submission, OSM notified Ohio of the requirement at
30 CFR 840.14(c)
that requires that the records (or the description thereof) be available at a Federal, State or local government office in the county where the mining is occurring or proposed to occur, and Ohio restored the language it had deleted in order to keep its rule as
(
printed page 67205)
effective as the Federal rule. In the program amendment docketed at SATS No. OH-252-FOR, OSM deferred its decision on Ohio's 2009 revision until OSM could address it together with Ohio's 2016 correction.
See
91 FR 51324
,
51347
(Aug. 7, 2026). Because OSM had not approved Ohio's 2009 revision, it had not taken effect.
See
30 CFR 732.17(g)
. Therefore, OSM need not approve Ohio's correction but reiterates that Ohio's corrected rule continues to be as effective as the Federal rule at
30 CFR 840.14(c)
. Secondly, OSM notes that
30 CFR 840.14(c)(2)
requires only that in providing copies by mail, the regulatory authority must provide such copies at its own expense at the request of residents of the area where mining is occurring or proposing to occur. Therefore, Ohio's election to provide copies at no charge for residents and at a fee consistent with ODNR policy for nonresidents is no less effective than the Federal rule, and OSM approves Ohio's revisions to OAC 1501:13-1-10(B)(2)(b).
OAC 1501:13-4-03 Permit Applications; Requirements for Legal, Financial, Compliance and Related Information
Ohio revised subsection (D)(2) to narrow when a permit applicant mining a private mineral estate that has been severed from the private surface estate must submit a consent for right of entry from the landowner, a document of conveyance that expressly grants or reserves the right to extract the coal, and/or other documentation acceptable under state law that demonstrates that the applicant has that legal right. Ohio's revisions to subsection (D)(2) and its subordinate clauses add that such documents are required when surface disturbance will result from the applicant's proposed use of surface mining methods, and that the documents demonstrate that the landowner consents to, or the other documents convey the right to, cause the surface disturbance. Ohio also revised subsections (E)(3) and (E)(4) to specify that the distance limitations of coal mining operations from occupied dwellings and roads are measured horizontally.
OSM Finding:
Ohio's revisions to this rule reflect revisions to Ohio's statutes at ORC 1513.07(E)(2) and ORC 1513.073 from Ohio House Bill 163 (approved June 30, 2011), 2011 Ohio Laws 36, which OSM approved in a separate program amendment docketed at SATS No. OH-252-FOR.
See
91 FR 51324
,
51343
(Aug. 7, 2026). OSM incorporates its discussion of those revisions here and approves the revisions to OAC 1501:13-4-03.
OAC 1501:13-4-04 Permit Application Requirements for Information on Environmental Resources
Ohio added subsection (D)(6), which consists of numerous provisions that outline the methodology a permit applicant must use to identify seasonal variations for groundwater and surface water, including a process for collection and submission of water samples and a table showing periods throughout the year that exhibit low flow, transition flow, intermediate flow, and high flow conditions.
In addition, Ohio included the Division's Permitting and Hydrology Policy/Procedure Directive 2002-2 (PPD 2000-2), so it would be applied consistently to all statewide mining permit applications. Ohio also added subsection (D)(7) to allow applicants to collect water quality and quantity data in a manner other than described in subsection (D)(6), so long as DMRM determines that the alternative data is adequate to identify the necessary seasonal variations for the hydrologic assessments required by ORC Chapter 1513 and its related regulations.
Ohio deleted subsections (J) and (K), which contained the requirements for maps, supplementary maps, cross-sections, designs and plans, and moved those provisions to OAC 1501:13-4-08 (discussed below), and a new rule at OAC 1501:13-4-08.1 (discussed above in Part A).
OSM Finding:
The proposed revisions relate to Ohio's requirements for permit applications for information on environmental resources for the proposed mining area. The Federal regulations at
30 CFR 780.21(b)
and
784.14(b)
require that permit applicants include certain baseline hydrologic information, including the seasonal quality and quantity of groundwater and information on surface water quality and quantity sufficient to demonstrate seasonal variation, with quantity descriptions to include, at a minimum, baseline information on seasonal flow rates. OSM has determined that the proposed revisions have no Federal counterpart. Ohio incorporated these provisions into its regulations from its guidance document entitled, “Permitting and Hydrology Policy/Procedure Directive 2002-2(PPD 2000-2)” due to a 2007 State court decision in the matter
Buckeye Forest Council, Inc.
v.
Div. of Mineral Res. Mgmnt.
172 Ohio App.3d 440. In
Buckeye,
the Court of Appeals of Ohio, Seventh Appellate District, found that Ohio's guidance applied to all mining applications statewide, it constituted an improperly promulgated rule that was therefore unenforceable (though that issue was not outcome determinative to the case).
Id.
at 446-47. Because Ohio simply adopted into regulation its existing guidance for complying with its approved SMCRA program, OSM considers these revisions non-substantive and find that they do not affect the meaning or effectiveness of Ohio's program. This rule continues to be no less effective than the Federal regulations requiring certain baseline hydrologic information at
30 CFR 780.21(b)
and
784.14(b)
and no less stringent than Section 507(b)(11) of SMCRA and are approved. OSM addresses the map requirements from subsections (J) and (K) as they appear in their new locations at OAC 1501:13-4-08 and -08.1 and approves their deletion here.
OAC 1501:13-4-05 Permit Application Requirements for Reclamation and Operation Plans
Ohio revised subsection (A)(2)(b) to require that certain facilities that the applicant proposes to retain on the property after the completion of reclamation be necessary for the approved postmining land use. Ohio's revision restores the requirement to the version that existed prior to April 30, 2009, when Ohio began to require that retention of the facilities need only be approved by DMRM. Subsection (G)(2) requires that the reclamation plan contain a copy of comments from the surface landowner and relevant government authorities concerning the proposed postmining land use. Ohio added a proviso to this subsection to specify that this requirement will not apply where no surface disturbance will result from proposed auger/highwall mining. Ohio also added subsection (H)(7) to incorporate by reference Soil Conservation Service Technical Release No. 60 and direct the reader to OAC 1501:13-9-04(H)(1)(a) for information on obtaining a copy.
OSM Finding:
OSM addressed Ohio's restoration of subsection (A)(2)(b) in the program amendment docketed at SATS No. OH-252-FOR. In OH-252-FOR, OSM explained that because Ohio restored the requirement as OSM originally approved it, OSM did not need to address its deletion.
See
91 FR 51324
,
51349
(Aug. 7, 2026). Likewise, OSM does not need to further address its restoration.
Ohio explained that its new proviso for auger/highwall mining at subsection (G)(2) was predicated on a related revision to its statutes at ORC 1513.07(E) by Ohio House Bill 163, referenced above, that written consent
(
printed page 67206)
for right of entry by the landowner (or written conveyance for the right to mine) was required only where the mining would result in surface disturbance. OSM also addressed that revision in OH-252-FOR, where OSM explained that when an operation will not disturb the surface, the surface rights owner will not be affected.
Id.
at 51349. However, OSM added that in the case of room-and-pillar or auger mining, access points would qualify as surface disturbance. In Ohio's Rule Summary and Fiscal Analysis form dated November 2, 2015, which accompanied the current revision, Ohio explained that “the landowner will have full, undisturbed use of the land above auger/highwall mining before, during, and after mining” and that even with the new proviso, subsection (G)(2) remains as effective as the Federal provision at
30 CFR 780.23(c)
because the proviso relates only to “the area above a highwall or auger mining operation that will not have surface disturbance.” Even though the text of the proviso itself does not make this distinction between areas above the highwall and access points, OSM approves this revision with the understanding that the proviso does not apply to access points of these operations, which OSM explained in OH-252-FOR constitute surface disturbance. Under Ohio's interpretation of the proviso, subsection (G)(2) remains as effective as the Federal rule at
30 CFR 780.23(c)
at meeting the requirements of the Act and is consistent with our approval of Ohio's revision to ORC 1513.07(E) in OH-252-FOR, and OSM will continue to monitor Ohio's implementation of this rule through our regular oversight function to determine whether future clarification is necessary. Finally, Ohio's addition of subsection (H)(7) has no substantive effect on Ohio's rules pertaining to ponds, impoundments, banks, dams, and embankments included in the reclamation plan and only provides additional reference for informational purposes. Therefore, OSM approves it.
OAC 1501:13-4-08 Application, Supplemental and Hydrologic Maps, and Cross-Sections, Designs and Plans
Ohio revised this rule, which formerly pertained only to hydrologic maps and cross-sections, to also include the map, cross-section, design and plan requirements for surface coal mining operations and the surface operations of underground mines that Ohio deleted from subsections (J) and (K) of both OAC 1501:13-4-04 (related to surface mining permit applications) and 1501:13-4-13 (related to underground mining permit applications). Subsection (A) relates to maps submitted with the permit application, and subsection (B) relates to supplementary maps, cross-sections, designs and plans. Ohio made several additional revisions, such as replacing the phrase “permit area” with “proposed permit area” and clarifying that certain features must be shown if they are within the proposed permit area, and certain other features must be shown if they are located in and within a certain distance from the proposed permit area. Ohio revised subsection (A)(25) to require that the application map show the location of gas and oil wells in and within twenty-five feet of the proposed permit area, rather than simply in the permit area, and the location of producing gas and oil wells in and within three hundred feet of the proposed permit area. With this revision, Ohio also segregated out the requirement that the map show the location of water wells into its own provision at subsection (A)(26).
OSM also deferred addressing revisions Ohio made to these provisions in 2010 that were part of OH-252-FOR, referenced above.
See
91 FR 51324
,
51348
(Aug. 7, 2026). Ohio deleted from the provision that now exists at subsection (A) that enabled an applicant to have its application maps certified by an engineer and added language allowing that they be certified by either a surveyor, or jointly by an engineer and surveyor to the extent such joint certification is required by State law. Similarly, Ohio deleted from the provision that now exists at subsection (B)(2) language that enabled an applicant to have its supplementary maps and cross-sections certified by a surveyor, now allowing that they be certified by an engineer or jointly by an engineer and a surveyor to the extent such joint certification is required by State law.
Finally, Ohio re-lettered the existing hydrologic map and cross-sections provisions as subsections (C)-(F) and revised internal citations accordingly. Ohio also revised subsection (C)(11), which required that the hydrologic map show all underground coal mine entries within one thousand feet of the proposed permit area, to now require the location and extent of known workings of active, inactive, or abandoned underground mines, including mine openings to the surface, within the proposed permit and adjacent areas.
OSM Finding:
Ohio's transition to the phrase “proposed permit area” and additional phrasing to denote whether a feature must be within the proposed permit area are minor clarifications that reflect our use of those qualifying phrases in the mapping requirements of
30 CFR Chapter VII
, subchapter G. Ohio's revision to subsection (A)(25) to extend the rule to gas and oil wells within 25 feet of the proposed permit area, and out to 300 feet for producing gas and oil wells, is no less effective than the corresponding Federal requirements at
30 CFR 779.25(a)(10)
and
783.25(a)(10)
, which only requires showing gas and oil wells within the proposed permit area. As OSM has explained before, Section 505(b) of SMCRA,
30 U.S.C. 1255(b)
, provides the States discretion to require more stringent regulations. Next, Ohio's revisions to limit who prepares and certifies maps, plans and cross-sections are no less effective than
30 CFR 779.25(b)
and
783.25(b)
at meeting the requirements of the Act. As OSM explained when OSM promulgated the Federal regulations, Congress amended SMCRA in 1983 to allow the preparation and certification of maps, plans and cross-sections to professional surveyors where authorized by State law.
See
50 FR 16194
(Apr. 24, 1985). Ohio retains the discretion to direct which components of its mapping requirements are prepared by professional engineers, surveyors, or in combination, as appropriate under State law. Finally, Ohio's decision to require the location and extent of known workings of active, inactive, or abandoned underground mines on its hydrologic maps, in addition to the existing requirement to show the mine openings, is also no less effective than the Federal requirements. The Federal regulations at
30 CFR 779.25(a)(5)
and
783.25(a)(5)
require those features to be shown on the application maps, as does Ohio's regulation at subsection (A)(21), but does not otherwise require those be shown on the hydrologic map. Accordingly, OSM finds that Ohio's revisions to this rule render it no less effective, and in some cases more stringent, than the Federal mapping requirements of
30 CFR Chapter VII
, subchapter G, and OSM approves them.
OAC 1501:13-4-09 General Map Requirements
Ohio revised subsection (B) to specify that the map legend must indicate which symbols from OAC 1501:13-4-10(C) appear on the map. Ohio also revised subsection (D)(1) to include supplemental maps and hydrologic maps in the list of map-types that could appear in the title, which must describe the map.
OSM Finding:
These revisions relate to Ohio's general requirements for maps
(
printed page 67207)
submitted with permit applications for proposed mining operations. The Federal regulations do not contain any specific requirements for map legends nor titles. Consequently, each regulatory authority may provide map legend or title requirements it believes will aid in the effective implementation of its approved program. Therefore, the proposed revisions are no less effective than the various mapping requirements under
30 CFR Chapter VII
, subchapter G, parts 777, 779, 780, 783 and 784, and no less stringent than Sections 507(b)(9), (b)(13) and (b)(14) of SMCRA, and OSM approves them.
OAC 1501:13-4-10 Uniform Color Code and Map Symbols
In updating this rule, Ohio determined that its changes and additions to the map symbols were significant enough that rescinding the existing rule and replacing it with the amended version was preferable to making line-by-line revisions. For our purposes, OSM simply notes the differences between the previous rule and the new rule as if they were revisions. Ohio revised subsection (A) to specify that supplemental maps and hydrological maps must also use the uniform color codes laid out in the rule. Ohio revised subsection (A)(3) to establish a color code for area lines and shading designating existing impoundments and wetlands, with the latter distinguished by whether the wetlands have been verified by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or not, and if they are proposed/restored/mitigated wetlands. Ohio revised subsection (A)(4) to clarify that the streams to which it applies may be perennial or intermittent, to change the coloring, and to add a distinction for areas within 100 feet of a perennial or intermittent stream where the buffer area will not be disturbed. Ohio also added color codes for any shadow areas at new subsection (A)(7), and, on annual maps, for remining areas affected during each mining year that are not to be reaffected during the following mining year at new subsection (B)(3). Finally, Ohio revised subsection (C) to add a requirement that the size and location of each symbol must not obscure other necessary information on the map, and to modify and add to the list of uniform map symbols, which appear at paragraphs (1) through (82) (up from thirty-nine).
OSM Finding:
The Federal regulations do not contain any specific requirements pertaining to mapping color codes or symbols. Like OSM found above with map legends and titles, each regulatory authority may provide color code or symbol requirements it believes will aid in the effective implementation of its approved program. Therefore, the proposed revisions are no less effective than the various mapping requirements under
30 CFR Chapter VII
, subchapter G, parts 777, 779, 780, 783 and 784, and no less stringent than Sections 507(b)(9), (b)(13) and (b)(14) of SMCRA, and OSM approves them.
OAC 1501:13-4-11 Maps Showing Reaffection of Permit Area
In addition to some miscellaneous editorial updates and corrections, Ohio revised subsections (B), (B)(2) and (B)(5) to restore the use of the phrase “valid existing rights,” which Ohio had changed to “a valid right to the mineral resource” in 2009.
OSM Finding:
OSM need not discuss the substance of these provisions, the reason for Ohio's 2009 change, which Ohio asserts was in error, nor its subsequent reversal. OSM neither addressed nor approved Ohio's 2009 revisions and, therefore, as mentioned elsewhere in this amendment, OSM need not address Ohio's subsequent correction.
OAC 1501:13-4-13 Underground Mining Permit Application Requirements for Information on Environmental Resources
Ohio made the same revisions to the mapping and seasonal variation of water provisions to this rule that it made to OAC 1501:13-4-04, the equivalent regulation for surface coal mining permit applications that OSM discusses above.
OSM Finding:
OSM incorporates its discussion above of those changes here and approves the revisions to this rule for the same reasons.
OAC 1501:13-4-14 Underground Mining Permit Application Requirements for Reclamation and Operations Plans
Like its companion rule for surface mining permits at OAC 1501:13-4-05, addressed above, Ohio revised subsection (A)(2)(b) to require certain facilities the applicant proposes to retain on the property after the completion of reclamation be necessary for the approved postmining land use. Ohio's revision restores the requirement to the version that existed prior to April 30, 2009, when Ohio began to require that retention of the facilities need only be approved by DMRM. Ohio also added subsection (H)(7) to incorporate by reference Soil Conservation Service Technical Release No. 60 and direct the reader to OAC 1501:13-9-04(H)(1)(a) for information on obtaining a copy.
OSM Finding:
As OSM discussed above, OSM need not address any further Ohio's revisions restoring the requirements of subsection (A)(2)(b). OSM also incorporates our findings from above regarding Ohio's revision to subsection (H)(7) of OAC 1501:14-4-05, and OSM approves the identical revision here for the same reasons.
OAC 1501:13-5-01 Review, Public Participation, and Approval or Disapproval of Permit Applications and Permit Terms and Conditions
Ohio revised subsection (E)(6) to specify that DMRM must review the permit application to ensure that the applicant has provided proper right-of-entry documentation for areas where the proposed operation results in surface disturbance. Ohio also revised subsection (G)(3), which requires that each permit has a specific condition that coal mining and reclamation operations are conducted only on those lands specifically designated on maps submitted pursuant to certain rules, to add a reference to its new mapping rule for underground workings at OAC 1501:13-4-08.1, which OSM approved above.
OSM Finding:
As OSM explains above in our approval of revisions to OAC 1501:13-4-03(D)(2), Ohio's revisions to this rule reflect revisions to Ohio's statutes at ORC 1513.07(E)(2) and ORC 1513.073 from Ohio House Bill 163 of 2011, which OSM approved in a separate program amendment docketed at SATS No. OH-252-FOR.
See
91 FR 51324
,
51342-43
(Aug. 7, 2026). OSM incorporates our discussion of those revisions here and approves this revision. OSM notes that Ohio made a subsequent revision to a citation to OAC 1501:13-4-03 due to a revision Ohio made to that rule in 2018. The 2018 revision, and by extension the 2020 correction, are part of a separate program amendment docketed at SATS No. OH-256-FOR, and OSM does not make any determination on them here.
Ohio's revision to subsection (G)(3) does not substantively change the rule's requirements, which OSM had already found as effective as the corresponding Federal regulation at
30 CFR 773.17(a)
. The Federal rule more broadly describes “maps submitted with the application” without enumerating the required maps. Ohio made a subsequent revision to subsection (G)(3) that is a part of OH-256-FOR, and which OSM does not address here.
OAC 1501:13-7-07 Liability Insurance
Ohio revised subsection (A) to allow a permit applicant with an existing permit to include in a new permit
(
printed page 67208)
application a notarized certification recognizing that proof of liability insurance, along with the rider required by subsection (B)(3), exist in the applicant's central file for identity information authorized by OAC 1501:13-4-03(J), in lieu of a separate, independent certificate of insurance.
OSM Finding:
The Federal regulations at
30 CFR 800.60
require that an applicant must submit as part of its permit application a certificate of insurance that meets the requirement of that rule, including a rider that requires that the insurer notify the regulatory authority whenever substantive changes are made in the policy including termination or failure to renew. The Federal regulation does not expressly provide that in lieu of that certificate, an operator may provide a notarized certification that a certificate of insurance exists in a central file that exists for the applicant. However, OSM finds that this measure, meant to avoid duplication of documents for applicants that hold several permits, is no less effective than the Federal requirement, and OSM approves it. In promulgating
30 CFR 800.60
, OSM specified in response to public comments that one policy could cover multiple operations.
See
48 FR 32910
,
32958
(July 19, 1983). OSM approved Ohio's creation of the central file authorized by OAC 1501:13-4-03(J) in 2015, noting that while it has no precise Federal counterpart, that it provides an acceptable alternative means for submitting, updating, and maintaining identification information.
See
80 FR 63120
,
63123
(Oct. 19, 2015).
OAC 1501:13-9-01 Signs and Markers
Ohio limited the types of markers that may be used at the operation to fence posts, trees, engineering lath or stakes by deleting from subsection (C)(1) the phrase “but shall not be limited to.” Ohio also revised the marker requirements for buffer zones at subsection (E) by requiring those markers include orange and black stripes to distinguish them from the solid orange required of other markers and require that they clearly define the limits of the buffer zone so that adjacent buffer zone makers are visible in either direction along the boundary. Ohio also reduced the number of paragraphs from subsection (C) that apply to buffer zones, eliminating the application of paragraphs (2), (4), and (6), that apply to the permit boundary and permit area more broadly, and added a reference to its rule describing buffer zones at OAC 1501:13-9-04(E).
OSM Finding:
The Federal regulations concerning signs and markers at
30 CFR 816.11
and
817.11
only require that they are of uniform design, can be easily seen and read, are made of durable material, and conform to local ordinances and codes, among other general performance standards. Regarding buffer zones, the Federal regulations require that they are marked only along their boundaries. Ohio's revisions relate to details that do not exist in the Federal regulations and do not diminish Ohio's existing requirements, which OSM had originally found to be as effective as the Federal regulations at the time OSM approved of the Ohio program. Therefore, OSM approves these revisions.
OAC 1501:13-9-07 Disposal of Excess Spoil
Ohio revised subsection (K), which requires that underground disposal of excess spoil occur according to a plan approved by DMRM and MSHA under OAC 1501:13-4-14(N), by adding a citation to subsection (O). Ohio also corrected applicable internal citations at subsection (M), related to durable rock fills, and subsection (N), restoring an earlier requirement that placement of spoil on preexisting benches meet the engineering and design requirement of subsection (B). Also, at subsection (N), Ohio disallows placement of excess spoil on the downslope below the upper bench except on designated gravity transport courses properly prepared according to OAC 1501:13-9-03. Ohio revised this provision to add that the courses also be prepared according to OAC 1501:13-9-14, which also contains requirements for postmining graded slopes.
OSM Finding:
OSM finds that none of the citations Ohio added or revised in this rule changed the basic existing requirements that already conformed to the Federal requirements at
30 CFR 816.71
(Disposal of excess spoil: General requirements), 816.73 (Disposal of excess spoil: Durable rock fills) and 816.74 (Disposal of excess spoil: Preexisting benches), and their correlating provisions in
30 CFR part 817
. In restoring the requirement that design be certified by a registered professional engineer, Ohio explained that it was unclear why the reference was removed through a rulemaking in 1988, but that it is required by subsection (c) of both
30 CFR 816.74
and
817.74
. OSM notes that OSM also did not approve its removal in 1988, so OSM considers this correction typographical. Following Ohio's revisions, OAC 1501:13-9-07 remains as effective as the Federal regulations in meeting the requirements of the Act, and, therefore, OSM approves them.
OAC 1501:13-9-08 Protection of Underground Mining
Ohio added subsections (B) and (C) to this rule to create a two-hundred-foot distance limitation between underground mining operations and other active and abandoned underground mining operations, as well as from coal exploration drilling operations. Ohio made a corresponding revision to subsection (A) to clarify that subsection (A) regulates surface mining operations.
OSM Finding:
Neither of Ohio's new provisions require our approval because they do not regulate activities subject to SMCRA and its implementing regulations. Subsection (B) regulates the underground activities of underground coal mining operations; it does not regulate the surface operations or surface effects of underground mines regulated by SMCRA.
See
30 U.S.C. 1291(28)
. Subsection (C) regulates the distance that must remain between coal exploration drilling and underground coal mines. While SMCRA does regulate some components of coal exploration activities,
see
30 U.S.C. 1262
and
30 CFR parts 772
and
815
, the distance between coal exploration drilling and underground workings is not a component of the Federal program. Ohio's revisions to subsection (A), which reflects the Federal requirement for surface mining activities at
30 CFR 816.79
, are merely editorial to distinguish it from subsections (B) and (C), and OSM approves them.
OAC 1501:13-9-15 Revegetation
Ohio revised subsection (F)(6), which requires that permanent vegetation that is established or reestablished on areas unavoidably disturbed in order to meet reclamation standards, or in the course of gaining access for the removal of sediment control structures, must have been seeded a minimum of twelve months before the request for phase III bond release. Ohio's revision to this subsection allows DMRM to determine that the 12-month requirement does not apply if the area of repair was limited in size and the permittee is in compliance with subsection (G)(3)(b), which is a standard of revegetation success requiring the ground cover to equal or exceed 90 percent and no single area with less than thirty percent cover shall exceed the lesser of three thousand square feet or 0.3 percent of the land affected.
OSM Finding:
When OSM initially approved subsection (F)(6) and its related provisions in 1998, OSM explained that the 12-month minimum requirement should be sufficient to
(
printed page 67209)
establish a permanent and diverse vegetative cover as required by SMCRA because the lands typically involved will be small in size, widely dispersed, and surrounded by vegetative lands.
See
63 FR 51829
,
51831
(Sept. 29, 1998). OSM also explained that the 12-month minimum requirement in no way reduces or eliminates any of Ohio's standards for reclamation success or bond release. Both of these findings remain true for areas which DMRM relieves the operator from the 12-month requirement based on a determination that the area of repair is limited in size and complies with OAC 1501:13-9-15(G)(3)(b). Therefore, OSM finds that Ohio's revision does not render OAC 1501:13-9-15 any less effective than the Federal regulations at
30 CFR 816.116(c)(4)
and
817.116(c)(4)
at meeting the requirements of Sections 515(b)(19), (b)(20)(A) and (b)(20)(B) of SMCRA, and OSM approves it.
OAC 1501:13-9-17 Postmining Use of Land
Ohio revised subsection (D) to add two additional criteria that must be met for DMRM to approve an alternative postmining land use. Ohio added paragraph (2), which requires that the use not be impractical or unreasonable, and paragraph (7), that the use will not cause or contribute to violation of Federal, State, or local law.
OSM Finding:
Ohio's proposed revisions to add these criteria make Ohio's regulation consistent with the Federal regulations at
30 CFR 816.133
and
817.133
, which include the same requirements at subsections (c)(3)(i) and (iv) of each rule. Therefore, OSM approves Ohio's revisions to OAC 1501:13-9-17.
OAC 1501:13-11-02 Support Facilities and Utility Installations
Ohio revised subsection (C) to add to the list of utility installations to which coal mining operations must minimize damage, destruction or disruption of services, to include oil, gas, and water wells, water and sewage lines and telecommunication lines (in addition to telephone lines, which already existed in the regulation).
OSM Finding:
Ohio's proposed revisions to include oil, gas and water wells, water and sewage lines, and telecommunications lines, make Ohio's regulation consistent with the Federal regulations at
30 CFR 816.80
and
817.180
, which explicitly include those wells and lines. OSM also interprets “other telecommunication lines” to be a necessary and natural interpretation of the Federal requirement to include telephone lines. Therefore, OSM approves Ohio's revisions to OAC 1501:13-11-02.

Executive Order 13175
—Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
The Department of the Interior strives to strengthen its government-to-government relationship with Tribes through a commitment to consultation with Tribes and recognition of their right to self-governance and tribal sovereignty. Executive Order 13175

In making the determination as to whether this rule would have a significant economic impact, the Department relied upon the data and assumptions for the corresponding Federal regulations.
Congressional Review Act
This rule is not a major rule under
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
, the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act. This rule: (a) does not have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million; (b) will not cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, Federal, State or local government agencies, or geographic regions; and (c) does not have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S.-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises. This determination is based on an analysis of the corresponding Federal regulations, which were determined not to constitute a major rule.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
This rule does not impose an unfunded mandate on State, local, or Tribal governments, or the private sector of more than $100 million per year. The rule does not have a significant or unique effect on State, local, or Tribal governments or the private sector. This determination is based on an analysis of the corresponding Federal regulations, which were determined not to impose an unfunded mandate. Therefore, a statement containing the information required by the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (
2 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
) is not required.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; reallocation.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is reallocating the projected unused amounts of Pacific cod from catcher vessels using trawl gear to catcher vessels less than 60 feet (18.3 meters (m)) length overall (LOA) using hook-and-line or pot gear and American Fisheries Act (AFA) trawl catcher/processors in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands management area (BSAI). This action is necessary to allow the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod in the BSAI to be harvested.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 26, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Andrew Olson, 907-206-5813.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the BSAI according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC specified for catcher vessels using trawl gear in the BSAI is 25,706 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (
91 FR 11750
, March 10, 2026) and reallocation (
91 FR 64806
, October 13, 2026).
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC specified for catcher vessels less than 60 feet (18.3 m) LOA using hook-and-line or pot gear in the BSAI is 4,557 mt as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (
91 FR 11750
, March 10, 2026) and reallocations (
91 FR 16583
, April 2, 2026,
91 FR 55499
, August 28, 2026, and
91 FR 64806
, October 13, 2026).
The 2026 Pacific cod TAC specified for AFA trawl catcher/processors in the BSAI is 2,712 mt as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (
91 FR 11750
, March 10, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that catcher vessels using trawl gear will not be able to harvest 475 mt of the 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to those vessels under § 679.20(a)(7)(ii)(A)(
9
). The Regional Administrator has also determined that catcher vessels less than 60 feet (18.3 m) LOA using hook-and-line or pot gear have the capability to harvest an additional 400 mt of Pacific cod TAC and AFA trawl catcher/processors have the capability to harvest an additional 75 mt of Pacific cod TAC.
Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(a)(7)(iii)(A), NMFS reallocates 400 mt of Pacific cod from catcher vessels using trawl gear to the annual amount specified for catcher vessels less than 60 feet (18.3 m) LOA using hook-and-line or pot gear. In accordance with § 679.20(a)(7)(iii)(B), NMFS reallocates 75 mt of Pacific cod from catcher vessels using trawl gear to the annual amount specified for AFA trawl catcher/processors.
The harvest specifications for 2026 Pacific cod TAC included in final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (
91 FR 11750
, March 10, 2026) and reallocations (
91 FR 16583
, April 2, 2026,
91 FR 55499
, August 28, 2026, and
91 FR 64806
, October 13, 2026) are revised as follows: 25,231 mt to catcher vessels using trawl gear and 4,957 mt to catcher vessels less than 60 feet (18.3 m) LOA using hook-and-line or pot gear and 2,787 mt to AFA trawl catcher/processors.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by
50 CFR part 679
, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on Pacific cod catch in a timely fashion and would not allow for the full harvest of the Pacific cod TACs by the sectors with harvesting capability. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on the catch of Pacific cod by sectors operating in the BSAI and the capability of certain sectors to harvest additional TAC only became available as of October 21, 2026.
There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to waive the 30-day delay in the effective date of this action. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of a new system of records.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended (Privacy Act), the U.S. Department of Education (Department) publishes this notice of a new system of records titled “National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE) Evaluation Studies” (18-14-49) and rescindment of the following system of records notices, as the records previously covered by those notices are now covered by the NCEE Evaluation Studies system of records: DC Choice Program Evaluation (18-13-07), Evaluation of Teacher Residency Programs (18-13-24), National Longitudinal Transitions Study 2012 (18-13-27), Evaluation of the Pell Grant Experiments Under the Experimental Sites Initiative—2012 (18-13-31), Study of Enhanced College Advising in Upward Bound (18-13-36), National Evaluation of the Striving Readers Comprehensive Literacy and Comprehensive Literacy State Development Programs (18-35-45), Connecting Adults to Success: Evaluation of Career Navigator Training (18-13-46), and Impact Evaluation of Training in Multi-Tiered Systems of Support for Reading In Early Elementary School (18-13-48). The Department proposes this new system of records to cover records from the identified studies and future NCEE evaluation studies that fall within the categories of individuals, categories of records, purposes, routine uses, and other terms described in this notice, in order to promote efficiency across its research and evaluation functions.
DATES:
Submit your comments on this notice of a new system of records on or before November 25, 2026. This new system of records will become applicable upon publication in the
Federal Register
on October 26, 2026, unless it needs to be changed as a result of public comment. The routine uses outlined in the section titled “ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND PURPOSES OF SUCH USES” will become effective on the expiration of the 30-day period of public comment on November 25, 2026, unless they need to be changed as a result of public comment. The Department will publish any significant changes to the system of records or routine uses resulting from public comment.

regulations.gov
. However, if you require an accommodation or cannot otherwise submit your comments via
regulations.gov
, please contact the program contact person listed under

. The Department will not accept comments submitted by fax or by email, or comments submitted after the comment period closes. To ensure that the Department does not receive duplicate copies, please submit your comments only once. In addition, please include the Docket ID at the top of your comments.

www.regulations.gov
to submit your comments electronically. Information on using

, including instructions for accessing agency documents, submitting comments, and viewing the docket, is available on the site under “FAQ”.

www.regulations.gov
.
Therefore, commenters should be careful to include in their comments only information that they wish to make publicly available.
Assistance to Individuals with Disabilities in Reviewing the Rulemaking Record:

NCEE conducts large-scale evaluations of education programs in accordance with the Education Sciences Reform Act (
20 U.S.C. 9501
et seq.
) and other applicable laws, supports applied research studies related to questions of education policy and practice, provides technical assistance, and supports the development and use of research and evaluation findings throughout the United States. This system of records is used to fulfill NCEE's legislative mandate to conduct research and evaluation activities related to education policy, programs, and practices and to support the wide dissemination of the results of evaluation, research, and products developed to stakeholders such as policymakers, practitioners, and researchers. By law, NCEE research, evaluations, and data projects must be timely, objective, and non-ideological; free of political influence and bias; and relevant and useful to practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and the public.

SYSTEM NAME AND NUMBER:
National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance Evaluation Studies (18-14-49).
SECURITY CLASSIFICATION:
Unclassified.
SYSTEM LOCATION(S):
National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences (IES), U.S. Department of Education, 400 Maryland Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20202.
A current list of contractor sites where system records are maintained is available from the System Manager and at
https://ies.ed.gov/​about
.
SYSTEM MANAGER(S):
Commissioner, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education, 400 Maryland Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20202.
AUTHORITY FOR MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM:
This system of records is authorized under sections 171, 173 and 174 of the Education Sciences Reform Act (
Pub. L. 107-279
), codified at
20 U.S.C. 9561
,
9563
, and
9564
. The collection of Social Security numbers, where necessary for a particular study, is authorized under
Executive Order 9397
(November 22, 1943) as amended by
Executive Order 13478
(November 18, 2008).
PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:
The records in this system are used for the purpose of conducting research, evaluation, and data analytic projects commissioned by the National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. Each project may involve: (a) the analysis of data from various sources; (b) the collection of data through assessments, surveys, interviews, focus groups, and other methods; (c) the evaluation of programs and services; (d) the provision of services to populations and evaluating their outcomes; (e) the provision of technical assistance to outside entities; and (f) other research, evaluation, and data related activities within NCEE's statutory authority.
This work may be supported or accomplished by Federal staff or by contractors, vendors, grantees and other partners working on behalf of NCEE.
A current list of studies covered under this system of records notice is available from the System Manager and at
https://ies.ed.gov/​about
.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
The system will include records about the following categories of individuals: (a) individuals who are considered for inclusion or are included in an NCEE study (
e.g.,
State, district, and school staff and other individuals who are involved with the administration of programs and strategies under study such as staff at institutes of higher education and adult education centers; individuals and families who participate in or may benefit from programs and strategies under study); (b) individuals who provide information about those considered or selected for an NCEE study (
e.g.,
state officials, school or grantee staff); and (c) individuals whose information is contained within an extant dataset needed to conduct an NCEE study (
e.g.,
educators, students, grantee staff). This includes administrative datasets created by offices, agencies, or organizations outside of NCEE when those datasets are necessary for an NCEE study.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
The records maintained about a specific individual will depend on which NCEE study the individual was considered for or included in and the individual's role in the study. As relevant and necessary for a particular NCEE study, the system may include the individual's personally identifiable information (
i.e.,
name, address(es), telephone number(s), email address(es), Social Security number); date of birth; sociodemographic characteristics (
e.g.,
race, ethnicity, gender); language preferences and proficiencies; responses to assessments and collections (
e.g.,
surveys and interviews); voice and video recordings and transcripts; correspondences; identifiers specific to the applicable study or series of studies in which the individual is involved; and administrative records (
e.g.,
participation in courses or programs, attendance). As relevant and necessary for a particular NCEE study, it may also collect records about an individual's current and prior education; employment; current and previous addresses; mental and physical health and well-being; involvement with the criminal justice system; behaviors that increase the risk of harm to educational and other outcomes (
e.g.,
illicit drug use); household structure and dynamics (
e.g.,
marriage, relationships); disabilities; social service and benefit use; other characteristics; experiences relevant to Federal education programs or strategies related to such programs; perceptions relevant to Federal education programs and strategies.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
The sources of records in the system may include, as relevant to a particular study: the record subject; the Department; other governmental agencies (
e.g.,
Federal, state, tribal, and local) and their agents; NCEE contractors and subcontractors; research institutions, foundations, and similar organizations; publicly available documents and data sets; commercial sources; individuals who know the record subject (
e.g.,
relatives, district staff, school and postsecondary institution staff, and service providers) and other third parties such as vendors and the National Student Clearinghouse.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
The Department may disclose information contained in a record in this system of records under the routine uses listed in this system of records notice without the consent of the individual if the disclosure is compatible with the purposes for which the record was collected. The Department may make these disclosures on a case-by-case basis or, if the Department has complied with the computer matching requirements of the Privacy Act of 1974, pursuant to a computer matching agreement. Any disclosure of personally identifiable information from a record in this system must also comply with the requirements of section 183 of ESRA (
20 U.S.C. 9573
) providing for confidentiality standards that apply to all collections, reporting, and publication of data by IES. Any disclosure of personally identifiable information from student education records that were obtained from schools, school districts, postsecondary institutions, and other sources must also comply with the requirements of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) (
20 U.S.C. 1417(c)
;
34 CFR 300.610-300.611
,
300.613-300.623
, and
300.625-300.627
), the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) (
20 U.S.C. 1232g
;
34 CFR part 99
), and, where applicable, the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA) (
20 U.S.C. 1232h
;
34 CFR part 98
), which protect the privacy of student education records.
(1)
Contract Disclosure.
If the Department contracts with an entity for the purposes of performing any function that requires disclosure of records in this system to employees of the contractor or its subcontractors or consultants, as applicable, the Department may disclose the records to those employees. As part of such a contract, the Department will require
(
printed page 67306)
the contractor and any subcontractors or consultants, if applicable, to agree to maintain safeguards to protect the security and confidentiality of the records in the system and to comply with applicable Privacy Act requirements under
5 U.S.C. 552a(m)
.
(2)
Research Disclosure.
The Department may disclose records to a researcher if the Department determines that the individual or organization to which the disclosure would be made is qualified to carry out specific research related to the functions or purposes of this system of records. The researcher must agree to safeguards and use restrictions, consistent with section 183(c) of the ESRA (
20 U.S.C. 9573(c)
), to protect the security and confidentiality of the records disclosed from this system. When personally identifiable information from a student's education record will be disclosed to the researcher, under FERPA (
20 U.S.C. 1232g(b)
and
34 CFR 99.31
), the researcher also must agree to comply with applicable FERPA requirements.
(3)
Obtaining Participants' Academic, Employment, Financial, and Benefits Records.
The Department may disclose information from this system of records to Federal, State and local agencies as well as other organizations (
e.g.,
the National Student Clearinghouse, high school equivalency test vendors) to obtain participants' academic, employment, financial, or benefits records.
(4)
Participant Identification Disclosure.
The Department may disclose information from this system to staff at sites participating in a study for purposes consistent with the conduct of the study. For instance, the Department may disclose information that is necessary for sites to provide education records linked to study participants or to provide services that are part of the study.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:
Electronic records are stored in databases on IES' or its contractors' or subcontractors' secure servers.
Records stored in paper copy are stored in secure areas within locked drawers or cabinets.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:
Records in this system are indexed and retrieved by a unique number, name, or other identifying particular assigned to or associated with each individual that can be cross-referenced when needed with the separately stored direct personal identifiers.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:
The Department has submitted a retention and disposition schedule that is intended to cover the records contained in this system to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) for review. Pending NARA approval, the records will be treated as unscheduled records and will not be destroyed except as authorized by NARA.
ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:
Department and its contractors and subcontractors are required to maintain appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the records from unauthorized access. Administrative controls include training individuals who have access to the records on how to handle them appropriately, incident response plans, and limiting access to individuals who need to know the information. Technical controls include the use of antivirus software, vulnerability patching, and multi-factor authentication when required. Physical controls include storing hard copy records and computer systems used to access electronic records in physically locked locations when not in use.
Department, contractor, and subcontractor employees who collect or maintain data in this system shall comply with the requirements of the confidentiality standards in section 183 of the ESRA (
20 U.S.C. 9573
).
RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES:
If you wish to gain access to a record that exists regarding you in this system, contact the system manager at the address listed above. Your request must provide necessary particulars such as the study in question, your full name, current address, the date and place of your birth, and any other identifying information requested by the Department while processing the request to distinguish between individuals with the same name. Your request must meet the requirements in
34 CFR 5b.5
, including proof of identity.
CONTESTING RECORD PROCEDURES:
If you wish to contest the content of a record regarding you, you must contact the system manager at the address listed above. Requests must contain your full name, address, and telephone number. Your request must meet the requirements of the regulations at
34 CFR 5b.7
.
NOTIFICATION PROCEDURES:
If you wish to determine whether a record exists regarding you in this system of records, you must contact the system manager at the address listed above. Your request must provide necessary particulars such as the study in question, your full name, current address, the date and place of your birth, and any other identifying information requested by the Department, while processing the request, to distinguish between individuals with the same name. Your request must meet the requirements in
34 CFR 5b.5
, including proof of identity.
EXEMPTIONS PROMULGATED FOR THE SYSTEM:
None.
HISTORY:
None.

ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is amending its regulations to facilitate direct leveraging of prior U.S. Department of Energy or Department of War authorizations of demonstration reactors into the NRC's licensing reviews of commercial reactor facility applications that reference those designs. This rulemaking improves NRC licensing review efficiency, where applicable, by explicitly establishing by regulation an additional means for reactor applicants to demonstrate the safety functions of their reactor designs, thereby contributing to the safe and secure use and deployment of civilian nuclear energy technologies.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on November 25, 2026.

I.
Executive Order 14300
: Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission
On May 23, 2025, President Donald J. Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.” Section 5, “Reforming and Modernizing the NRC's Regulations,” directed the NRC to undertake a review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents as guided by the policies set forth in section 2 of the E.O. This rulemaking addresses section 5(d), which contemplates an expedited pathway to approve reactor designs that the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) or the Department of War (DOW) have tested and that have demonstrated the ability to function safely.
[
1
]
E.O. 14300
further states that NRC review of such designs should focus solely on risks that may arise from new applications permitted by NRC licensure, rather than revisiting risks that have already been addressed in the DOE or DOW processes.
II. Discussion
Consistent with its authority and historical practice under section 161 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (AEA) to make, promulgate, issue, rescind, and amend rules and regulations as well as that under section 182 of the AEA to determine the information that enables the Commission to make the findings required to grant an application for a utilization facility, the NRC is amending title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) section 50.43, “Additional standards and provisions affecting class 103 licenses and certifications for commercial power,” and section 53.440, “Design requirements.” These changes explicitly establish a pathway for streamlined reviews for licensing commercial reactor designs that have previously received
(
printed page 67196)
DOE or DOW authorization and that have been tested and have demonstrated the ability to function safely. The amendment to § 50.43 explicitly establishes such a pathway for the licensing frameworks under
10 CFR part 50
, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” and part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” and the amendment to § 53.440 does so for the
10 CFR part 53
, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Commercial Nuclear Plants,” licensing framework. A similar provision is included in a separate proposed rule, “Licensing Requirements for Microreactors and Other Reactors With Comparable Risk Profiles,” which, if finalized, would apply to the associated proposed
10 CFR part 57
, “Licensing Requirements for Microreactors and Other Reactors with Comparable Risk Profiles,” licensing framework (
91 FR 23628
; May 1, 2026). The primary intent of this rulemaking is to improve NRC licensing review efficiency, and in turn increase capacity, for conducting licensing reviews. At the same time, this rulemaking maintains flexibility for the NRC to leverage a broad range of technologies, testing methods, and information from previously authorized and evaluated designs, as appropriate and supported by an applicant in its commercial license application. In turn, this contributes to the safe and secure use and deployment of civilian nuclear energy technologies.
Section 50.43(e) provides two options for license applicants to demonstrate how newer reactor designs, including those that use simplified, inherent, passive, or other innovative means, accomplish their safety functions. The final rule adds the option, to be codified in § 50.43(f), for an applicant to reference information from a prior DOE or DOW authorization as a means for an NRC license applicant to show that the design can accomplish its safety functions, as required by § 50.43(e).
The amendment to § 50.43 explicitly reflects the option for NRC Class 103 license applicants to directly reference a prior DOE or DOW authorization when demonstrating compliance with NRC regulatory requirements. Applicants using this option are required to identify how aspects of the prior authorization satisfy NRC regulations, including § 50.43(e). Applicants are also required to address how any changes to the design, its functionality, associated hazards, siting information, or underlying safety assumptions from those considered in prior authorization reviews meet applicable NRC requirements.
Under the part 53 licensing framework, § 53.440 provides a series of design requirements. The requirements in § 53.440(a)(1) reflect an essential element of ensuring a proposed design can comply with the performance criteria in part 53, namely that the abilities of design features to fulfill their safety functions are demonstrated by a combination of analyses, test programs, prototype testing, and operating experience. This requirement closely aligns with the language in § 50.43(e) and reflects the same foundational requirement.
The amendment to § 53.440(a)(1) explicitly accommodates the option for NRC Class 103 license applicants to directly reference a prior DOE or DOW authorization for the purpose of demonstrating that the design features required by § 53.400, “Design features for licensing-basis events” meet the defined functional design criteria required by §§ 53.410, “Functional design criteria for design-basis accidents,” and 53.420, “Functional design criteria for licensing-basis events other than design-basis accidents.” Such a demonstration is required to consider interdependent effects throughout the commercial nuclear plant and the range of conditions under which the design features required by § 53.400 must function throughout the plant's lifetime. Applicants using this option are required to identify how aspects of the prior authorization satisfy applicable NRC regulations.
The new §§ 50.43(f) and 53.440(a)(1) pathways will be supported by the draft Interim Staff Guidance (ISG), DANU-ISG-2026-XX, “NRC Application Pathway for Reactor Designs Previously Authorized by U.S. Department of Energy or Department of War.” The guidance is not part of this rulemaking but was published for public comment on April 17, 2026 (
91 FR 20717
). The scope of such guidance is intended to facilitate staff review of future commercial nuclear plant license applications, including advanced reactor designs that may not employ light-water technology.
The NRC also recognizes significant public interest in this rule and has provided a separate public comment response document as discussed in Section IV of this document, “Public Comment Analysis.” While that document provides comprehensive responses to comments, several points are highlighted below.
Some comments expressed concern that this rulemaking would impact the NRC's performance of independent evaluations of license applications mandated under the AEA. Specifically, section 103 of the AEA and title II of the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 (88 Stat. 1242) authorize the NRC to, among other things, issue licenses for commercial nuclear power plants if in the opinion of the Commission, issuance of the license would not be inimical to the common defense and security or to the health and safety of the public. First and foremost, this rulemaking does not affect the NRC's commitment to conducting independent reviews, nor does this rulemaking alter any underlying regulatory requirements an applicant must meet. Nothing in this rule delegates to DOE, DOW, or any other agency the NRC's functions to evaluate a request for NRC approval, and nothing in this rule allows the NRC to forego an independent review. Regardless of whether an applicant references a prior DOE or DOW authorization, it remains the applicant's responsibility to demonstrate compliance with all applicable requirements, under the AEA and NRC regulations, and the NRC will continue to conduct the independent assessments necessary to confirm whether such requirements have indeed been satisfied. Where an NRC applicant references information from a prior design authorized and tested by DOE or DOW, the applicant is responsible for justifying the applicability and relevance of the information it seeks to rely upon, and where it does so, the NRC may be able to tailor the focus and depth of its review.
Under this approach, the NRC notes that the extent to which prior DOE or DOW information can be leveraged depends on the information an applicant provides and the associated justification as to how it meets NRC requirements. For example, the scope of a DOE or DOW authorization or associated testing may not fully represent a commercial reactor configuration or the breadth of analyses necessary for an NRC licensing basis. The final rule is intentionally structured to reflect that not all prior DOE or DOW authorizations may meet the full scope of requirements specified in § 50.43 and, in recognition of this, to nevertheless make clear that the NRC retains the flexibility to leverage information from such authorizations to the maximum extent practical.
In addition, some comments highlighted that it would be beneficial for the NRC to provide additional clarity as to the type of information an NRC application might include in a discussion of how a prior DOE or DOW authorization supports the application.
(
printed page 67197)
In light of these comments, the NRC is clarifying that, when demonstrating compliance with applicable regulations, an NRC applicant may, for example, consider including a discussion of the following: (A) the scope of the prior authorization, including the testing, analyses, and operational experience on which it relied, as applicable; (B) the safety functions and design features addressed by such authorization; and (C) any differences from the prior authorization in design, operational, or siting factors relevant to the application that are material to the Commission's licensing review.
Finally, several commenters expressed concerns that the proposed § 50.43(e)(3) would establish a lower safety standard than that required by § 50.43(e)(1)-(2) and § 53.440(a)(1). As explained in the public comment response document, the NRC has revised the language originally proposed to be codified in § 50.43(e)(3) and has added it as a new subsection § 50.43(f) to clarify and to reaffirm that this rulemaking does not alter the safety standard established in§ 50.43(e) and to enhance consistency with the approach taken in the rule revision to § 53.440(a)(1). As such, the final rule language makes clear that § 50.43(f) is one option that a commercial license applicant may use to satisfy the requirements, or a subset of the requirements, contained in section(e). As previously noted, applicants must still meet all applicable NRC and statutory requirements. Although § 50.43(f) provides a pathway for reactor technologies to demonstrate the ability to accomplish safety functions under § 50.43(e), if an authorization does not supply all necessary information, the final rule language in § 50.43(f) reflects that applicants must address any remaining gaps to ensure full compliance with NRC requirements.
III. Opportunities for Public Participation
The proposed rule was published in the
Federal Register
on April 2, 2026 (
91 FR 16584
) for a 30-day comment period ending May 4, 2026. The NRC held a public meeting on April 14, 2026, and developed a public meeting summary (ML26131A245).
IV. Public Comment Analysis
The NRC prepared a summary and analysis of public comments (“NRC Response to Public Comments: NRC Reviews of Reactor Designs Previously Authorized by U.S. Department of Energy or Department of War”) received on the proposed rule, as referenced in the “Availability of Documents” section. In response to the proposed rule, the NRC received 136 unique comment submissions.
The public comment submissions are available from the Federal rulemaking website at
https://www.regulations.gov
under Docket ID NRC-2025-1503. Responses to the public comments, including a summary of how this final rule changed as a result of the public comments, can be found in the public comment response document as indicated in the “Availability of Documents” section of this document.
V. Regulatory Flexibility Certification
Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
), the NRC certifies that this rule does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. This final rule affects only the licensing and operation of nuclear power plants. The companies that own these plants do not fall within the scope of the definition of “small entities” set forth in the Regulatory Flexibility Act or the size standards established by the NRC (
10 CFR 2.810
).
VI. Regulatory Analysis
The NRC has not prepared a separate regulatory analysis. However, the NRC performed a qualitative economic analysis of the rule's impacts. As a result of this final rule, the NRC expects that the NRC will not need to repeat technical reviews previously performed by DOE or DOW, to the extent that those reviews cover the same scope as the related content in the NRC license application. The final rule language at § 50.43(f) offers an option to meet the requirements in § 50.43(e), and the final rule language in § 53.440(a) provides an option for how to demonstrate that the design features required by § 53.400 meet the design criteria required by §§ 53.410 and 53.420. Therefore, the NRC does not anticipate that an application under the new § 50.43(f) or the revised § 53.440(a)(1) would require more review work than under the existing requirements. Furthermore, the NRC assumes that applications under these sections will be high-quality applications.
In general, the NRC expects cost savings to both applicants in preparing an application and the NRC in reviewing that application. The NRC was not able to quantify these potential savings in a useful way at this time. These savings depend on the applicability of the DOE/DOW reviews to NRC requirements and the ability of applicants to demonstrate that applicability, the number of applications that may reference a previous DOE/DOW authorization, as well as how any potential differences (
e.g.
, changes to the design or site-specific factors) from the previously authorized design also meet NRC requirements. The NRC anticipates that use of the approaches provided by § 50.43(f) or 53.440(a)(1) will become more efficient as experience is gained,
i.e.
, there may be an initial learning curve which may result in greater cost savings over time, to both the NRC and applicants, as a result of the additional flexibility this final rule provides to applicants. Therefore, the NRC expects that this final rule will be cost beneficial to both the NRC and future applicants.
VII. Backfitting and Issue Finality
The changes to §§ 50.43(f) and 53.440(a)(1) do not impose new or revised requirements on existing licensees or approval holders because they include an option that would apply only to future applicants. Therefore, the changes do not constitute backfitting as defined in § 50.109(a)(1) or 53.1590(a)(1) or affect the issue finality of an existing approval issued under
10 CFR part 52
, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants.”
VIII. Cumulative Effects of Regulation
The NRC seeks to minimize any potential negative consequences resulting from the cumulative effects of regulation (CER). The CER describes the challenges that licensees, or other impacted entities such as State partners, may face while implementing new regulatory positions, programs, or requirements (
e.g.
, rules, generic letters, backfits, inspections). The CER is an organizational effectiveness challenge that may result from a licensee or impacted entity implementing a number of complex regulatory actions, programs, or requirements within limited available resources.
The goals of the NRC's CER effort were met throughout the development of this final rule. The NRC engaged with external stakeholders at a public meeting and solicited public comments on the proposed rule. The NRC included in the proposed rule a request for feedback related to CER. Specifically, the NRC requested feedback on the implementation and potential unintended consequences of the proposed rule, and invited comments on the regulatory analysis. The NRC received several comment submissions in response to these CER questions, which are addressed in the public comment response document as indicated in the “Availability of Documents” section of this document.
(
printed page 67198)
IX. Plain Writing
The Plain Writing Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-274
) requires Federal agencies to write documents in a clear, concise, and well-organized manner. The NRC has written this document to be consistent with the Plain Writing Act as well as the Presidential Memorandum, “Plain Language in Government Writing,” published June 10, 1998 (
63 FR 31885
).
X. National Environmental Policy Act
The NRC has determined that this final rule is the type of action eligible for categorical exclusion because it meets the criterion described in § 51.22(a)(1). This provision includes amendments to parts 50 and 53 related to procedures for filing and reviewing applications for licenses or construction permits or early site permits or other forms of permission or for amendments to or renewals of licenses or construction permits or early site permits or other forms of permission. The action belongs to a category of actions that the Commission, by rule or regulation, has declared to be a categorical exclusion, after first finding that the actions within the category do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment. Therefore, neither an environmental impact statement nor environmental assessment has been prepared for this final rule. For any particular licensing action that would use the pathways from this rule, the NRC will comply with its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, including by developing or using an environmental impact statement, environmental assessment, or categorical exclusion, as applicable.
XI. Paperwork Reduction Act
This final rule does not contain any new or amended collections of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). Existing collections of information were approved by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), approval numbers 3150-0011 and 3150-0274.
Public Protection Notification
The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting or requiring the collection displays a currently valid OMB control number.
XII. Executive Orders
The following are Executive orders that are related to this final rule:
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review (as Amended by
Executive Order 14215
, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)
E.O. 12866
provides that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within the OMB will review all significant rules. OIRA has determined that this final rule is a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
; though not economically significant under section 3(f)(1). Accordingly, the NRC submitted this final rule to OIRA for review. The NRC has prepared an economic analysis in accordance with section 6(a)(3)(B) of
E.O. 12866
. More can be found in Section VI, of this document, “Regulatory Analysis.”
B.
Executive Order 14154
: Unleashing American Energy
NRC has examined this final rule and has determined that it is consistent with the policies and directives outlined in
E.O. 14154
.
C.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is a deregulatory action as defined by
E.O. 14192
. Details on the estimated costs of this final rule can be found in Section VI of this document, “Regulatory Analysis.”
D.
Executive Order 14270
: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash American Energy
E.O. 14270
, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) promulgated under the AEA, the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC determined that the regulatory changes proposed in this rule are part of the NRC's regulatory permitting scheme authorized by the AEA, ERA, or NWPA. Therefore, the NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of
E.O. 14270
and did not insert conditional sunset dates for the regulatory changes in this final rule.
XIII. Congressional Review Act
This final rule is a rule as defined in the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 801-808
). However, OMB has found that it does not meet the criteria at
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
.
XIV. Voluntary Consensus Standards
The National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995,
Public Law 104-113
, requires that Federal agencies use technical standards that are developed or adopted by voluntary consensus standards bodies unless the use of such a standard is inconsistent with applicable law or otherwise impractical. In this final rule, the NRC revised its regulations to facilitate direct leveraging of prior DOE or DOW authorizations of demonstration reactors into the NRC's licensing reviews of commercial reactor facility applications that utilize those designs. This action does not constitute the establishment of a standard that contains generally applicable requirements.

Federal Register
notices announcing the availability of the new guidance documents. The documents will be available at
https://www.regulations.gov
by searching on Docket ID NRC-2026-0760.
