International Trade Administration
[A-201-847]
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is simultaneously initiating and issuing the preliminary results of a changed circumstances review (CCR) of the antidumping duty (AD) order on heavy-walled rectangular welded carbon steel pipes and tubes (HWR) from Mexico, consistent with section 751(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and
19 CFR 351.216
and
351.221(c)(3)(ii)
. Based on the information on the record, we preliminarily determine that Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V. (PLM) is the successor-in-interest to Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V. (PyH). Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Paola Aleman Ordaz, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-4031.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 13, 2016, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD order on HWR from Mexico.
[
1
]
On August 19, 2026, PLM informed Commerce that, effective July 11, 2017, it had changed its name from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PyH) to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PLM) and requested that Commerce conduct a CCR under
19 CFR 351.216(b)
to determine that PLM is the successor in-interest to PyH for purposes of determining PLM's AD cash deposits and liabilities.
[
2
]
On September 3, 2026, Commerce declined to initiate the CCR that PLM requested, citing the need for additional information pertaining to any changes in management, production facilities, customers, and suppliers.
[
3
]
Therefore, Commerce issued a supplemental questionnaire to PLM, to which we received a timely response on September 21, 2026.
[
4
]
We did not receive comments from other interested parties concerning this request.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the scope of the
Order
is HWR from Mexico. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
5
]
Initiation of Changed Circumstances Review
Pursuant to section 751(b)(1) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.216
, Commerce will conduct a CCR of an order upon receipt of information or a review request from an interested party for a review of an order which shows changed circumstances sufficient to warrant a review of the order.
[
6
]
In the past, Commerce has used CCRs to address the applicability of cash deposit rates after there have been changes in the name or structure of a respondent, such as a merger or spinoff (“successor-in- interest,” or “successorship,” determinations).
[
7
]
The information submitted by PLM supporting its claim that it is the successor-in-interest to PyH demonstrates changed circumstances sufficient to warrant such a review.
[
8
]
The information submitted by PLM substantiates that its request is based solely on a change in the name of the company from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” effective on July 11, 2017.
[
9
]
Moreover, the evidence submitted in support of PLM's request demonstrates that PLM is otherwise the same business entity as PyH. Therefore, in accordance with the regulation referenced above, Commerce is initiating a CCR to determine whether PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH.
Preliminary Results
Commerce is permitted by
19 CFR 351.221(c)(3)(ii)
to combine the notice of initiation of a CCR and the preliminary results if Commerce concludes that expedited action is warranted. In this instance, because the record contains information necessary to make a preliminary finding, we find that expedited action is warranted and we have combined the notice of initiation and the preliminary results.
Accordingly, pursuant to section 751(b) of the Act, we have conducted a successor-in-interest analysis in response to PLM's request. In making a successor-in-interest determination in an AD CCR, Commerce examines several factors, including, but not limited to, changes in the following: (1) management and ownership; (2) production facilities; (3) supplier relationships; and (4) customer base.
[
10
]
While no single factor or combination of factors will necessarily provide a dispositive indication of a successor-in-interest relationship, generally, Commerce will consider the new company to be the successor to the
(
printed page 67290)
previous company if the new company's resulting operation is not materially dissimilar to that of its predecessor.
[
11
]
Thus, if the evidence demonstrates that, with respect to the production and sales of the subject merchandise, the new company operates as essentially the same business entity as the former company, Commerce will assign to the new company the cash deposit rate of its predecessor.
[
12
]
In its CCR request, PLM provided evidence demonstrating that PLM's operations are not materially dissimilar from those of PyH. Based on the record, we preliminarily determine that PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH, as the change in the name was not accompanied by significant changes to its management and ownership, production, facilities, supplier relationships, or customer base. There is also no evidence of significant changes between PyH and the successor-in-interest company PLM's operations, ownership, or corporate or legal structure during the relevant period that could have impacted the successor-in-interest company's subsidy levels.
[
13
]
Thus, we preliminarily determine that PLM operates as essentially the same business entity as PyH, that PLM is the successor-in- interest to PyH, and that PLM should receive the same AD cash deposit rate with respect to subject merchandise as its predecessor, PyH.
For a complete discussion of the information that PLM provided, and the complete successor-in-interest analysis,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum. A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included as an appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Public Comment
Case briefs or other written comments may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance. Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.309(c)(1)(ii)
, we have modified the deadline for interested parties to submit case briefs to Commerce to no later than seven days after the date of the publication of this notice.
[
14
]
Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in the case briefs, may be filed not later than seven days after the date for filing case briefs.
[
15
]
Interested parties who submit case briefs or rebuttal briefs in this review must submit: (1) a table of contents listing each issue; and (2) a table of authorities.
[
16
]
All briefs must be filed electronically using ACCESS. An electronically filed document must be received successfully in its entirety in ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)(iii)
and
(d)(2)(iii)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public, executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
17
]
Further, we request that interested parties limit their executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final results in this CCR. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
18
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, filed electronically via ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time within seven days after the date of publication of this notice. Requests should contain: (1) the party's name, address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants, and whether any participant is a foreign national; and (3) a list of issues to be discussed. Oral presentations at the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the briefs. If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce will inform parties of the scheduled date for the hearing.
[
19
]
Parties should confirm the date and the time of the hearing two days before the scheduled date.
Final Results of Review
Should our final results remain unchanged from these preliminary results, we intend to instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection to assign entries of subject merchandise exported by PLM the AD cash deposit rate applicable to PyH. Consistent with
19 CFR 351.216(e)
, we intend to issue the final results of this CCR no later than 270 days after the date on which this review was initiated, or within 45 days if all parties agree with our preliminary finding.
Notification to Interested Parties
This initiation and preliminary results notice is published in accordance with sections 751(b)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.216(b)
,
351.221(b)
and
351.221(c)(3)
.
Dated: October 20, 2026.

Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
This notice advises the public that two direct take permits 1454-3R and 1455-3R have been issued for operation, monitoring, and evaluation of a hatchery program rearing and releasing sockeye salmon in the Snake River basin of Idaho, and that the decision documents are available upon request.
DATES:
Permits 1454-3R and 1455-3R were issued on October 7, 2026, subject to certain conditions set forth therein. The permits expire on September 27, 2036.
ADDRESSES:
Requests for copies of the decision documents or any of the associated documents should be directed to the West Coast Region NMFS Office, 1201 NE Lloyd Blvd., Portland, OR 97232.
The documents are also available on the internet at:
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/​action/​snake-river-sockeye-salmon-production-program
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Andreas Raisch at (503) 230-5405 or
andreas.raisch@noaa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
ESA-Listed Species Covered in This Notice
Sockeye salmon (
Oncorhynchus nerka
): endangered, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Sockeye Evolutionary Significant Unit (ESU);
Chinook salmon (
O. tshawytscha
): threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Spring/Summer-run ESU; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Lower Columbia River Chinook salmon ESU;
Steelhead (
O. mykiss
): threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Steelhead Distinct Population Segment (DPS); threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Lower Columbia River Steelhead DPS; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Middle Columbia River Steelhead DPS; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Upper Columbia River Steelhead DPS.
Background
The operators and funding agencies, including Idaho Fish and Game, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribe, Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, NMFS's Northwest Fisheries Science Center, the Nez Perce Tribe and Bonneville Power Association, submitted a Hatchery and Genetic Management Plan to NMFS pursuant to NMFS' ESA section 10(a)(1)(A) for hatchery activities in the Snake River basin.
The programs are intended to contribute to the survival and recovery of Snake River Sockeye salmon in the Snake River basin. The proposed program would maintain the Snake River sockeye salmon captive broodstock, collect and spawn adult
(
printed page 67302)
sockeye salmon returning to the Snake River basin, rear juveniles, and release eggs, juveniles, and adult fish in upper Salmon River basin lakes, as well as into Tanner Creek, Oregon. Adult fish that return to Tanner Creek, would be transported to Eagle Fish Hatchery, Idaho for processing, and released to spawn upstream in Redfish and Pettit Lake. The proposed continuation of the program would indicate best management practices to minimize adverse effects on the ESU.
(Authority:
16 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
)
Dated: October 21, 2026.
Jennifer Quan,
Regional Administrator, West Coast Region, National Marine Fisheries Service.

ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
This proposed rule sets forth regulations that would implement Subtitle C of the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, which is codified at Title VIII of the Defense Production Act. The proposed rule would require United States persons to provide notification to the U.S. Department of the Treasury regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in notifiable technologies; and prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in prohibited technologies. Where consistent with Title VIII, the proposed rule incorporates certain definitions and concepts from the current regulations governing the Outbound Investment Security Program. The proposed rule also would add applicability dates to the regulations, such that those regulations would continue to apply to activities that occurred within the relevant timeframe.

Written comments must be received by December 7, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A.
Executive Order 14105
and Current Outbound Investment Security Program
On August 9, 2023,
Executive Order 14105
(
88 FR 54867
), “Addressing United States Investments in Certain National Security Technologies and Products in Countries of Concern” (the Outbound Order), was issued. The Outbound Order described the threat posed to the United States by countries of concern that exploit, or have the ability to exploit, certain U.S. outbound investments, including certain intangible benefits that often accompany U.S. investments and that help companies succeed. The Outbound Order identified the People's Republic of China (PRC), along with the Special Administrative Regions of Hong Kong and Macau, as a country of concern, and identified three technology areas for coverage.
On November 15, 2024, the Department of the Treasury (Treasury Department) published regulations to implement the Outbound Order. These regulations are found at
31 CFR part 850
(Part 850 Regulations), and they established the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP), which went into effect on January 2, 2025. Among other things, the Part 850 Regulations (1) require U.S. persons to provide notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions involving persons of a country of concern that are engaged in specified activities in the semiconductor and microelectronics and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors that may contribute to the threat to the national security of the United States; and (2) prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving persons of a country of concern that are engaged in other specified activities in the semiconductor and microelectronics, quantum information technologies, and AI systems sectors that pose a particularly acute national security threat to the United States.
In the time since the OISP went into effect (approximately 21 months), the Treasury Department has received approximately 100 notifications of investments in the semiconductor and AI industries from a range of transaction parties, including venture capital firms, asset managers, investment banks, and individual investors and entrepreneurs. Many other transaction parties and their counsel have engaged with the Treasury Department during this time. The Treasury Department also has been closely monitoring investment activity that may be subject to the OISP, because such investment was either potentially prohibited or not notified. Additionally, the Treasury Department has engaged with a wide range of stakeholders across industries, issued guidance and responses to more than 50 Frequently Asked Questions, and launched a website dedicated to the OISP that includes an online portal for submission of notifications.
B. Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025
On December 18, 2025, Congress enacted the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26 NDAA). In passing the COINS Act, Congress made clear that restricting certain U.S. outbound investments into dual-use strategic technologies that benefit a foreign adversary's military modernization efforts, surveillance states, and human rights abuses is necessary to prevent harm to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. In addition, Congress stated that the President should exercise the authorities granted in the COINS Act to prevent countries of concern from exploiting U.S. capital to undermine U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
Subtitle C of the COINS Act adds Title VIII to the Defense Production Act of 1950,
50 U.S.C. 4581-4589
(Title VIII), and establishes a statutory basis for the OISP. In the COINS Act, Congress codified the framework for the Secretary of the Treasury (Secretary) to (1) require United States persons to provide
(
printed page 67397)
notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons engaged in notifiable technologies, and (2) prohibit United States persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving foreign persons engaged in prohibited technologies. Title VIII maintains various aspects of the current OISP—such as its application to certain transactions involving the semiconductor and microelectronics, AI systems, and quantum information technologies sectors in the PRC including the Hong Kong and Macau Special Administrative Regions—while broadening the program to address threats to U.S. national security posed by other advanced technologies. Specifically, Title VIII expands the OISP's jurisdiction to include two new technology sectors (in addition to the three already covered under the Part 850 Regulations): (1) high-performance computing and supercomputing; and (2) hypersonic systems. Title VIII also authorizes the Secretary—in consultation with the appropriate congressional committees and subject to notice and comment—to identify additional categories of notifiable and prohibited technologies beyond those specifically listed in the law that enable the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a country of concern, and to define the technical parameters of the technologies within those categories as reasonably needed for national security purposes.
Title VIII includes an expanded list of countries of concern. In addition to the PRC (including Hong Kong and Macau), Title VIII includes as
countries of concern
the Republic of Cuba, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the Russian Federation, and the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela under the regime of Nicolás Maduro Moros. Title VIII uses the terms
notifiable technology
and
prohibited technology
to capture the relevant technologies for coverage largely in place of the terms “notifiable transaction” and “prohibited transaction” found in the Part 850 Regulations. Title VIII uses the term
covered national security transaction
(in place of the term “covered transaction” found in the Part 850 Regulations) and explicitly excepts from its coverage, among other things, underwriting services (including where such services involve the acquisition of equity), bank lending, processing or clearing of payments, prime brokerage, and global custody services. Title VIII also includes exceptions for
de minimis
transactions, specifically for (1) any transaction the value of which the Secretary determines is
de minimis
and (2) certain investments made by a limited partner or the equivalent where committed capital is not more than a
de minimis
amount, as determined by the Secretary. Title VIII does not set such
de minimis
values and instead grants the Secretary the discretion to do so. Title VIII additionally defines a
covered foreign person
only in terms of such person's relationship to a
country of concern
and not in connection with the technology or technologies in which such person engages (in contrast to the Part 850 Regulations, where “covered foreign person” has a different meaning).
In addition to certain changes that expand the scope of the OISP, Title VIII includes certain new processes. In particular, Title VIII requires the Treasury Department to implement regulations establishing a process under which a person can request confidential non-binding feedback or anonymized public guidance for a potentially
prohibited transaction.
Title VIII also requires the Secretary to establish a mechanism for the public to submit evidence on a confidential basis with respect to whether a
foreign person
is a
covered foreign person
engaged in a
prohibited technology
or a
notifiable technology.
Title VIII further provides the Secretary with the discretionary authority to establish a publicly accessible, non-exhaustive database that identifies
covered foreign person
s that are engaged in a
prohibited technology
or a
notifiable technology.
II. The Proposed Rule
A. Scope and Structure of the Proposed Rule
The United States remains committed to maintaining a strong, open investment environment and supporting cross-border investment where consistent with the protection of U.S. national security. Certain U.S. investments, however, may be exploited by countries of concern to advance the development of sensitive technologies and products that contribute to those countries' military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities.
This current rulemaking seeks comment on the draft regulatory framework (Proposed Rule) to implement Subtitle C of the COINS Act. Consistent with the sense of Congress, in implementing the COINS Act, the Treasury Department seeks to (1) restrict certain U.S. outbound investments into certain technologies in countries of concern as is necessary to prevent harm to United States national security and foreign policy interests; and (2) balance the priority of protecting the national security interest of the United States while, to the extent practicable, minimizing the cost and complexity of compliance, adopting the least burdensome alternative that achieves regulatory objectives, and prioritizing transparency and stakeholder involvement in the process of issuing the rules.
To implement Title VIII, Congress has directed the Secretary to issue or update current regulations that, as necessary, amend, terminate, supersede, revoke, or streamline the existing requirements in the Part 850 Regulations. Where consistent with Title VIII, the Proposed Rule incorporates certain definitions and concepts from the Part 850 Regulations. Where Title VIII uses new or different terminology, the Treasury Department has made adjustments while seeking, to the extent consistent with congressional intent, to preserve relevant aspects of the Part 850 Regulations. This approach is intended to minimize the cost and complexity of compliance for affected parties by maintaining certain definitions and concepts with which the regulated community is already familiar.
The Proposed Rule, therefore, includes detailed definitions and descriptions of terms and elements to clearly delineate the scope of coverage and facilitate compliance by
U.S. persons.
At the same time, the Proposed Rule seeks to avoid loopholes that could undermine the intent of the COINS Act. The Treasury Department seeks input on how the Proposed Rule can best meet these objectives.

B. Discussion of the Proposed Rule
The following discussion provides an overview and narrative description of the key substantive provisions of the Proposed Rule to implement Title VIII. Because the Part 850 Regulations will remain in effect for transactions occurring during the relevant period, the Treasury Department views establishing a new Part 851 within
Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations
with the full process, procedures, and requirements under Title VIII as the most administrable approach. To make clear the applicability of the Part 850 Regulations, the Proposed Rule also would add a new § 850.105 to the Part 850 Regulations that sets the specific dates for the applicability of those regulations.
Many provisions of the Proposed Rule are substantively identical to the corresponding provisions in the Part 850 Regulations. The Proposed Rule should be read in its entirety as many terms are related and various features are discussed in different parts. The Treasury Department will carefully consider all comments provided to the Proposed Rule and is particularly interested in receiving comments relating to the new provisions and revisions described below.
Subpart A—General

Federal departments and agencies

Subpart A of the Proposed Rule would generally be identical in substance to §§ 850.101 through 850.104 in Subpart A of the Part 850 Regulations, with most differences focused on conforming the language of the regulatory text to terms used in Title VIII. SI Systems
Since publication of the Part 850 Regulations nearly two years ago, technology has undergone rapid transformation, with breakthrough advances in the capabilities and development of
SI systems.
A range of
SI systems
developed by
covered foreign persons
present significant national security risks—from the ability to autonomously conduct cyberattacks to the potential use by malign actors and foreign adversaries to develop weapons of mass destruction.
SI systems
can also provide
countries of concern
with the potential to substantially enhance military modernization efforts, surveillance, and real-time targeting and decision-making capabilities. A range of
SI systems
may pose novel national security risks in areas such as cyberattacks and the development of chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or explosive weapons, as well as expose novel security vulnerabilities. The Treasury Department has observed advances in the capabilities and development of
SI systems
directly through its market monitoring activity, receipt of notifications as part of the OISP, and other sources.
The Part 850 Regulations distinguished among “AI systems” for purposes of the prohibition, the notification requirement, or absence from OISP coverage based on the quantity of computing power for training, designed end uses, and intended end uses. Over the past two years, SI models have achieved notable performance gains through additional means other than the quantity of training compute. Therefore, no single measure, benchmark, or threshold is currently sufficient to distinguish advanced models. Although the quantity of training compute may continue to indicate a degree of SI model capability, developers increasingly rely on additional methods to improve model capability, including other research and development activities such as synthetic data generation, improved algorithmic or architectural efficiencies, and novel post-training techniques or increasing inference-time compute.
Similarly, the proliferation and adoption of SI capabilities have made SI system end uses more challenging to isolate. General-purpose SI models that were not necessarily designed to be used for relevant national security applications nevertheless may exhibit that functionality, and investors may lack insight into the capabilities of such models if model developers have not evaluated or advertised these capabilities. Additionally, the availability of capable open-source SI models that have fewer safeguards and oversight may lead to their utilization and incorporation into SI systems in contexts outside their intended scope.
Accordingly, the Secretary, in consultation with interagency partners and the Executive Office of the President, has determined that it is necessary for national security purposes to define
prohibited technology
to include the development of any
SI system.
The Treasury Department notes that this approach is consistent with the COINS Act's direction to balance the priority of protecting the national security interest of the United States, while, to the extent practicable, minimizing the cost and complexity of compliance for affected parties and adopting the least burdensome alternative that achieves regulatory objectives. Specifically, this approach seeks to protect U.S. national security and streamline compliance through clear proposed regulatory text that does not rely on a
U.S. person
ascertaining the technical capabilities or thresholds of
SI systems
being developed by a
covered foreign person
(which was the case in the Part 850 Regulations).
Importantly, the Treasury Department proposes to include clarifying language regarding when the use or incorporation of certain third-party SI systems would or would not constitute the development of an SI system. This language generally corresponds to Notes 2 and 3 to § 850.224 in the Part 850 Regulations.
The Treasury Department particularly welcomes feedback regarding the potential implications arising from defining

Subpart F—Violations
This subpart of the Proposed Rule describes conduct that would be treated as a violation of the Proposed Rule. Such conduct would include taking any action prohibited by the Proposed Rule, failing to take any action required by the Proposed Rule within the timeframe and in the manner required, taking action to evade or avoid—or conspiring to violate—the Proposed Rule's requirements, and making materially false or misleading representations to the Treasury Department when submitting any information required by the Proposed Rule.
The Treasury Department notes that the proposed anti-evasion language would apply to any action that evades or avoids, has the purpose of evading or avoiding, causes a violation of, or attempts to violate any of the Proposed
(
printed page 67411)
Rule's obligations, as well as to any conspiracies formed to violate the obligations of the Proposed Rule. Evasion may include the establishment by a
U.S. person
of an entity or corporate structure to effectuate a transaction that would be a
covered national security transaction
if undertaken by a
U.S. person.
While many U.S. investors or asset managers may have bona fide commercial reasons to establish non-U.S. investment vehicles to effectuate investments outside of the United States, in determining whether an entity was established or used for the purpose of evading the obligations of the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department may consider,
inter alia:
whether a
U.S. person
de facto controls the non-U.S. entity irrespective of formal corporate governance rights or voting interest held in the entity; the extent and nature of any shared personnel, services, facilities, or branding between a
U.S. person
and the non-U.S. entity, or commingling of funds; privity in limited partnership interest between a
U.S. person
and the non-U.S. entity (
i.e.,
does the non-U.S. entity have the same investors as an affiliated U.S. fund or fund controlled by a
U.S. person
); and shared beneficial ownership or right to proceeds (including any commercial arrangements effectuating the same) between the
U.S. person
and the non-U.S. entity.
Pursuant to Title VIII, the Treasury Department proposes adding a new § 851.605, which would establish that, in an enforcement action for a violation of the Proposed Rule, the burden of proof shall be upon the Secretary.
Subpart G—Penalties and Disclosures
This subpart of the Proposed Rule describes the penalties that would be applicable to violations of the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department notes that the current Part 850 Regulations contain text that allows for civil and criminal penalties. Title VIII, however, includes language regarding civil penalties but does not include language regarding criminal penalties. As such, the Treasury Department proposes to retain previous civil penalty language from the Part 850 Regulations in the Proposed Rule and to omit language that allows for criminal penalties from the Proposed Rule. The Proposed Rule would include civil penalties up to the maximum amount set forth in section 206 of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act,
50 U.S.C. 1701
et seq.
The Treasury Department may impose a civil penalty on any person that violates the Proposed Rule. Further, to implement Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would also state that the Secretary may compel the divestment of a
covered national security transaction
in a
prohibited technology.
This subpart would also describe the process for submission of a voluntary self-disclosure by a person that may have violated applicable rules. The Treasury Department may take self-disclosures into account as a mitigating factor in determining any appropriate response, including the potential imposition of penalties, if the Treasury Department determines that there was a violation. Consistent with Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would use corresponding language from the Part 850 Regulations but would modify the scope of a voluntary self-disclosure to require that such disclosures contain a proposal for mitigation of any harms associated with the violation, including divestment or a voluntary disgorgement of profits. The Proposed Rule would further specify the information that must be included in a voluntary self-disclosure letter.
Subpart H—Provision and Handling of Information
This subpart of the Proposed Rule would implement the section of Title VIII that provides that information or documentary material provided to the Treasury Department under this part is exempt from disclosure under section 552(b)(3) of Title 5 of the United States Code. Title VIII also identifies exceptions to this rule.
The Proposed Rule would incorporate this provision of Title VIII with certain clarifications. Title VIII excepts from the disclosure exemption certain information “[g]athered by the Secretary or the Secretary's designee where the disclosure is determined to be in the national interest.” Section 851.801(b)(6) would clarify that the determination is made by the Secretary or the Secretary's designee. Factors that the Secretary or the Secretary's designee may consider when determining if disclosure is in the national interest may include whether such disclosure will further national security interests, address law enforcement needs, or promote compliance with the rule. Circumstances in which the Secretary may determine the disclosure of information to be in the national interest can include, for example, in the context of notifying the public regarding an action taken by the Treasury Department to enforce compliance with the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department anticipates this exception to be invoked only in circumstances in which the Secretary identifies a national interest that disclosure could help to address.
Subpart I—Non-Binding Feedback
This subpart would implement Title VIII by establishing procedures by which an eligible person may request non-binding feedback from the Treasury Department regarding a
prohibited transaction.
The Treasury Department recognizes that parties may have questions regarding whether a specific investment would constitute a
prohibited transaction.
Indeed, since the Part 850 Regulations became effective in January 2025, transaction parties and the public have requested feedback on interpretations of the Part 850 Regulations, submitted questions regarding compliance with the regulations, and sought additional public guidance. In response, the Treasury Department has published on its website several tranches of Frequently Asked Questions designed to assist the public with understanding and complying with the regulations.
To make effective and efficient use of the Treasury Department's resources, limit frivolous requests as contemplated under Title VIII, and adhere to Title VIII's confidentiality requirements, the Proposed Rule would require that requests for feedback be submitted in writing by a
party
with a direct financial interest in an actual—not hypothetical—transaction. While an executed contract would not be required, the material terms of the prospective transaction would need to be identified in a binding written agreement or other binding document to demonstrate that the transaction is not hypothetical. Requesters would need to provide sufficient detail regarding the transaction—which could be in the form of an executed contract, term sheet, or other written documentation—to permit a meaningful review and potential determination by the Treasury Department as to whether the transaction is a
prohibited transaction.
The Treasury Department recognizes that a
person
that is not a
party
to a
covered national security transaction
may have tips or referrals related to compliance with the OISP, and the Treasury Department continues to encourage the submission of tips and referrals by email to
Outbound.Tips@treasury.gov
.
The Treasury Department will continue to monitor and evaluate such tips and referrals, but it does not intend to provide feedback to them.
The Treasury Department expects that a
party,
before submitting a request for non-binding feedback, will have conducted sufficient diligence with respect to a potential investment to provide the information that the
(
printed page 67412)
Treasury Department would need to evaluate such a request. This would include, at a minimum, information about the requester and any
party
to the transaction; a detailed description of the structure of the transaction (including the form of investment, governance and information rights, timing, and
completion date
); a detailed description of the products, services, technologies, or activities implicated by the transaction; all operative documents and material term sheets, draft agreements, side letters, and other written materials reflecting the transaction; and any other information that the requester believes would be relevant to the application of the Proposed Rule to the transaction.
The Proposed Rule would outline additional features of the submission process for non-binding feedback, including a required
certification
that the request contains true, correct, and complete disclosure of all material facts and circumstances known to the requester at the time of submission and that the requester will supplement the request if the requester learns of material changes or omissions. The Proposed Rule notes that the Treasury Department may request additional information or a meeting with the requester and any relevant parties to the transaction.
The Proposed Rule would state that receipt of a complete request for non-binding feedback would not obligate the Treasury Department to issue such feedback and would also state that the Treasury Department may, in its sole discretion, respond to a complete request by providing anonymized public guidance, issuing confidential, written non-binding feedback, or declining to provide feedback. The Proposed Rule would further state that non-binding feedback provided pursuant to this subpart would address only whether a transaction, as described in the request, would constitute a
prohibited transaction,
and that the Treasury Department may provide feedback that is responsive to some, but not all, of the questions or information presented by the requester. The Proposed Rule would also describe the non-binding nature of the feedback, noting that feedback provided pursuant to this subpart would not bind the Treasury Department, any other Federal or local department or agency, or any court; would not constitute an authorization, license, exemption, or waiver; and would not preclude the Treasury Department from taking any action authorized by the law with respect to the transaction, the requester, or any other person.
To further limit frivolous requests as authorized under Title VIII, the Proposed Rule would describe types of requests that the Treasury Department may identify as frivolous, including requests that concern hypothetical conduct, are incomplete or lack sufficient information to permit a meaningful review, or seek general advisory views or policy guidance that is not specific to the transaction that is the subject of the request.
The Treasury Department notes that this non-binding feedback process would be a new addition to the OISP, as the Part 850 Regulations do not include such a process, and welcomes comment on this subpart.

Subpart K—Other Provisions
This subpart of the Proposed Rule would implement provisions related to the delegation of the Secretary's authorities under Title VIII, any amendment or modification of the Proposed Rule, severability of the Proposed Rule, and a requirement for certain information regarding any transaction to be furnished upon demand. The Proposed Rule would also state that, consistent with Title VIII, the Treasury Department has the power to investigate conduct that may constitute a violation, hold hearings, call witnesses, and require in-person testimony or production of documents.
III. Request for Comment
The Treasury Department welcomes comment with respect to the Proposed Rule as a whole and to specific provisions discussed above in Section II, accompanied by empirical data or other specific information wherever possible.
IV. Rulemaking Requirements
This Proposed Rule is intended to implement Subtitle C of the COINS Act, which added Title VIII to the Defense Production Act of 1950. Title VIII establishes a statutory framework for the Secretary to (1) require
U.S. persons
to provide notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving
notifiable technologies,
and (2) prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving
prohibited technologies.
The Treasury Department has opted, as a matter of discretion, to undertake a high-level analysis of the anticipated costs and benefits of the Proposed Rule.
In addition, this section includes the required assessments of the reporting and recordkeeping burdens under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA),
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.,
and the potential impact on small entities pursuant to the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601

A. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives for certain types of rulemaking in certain circumstances and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. The Office of Management and Budget's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has designated this Proposed Rule a significant regulatory action under
E.O. 12866
. The Treasury Department conducted an assessment of the costs and benefits of the Proposed Rule, as well as the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives.
As noted above, Title VIII directs the Secretary to issue regulations to (1) require
U.S. person
s to provide
(
printed page 67413)
notification to the Treasury Department regarding certain transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving
notifiable technologies,
and (2) prohibit
U.S. person
s from engaging in certain other transactions involving foreign persons that are engaged in activities involving
prohibited technologies.
The Proposed Rule maintains the general framework of the Part 850 Regulations while making changes to implement Title VIII and address the effort by
countries of concern
to develop certain technologies that pose a threat to the national security of the United States.
Title VIII authorizes the Secretary, in consultation with the appropriate congressional committees and subject to notice and comment, to prescribe regulations defining the technical parameters of
notifiable technologies
and
prohibited technologies
in the following technology sectors: (1) semiconductor technology and microelectronics; (2) artificial intelligence systems; (3) quantum information technologies; (4) high-performance computing and supercomputing; and (5) hypersonic systems. As described above, the Treasury Department has determined that rapid advances in the development, adoption, and use of SI capabilities by
countries of concern
warrant an expansion in the prohibition of
U.S. person
investment in that sector. Additionally, for the reasons described above, the Treasury Department has expanded the prohibition on
U.S. person
investment into semiconductors and quantum computing in
countries of concern.
Title VIII also authorizes the Secretary, in consultation with the appropriate congressional committees, to add and define categories of technologies and products that enable the military, intelligence, surveillance, or cyber-enabled capabilities of a
country of concern.
The Secretary has determined for purposes of this Proposed Rule to add certain technologies and products within the biotechnology sector as
prohibited technologies.
Other changes include the coverage of additional
countries of concern:
Russia, Iran, Cuba, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, and Venezuela under the regime of Nicolás Maduro Moros. Title VIII also requires that the implementing regulations establish a process under which a person can request confidential non-binding feedback or anonymized public guidance for a potentially
prohibited transaction.
The Proposed Rule would apply to certain types of investments by
U.S. persons
in
covered foreign persons
engaged in the technologies and activities described above or meets the conditions of § 851.208(a)(8). These include certain acquisitions of equity interests, limited partner investments, greenfield investments, joint ventures, and certain debt financing transactions. The Proposed Rule would except from coverage certain activities or transactions that are identified in Title VIII, including investments in publicly traded securities, certain investment funds, any
de minimis
transaction, any ancillary transaction, an
intracompany transfer of funds,
or any ordinary or administrative business transaction, as well as other transactions secondary to a
covered national security transaction.
Title VIII also authorizes the Secretary to except from coverage any other transaction that the Secretary determines is in the national interest of the United States.
B. Costs
The primary direct costs to the public associated with the Proposed Rule would relate to (1) understanding the Proposed Rule, (2) conducting the transaction-specific diligence that would be needed for a
U.S. person
to determine whether its intended transaction would be subject to either the notification or prohibition provisions of the Proposed Rule; and (3) if applicable, preparing and submitting a mandatory notification of certain transactions or other information to the Treasury Department pursuant the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department requests comments on any of the assumptions and estimates in this analysis.
The Proposed Rule would apply to all
U.S. persons
undertaking a
covered national security transaction
with or involving a
covered foreign person.
To estimate the number of potential transactions subject to the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department considered the number of transactions filed under the notification requirement pursuant to the Part 850 Regulations, the scoping of the Proposed Rule, and a review of commercially available data on transactions that may be subject to the Proposed Rule based on the identified sector of the investment target.
For example, to estimate the number of entities and transactions that would be potentially affected by the Proposed Rule and would incur associated compliance costs, the Treasury Department considered publicly available data from PitchBook relating to transactions from approximately 2023 through 2025. This data indicated that over the relevant three-year period, almost 230 unique U.S.-based investors completed approximately 300 initial and add-on investment transactions in the semiconductor, artificial intelligence, quantum information technology, hypersonic system, high-performance computing and supercomputing, and biotechnology sectors (as such sectors are identified in the commercially available data) in
countries of concern.
This data suggests an annual average of 75 different investors collectively engaging in an annual average of approximately 100 potentially
covered national security transactions.
While granular details of U.S. private investment overseas cannot be determined with precision, the Treasury Department believes this figure to be a reasonable estimate. For purpose of this analysis, the Treasury Department then doubled the averages from this data over the relevant three-year period to account for the possibility that these average figures undercount transactions. For example, commercially available data may not include certain transactions that would be subject to the Proposed Rule, or such data may not identify certain transactions as occurring in the technology sectors subject to the Proposed Rule. Thus, the Treasury Department's analysis is based on the assumption that, annually, around 150 different investors collectively engage in 200 transactions that would be potentially covered by the Proposed Rule.
The Treasury Department is interested in comments regarding additional publicly available data sources that the Treasury Department should consider. The Treasury Department also welcomes comment on whether doubling the averages from publicly available data is a reasonable way to account for uncertainty or whether the Treasury Department should account for this uncertainty using a different methodology.
To derive an estimate for the costs related to the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department first estimated the associated labor costs. The Treasury Department expects that businesses reviewing the Proposed Rule and engaging in potentially relevant transactions would engage their own employees as well as lawyers from outside law firms.
For a low-end estimate, the Treasury Department relied on May 2025 Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), which reports the mean hourly wage for Standard Occupational Classification System Code (SOC Code) 231011—Lawyers to be $89.35 per hour and SOC Code
(
printed page 67414)
111021—General and Operations Managers to be $64.87 per hour.

In each instance the Treasury Department tripled the BLS mean hourly wage figure. This adjustment is meant not only to account for employee benefits and overhead, but also to reflect the presumption that, because these U.S. investors require attorneys and other staff with experience in cross-border investments that involve complex financial and corporate structures, the hourly labor costs of the investors and their advisers likely to be affected by the Proposed Rule will be systematically higher than the hourly mean wage in these occupational categories. Accordingly, the Treasury Department estimates that the impacted entities will each incur costs of $195 per hour for operations managers and $268 for lawyers. As the Treasury Department is unable to determine which particular tasks will be performed by managers as compared to lawyers, this cost analysis uses the average wage of the two positions for both the low-end and high-end estimate, which the Treasury Department assesses is a reasonable method for estimating the hourly cost. The average of these figures is $231 per hour, which is the low-end estimate.
For a high-end estimate, for the reasons discussed in the preceding paragraph, the Treasury Department acknowledges that the hourly rate billed for a lawyer performing the relevant type of work at an outside firm may be higher than the average hourly wage of a lawyer. Using BLS OEWS data from 2025, the average hourly attorney billing rate in Washington, DC, where many private practice attorneys who advise on the OISP are based, was $116.73 and the hourly cost for operations managers was $78.67.

Costs Associated With Understanding the Proposed Rule
Based on the above assumptions and estimates of affected entities, number of transactions, and labor costs, the Treasury Department has estimated the annual time and cost that would be spent by affected entities in understanding the Proposed Rule. While recognizing that the amount of time necessary to understand the Proposed Rule will vary, the Treasury Department arrived at the below estimates for purposes of this analysis.
The range of estimated aggregate annual costs for understanding the Proposed Rule begins at $462,000 on the low end and rises to $586,000 on the high end. This is based on the estimate of an average time burden to be 10 total person-hours per transaction for understanding the Proposed Rule. As such, 10 total person-hours per transaction multiplied by 200 annual transactions and the low-end hourly labor cost range and high-end hourly labor cost range described above, respectively, result in the total cost range for understanding the Proposed Rule.
Costs Associated With Diligence and Maintaining Records
Based on the above assumptions and estimates of affected entities, number of transactions, and labor costs, the Treasury Department has estimated the annual time and cost that would be spent by affected entities on conducting diligence. While recognizing that the extent of this diligence will necessarily vary from transaction to transaction and noting that these economic estimates should in no way be construed as relevant to a party's determination of what constitutes a reasonable and diligent inquiry in light of the particular facts and circumstances of a transaction and the requirements of the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department arrived at the following estimates for purposes of this regulatory analysis.
The Treasury Department estimates that the range of the annual additional cost for conducting diligence and maintaining records would range from $0 on the low-end to $2,344,000 on the high-end. In estimating the low-end, the Treasury Department recognizes that virtually all investment transactions, regardless of whether the investment is potentially subject to this Proposed Rule, require some minimum level of review, diligence, assessment, and recordkeeping by the investor. And, in most cases, the level of collected and retained information necessary to comply with the Proposed Rule would not give rise to an additional cost to the investor.
The Treasury Department estimates that with respect to those investment transactions where diligence and recordkeeping costs are expected to marginally exceed the normal costs due to more detailed inquiry regarding a technology or other detail relevant to the Proposed Rule, the average additional burden would not exceed 40 total person hours per transaction for conducting diligence and maintaining records.
As such, the Treasury Department arrived at the high-end estimate by multiplying 40 total person hours per transaction by 200 annual transactions by the high-end hourly labor cost range described above. The Treasury Department estimates 40 person-hours per transaction, based on a total of approximately eight person-hours across all involved employees and lawyers per business day for one week. However, the cost and duration of a
U.S. person
conducting diligence will vary depending on a transaction's complexity and may be higher for certain transactions, such as indirect transactions, including transactions undertaken by a
U.S. person'
s
controlled foreign entity.
The Treasury Department seeks comment on whether these figures are reasonable benchmarks and estimates for this analysis or whether there are specific sources of data or estimates it should consider.

Estimated Total Direct Cost
Based on the direct cost estimates above, the total annual direct costs associated with complying with the Proposed Rule can be expected to have a range of between $2,772,000 to $5,860,000 and the total annual time burden would be approximately 20,000 person-hours.
Additional Indirect Costs Associated With Prohibited Transactions
With respect to
prohibited transactions,
the Treasury Department does not believe that the Proposed Rule will have additional direct economic costs to U.S. investors beyond those described above. There may, however, be additional indirect costs associated with
prohibited transactions.
Investors who would have otherwise engaged in a
prohibited transaction,
absent the Proposed Rule, may have to seek less promising investment opportunities since they would be precluded from undertaking and benefiting from
prohibited transactions
that would be foreclosed to them by the Proposed Rule. These indirect costs amount to the difference between the return that would have been generated by the
prohibited transaction
and the return that would result from the best alternative transaction. In addition, while the Proposed Rule may have an economic impact on investment targets that are
covered foreign persons
because certain transactions would be prohibited, the Proposed Rule is not designed to, nor does it, prohibit all
U.S. person
investments into such persons, due to the several exceptions provided for in the Proposed Rule.
Costs to the U.S. Government
Administering the Proposed Rule would also entail costs to the U.S. Government. Such costs would include information technology (IT) development and ongoing annual maintenance, as well as processing electronic submissions of the transaction data. The Treasury Department estimates that IT development costs would be between $4 million and $5 million with an additional $2 million to $3 million required to maintain the new systems and the underlying technology being leveraged to support the new capabilities. This would include adjustments to address changes in the type of notification information being received, as well as implementing processes for the electronic submission of requests for confidential non-binding feedback, and information submissions regarding potentially
covered foreign persons,
among other changes.
The Treasury Department or other agencies may incur additional costs, besides those estimated above, while promoting compliance with the notification and prohibition requirements, potentially including providing training on the requirements, publishing documents such as guidance and frequently asked questions, and conducting outreach to and answering inquiries from the public. The Treasury Department does not currently have specific estimates for these costs but estimates that there would be personnel costs of less than $1 million associated with the Proposed Rule in Fiscal Year 2027. For future years, the Treasury Department may incur additional costs for ongoing outreach and enforcement, as well as ensuring there is sufficient personnel to review and timely respond to requests for confidential non-binding feedback.
The Treasury Department and other government agencies may also incur costs in enforcing compliance with the Proposed Rule. These may include additional personnel costs related to the expanded prohibition in existing technology sectors as well as new technology sectors added by Title VIII. The Treasury Department does not currently have estimates for these costs, and they are not included in the estimates above.
The Treasury Department plans to monitor compliance with the Proposed Rule, when finalized, by leveraging a variety of data sources, both internal and external. Because the external data sources may include third parties, the Treasury Department requests comment on what external data sources would be
(
printed page 67416)
appropriate to leverage in identifying non-compliance with the Proposed Rule and what potential costs may be incurred by such third parties. If the external data sources include third party commercial data, the Treasury Department assesses that the costs associated with accessing these databases would be modest and incremental, given that the Treasury Department regularly maintains access to such databases but may need to request additional licenses for employees. After identifying an instance of apparent non-compliance, the Treasury Department may initiate outreach to the involved entity, work with law enforcement to investigate the apparent non-compliance, or initiate an enforcement action. The Treasury Department's enforcement of the Proposed Rule would also involve coordination with law enforcement agencies. These law enforcement agencies may also incur costs (time and resources) while conducting investigations into potential non-compliance.
C. Benefits
As Congress noted in the COINS Act, there are countless known and unknown entities in
countries of concern
that are developing dual-use strategic technologies that benefit a foreign adversary's military modernization efforts, surveillance states, and human rights abuses. Advancement by
countries of concern
in sensitive technologies and products critical for the military, intelligence, surveillance, human rights abuse, or cyber-enabled capabilities of such countries constitutes a threat to the national security of the United States. Restricting certain U.S. outbound investments into certain technologies in
countries of concern
is necessary to prevent harm to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
The Proposed Rule is designed to complement existing tools of the U.S. Government and effectively address the threat to the national security of the United States described in Title VIII. While the benefit of protecting national security is difficult to quantify, the Treasury Department has identified specific benefits below. The notification function of the Proposed Rule is intended to provide key information that the Treasury Department could use to better inform the development and implementation of the OISP. Such notifications received under the existing OISP have increased the U.S. Government's visibility into transactions by
U.S. persons,
or their
controlled foreign entities,
in the SI and the semiconductor and microelectronics sectors in a
country of concern.
These have also assisted the U.S. Government by highlighting trends with respect to related capital flows and investment by non-U.S. persons in these technology sectors in a
country of concern.
Finally, these notifications have informed policy development for the Proposed Rule as well as other U.S. Government efforts to protect U.S. national security. The Treasury Department expects to receive similar benefits from notifications filed under the Proposed Rule. The Treasury Department does not currently propose a breakeven analysis for the Proposed Rule, as it continues to collect information on potential costs and benefits of the Proposed Rule through the rulemaking process.
D. Alternatives
The Proposed Rule is promulgated pursuant to Title VIII, which directs the Treasury Department to issue regulations to implement its requirements. However, the Treasury Department considered some alternative approaches that would be consistent with Title VIII. Specifically, the Treasury Department considered the following potential alternatives to the Proposed Rule:
Limited exceptions.
In the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department would define the term “covered national security transaction” largely as defined in Title VIII (as set forth in Subpart B) without further permitted additions and would provide for certain exceptions (in Subpart E), some of which are explicitly required by Title VIII and others that are permitted, but not required, under Title VIII. Therefore, as an alternative consistent with Title VIII, the Treasury Department could have proposed a broader definition of
covered national security transaction
and/or fewer exceptions. This alternative likely would result in the gathering of more information on U.S. investments in sensitive technologies and products in
countries of concern
through
notifiable transactions,
which would expand the information available to assist the development and implementation of the OISP. But the alternative approach also likely would impose higher compliance costs on
U.S. persons.
Prohibited and notifiable technology using broad definition of sectors rather than specific activities and technologies.
In the Proposed Rule, the Treasury Department would define
notifiable technology
and
prohibited technology
in § 851.218 and § 851.226, respectively, by reference to certain technologies and activities, and in some instance, end uses. Alternatively, and consistent with Title VIII, the Treasury Department could have proposed broad sectoral categorizations, such as, for example, defining a
prohibited technology
to include “all super intelligence” in a country of concern. If the Treasury Department had proposed that approach, the Treasury Department estimates that it would create ambiguity and uncertainty for
U.S. persons
about what investments were subject to the prohibition and notification requirements because of the lack of a clear, articulated nexus between a
covered foreign person
and the technology being described. This in turn would result in significant compliance costs and overall economic consequences on
U.S. persons
and the U.S. economy that could undermine potential national security benefits.

It is hereby certified that the Proposed Rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities within the meaning of section 601(6) of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
The Proposed Rule may impact any
U.S. person,
including a small business that engages in a
covered national security transaction
with a
covered foreign person.
The Treasury Department does not anticipate that the Proposed Rule would affect “small organizations” or “small governmental jurisdiction[s],” as defined in the RFA.
The Treasury Department expects the Proposed Rule to have a negligible baseline impact on small businesses because the Proposed Rule focuses on certain transactions that—based on the Treasury Department's experience with the type of U.S. investors involved in transactions currently subject to the existing OISP—are more likely to involve a small number of sophisticated investors managing substantial amounts of capital and with access to expertise in a number of emerging technology sectors. This expertise may be acquired through affiliated companies or the hiring of senior advisors with significant experience growing and managing successful technology companies, either of which financial investors that meet the requirements to be a small business are unlikely to have. Further, the
covered foreign persons
subject to the Proposed Rule are largely located outside of the United States, requiring U.S. investors to hire or retain staff skilled in assessing and structuring complex cross-border investments in foreign companies, which is not common to small businesses. In addition, and as discussed below, the Treasury Department has assessed that small businesses would be more likely to enter into the types of transactions excepted from coverage, including
de minimis
transactions and investments in publicly traded securities, if such businesses are investing at all into
covered national security transactions.
As an example, the Small Business Administration's (SBA's) Table of Size Standards with respect to North American Industry Classification System U.S. Industry Sector 52 “Finance and Insurance” defines a small business in this sector by dollar value rather than by number of employees. For example, SBA categories such as “open end investment funds,” and “other financial vehicles” are not considered small businesses if their average annual receipts exceed $40 million. A number of the U.S. investors who have submitted notifications pursuant to the Part 850 Regulations are investment firms or entities that exceed this threshold, as do most investment entities operating in the United States. As a reference point, according to the Investment Company Institute, there were 11,263 U.S. businesses in this
(
printed page 67418)
category with net sales of $1.58 trillion.

Extrapolating from this data, the average net sales per firm in this category would have been $140.4 million.
Given the applications of technologies and products in these sectors, the Treasury Department believes investments into these sectors involving a person of a
country of concern
is not typical for a small business, as these investor types are treated in the SBA's Table of Size Standards. Importantly, the Proposed Rule would also except certain types of transactions, including certain investments into publicly traded securities or into certain investment funds, as well as
de minimis

In the unlikely event that a small entity is subject to the requirements of the Proposed Rule, such entity would be expected to incur the costs described in the separate cost benefit analysis above. For submission of notifications, the Treasury Department has endeavored to develop information gathering procedures that minimize the burden on
U.S. persons,

U.S. persons
who file a notification will use a fillable form that will be available online and is intended to facilitate submission through an electronic format. This fillable form will benefit anyone who submits a notification, regardless of their size, but may be especially helpful for small businesses that will be able to submit directly to the Treasury Department through the online portal.
