Abstract of Proposed Collection
This information collection relates to three final rules published on January 27, 2026.
91 FR 3319
,
91 FR 3332
, and
91 FR 3345
. These rules implement the President's Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance (PHFFA) policy, by requiring recipients of U.S. foreign assistance funds to agree to certain terms and conditions. In summary, foreign NGOs, U.S. NGOs, and international organizations are required to comply with the policy (foreign governments and parastatals may also be required to comply with the policies, but those entities are not “persons” under the Paperwork Reduction Act, thus not covered by this notice) and agree that during the period of the award they will segregate records so that the Department can verify that they are not violating the terms of the foreign assistance grants that were provided to them. Full details are included in the three final rules.
Methodology
There is no form involved in this information collection. The final rules require recipients of U.S. foreign assistance funds to maintain records and make business records available upon request, which is a requirement governed by the Paperwork Reduction Act. In accordance with
2 CFR 200.334
, all recipients need to preserve records. The final rules require U.S. NGOs to ensure that any program, project, or activity for which funds are made available under a Department award must be organized so that the program, project, or activity is physically and financially separate from any “prohibited activities” undertaken using other funding sources. Foreign assistance grantees must ensure that all award terms flow down to any subrecipients of such assistance, as applicable.
Public Comments
The Department published a 60-day notice for this information collection on April 6, 2026.
91 FR 17322
. Four comments were received from three organizations. The Department is publishing a
Federal Register
notice, soliciting comment for 30 days. The Department published a 60-day notice for this information collection on April 6, 2026.
91 FR 17322
. Four comments were received from three organizations.
Summary of InterAction Comment
InterAction's central argument is that the Department's burden estimates fail to capture the real operational costs of PHFFA compliance, particularly because the regulations require organizations to assess activities and funding streams beyond a single U.S. Government award. Training costs are understated: one member organization consolidated training across three related regulations but still had to run both introductory and specialized HR-focused sessions, with more anticipated as interpretation evolves—meaning these are recurring, not one-time, costs. A second major cost driver is ambiguity around allowable activities; without clear definitions or standardized documentation expectations, organizations cannot direct compliance resources efficiently and must repeatedly engage legal review. Subaward relationships compound the burden further—prime recipients must determine which PHFFA requirements apply to which partners, monitor activities funded by non-U.S. donors to assess overall organizational compliance, and in some cases provide technical assistance to partners struggling to interpret the rules against their own funding structures. InterAction warns this could push smaller local and national organizations out of U.S.-funded programs altogether, given their limited administrative capacity. Finally, the comment flags unresolved retention-period questions (duration, post-award cost allocation, audit-triggered extensions, and translation of non-English records) as a gap likely to cause organizations to over-retain records defensively, inflating costs further. InterAction's asks are narrow and specific: clarify the scope of monitoring for non-federally-funded activities, and ensure any new compliance IT tools integrate with existing nonprofit systems rather than adding parallel administrative layers.
FAO Response
The Department of State acknowledges InterAction for its comment submitted in response to the 60-Day Notice of Proposed Information Collection: Foreign Assistance Requirements (Public Notice 12977,
91 FR 17322
, April 6, 2026).
The Department acknowledges the compliance requirements on prime and sub-recipients. and will consider further additional information regarding the scope of prime recipient monitoring obligations with respect to non-U.S. Government-funded activities. The Department also notes InterAction's concern regarding potential compliance costs and will take these issues into consideration.
Regarding InterAction's points on record retention, the guidance outlined in
2 CFR 200.334
(Uniform Guidance) shall apply. Records must generally be retained for three years from the date of the final expenditure report, subject to applicable exceptions.
Taking note of InterAction's observation on technology and automation, the Department does not require recipients to maintain technological or automated compliance systems for the purposes of PHFFA
(
printed page 67387)
compliance. To the extent a recipient implements a PHFFA-specific technological or automated monitoring system, the Department suggests that any technological solutions should be designed to integrate with existing compliance systems wherever possible. Regarding InterAction's observations on award budget structures appropriately accounting for PHFFA compliance costs, particularly for organizations managing complex partner networks, the Department takes seriously its obligations under the PRA to ensure burden estimates are accurate, information collections are clear and useful, and reporting burden is minimized.
See
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)-(C)
. The Department remains committed to maintaining an open dialogue for ongoing feedback in relation to the demonstrated burden estimates.
Conclusion
The Department thanks InterAction for its comment. The Department is committed to working with the implementing partner community to ensure that PHFFA compliance requirements are clear and accurately reflected in the burden estimates submitted to OMB.
Summary of National Catholic Bioethics Center Comment and FAO Response
The NCBC provided an argument focused on Title X of the Public Health Service Act. The Department does not implement Title X programs.
Summary of The Council for Global Equality Comment
CGE's comment is a procedural challenge under the Paperwork Reduction Act, not a policy critique of PHFFA's substance. The core claim is that the Notice fails all four PRA evaluation criteria because it discloses almost nothing about what records must be kept, why the collection is necessary, or how it will be used—stating only that recipients must maintain records “separate” from non-federally-funded activities and make them available on request. CGE identifies a specific legal defect here: the underlying Rules only require U.S. NGOs to keep separate records, yet the Notice/Supporting Statement extend this obligation to foreign recipients as well, a requirement they argue appears nowhere in the Rules themselves. On burden estimation, CGE documents two concrete numerical inconsistencies: a 52,500-hour gap between the Rules' estimate (652,500 hours) and the Notice's estimate (600,000 hours), and an approximately $85 million discrepancy in per-hour cost assumptions ($175/hour in the Rules versus $50/hour in the Supporting Statement, yielding $114M vs. $30M total cost estimates)—with no explanation offered for either gap. CGE also argues the Notice's respondent count (2,500) is unrealistic because it excludes subgrantees and subrecipients who are independently subject to monitoring obligations under the Rules; they cite an example of a single foreign NGO with roughly 1,500 subgrantees to illustrate how far off the estimate could be. Separately, CGE notes the Notice does not address burden-minimization for small entities as required by the PRA, and the Supporting Statement's response—that requirements apply “equally to large and small grantees”—does not satisfy that obligation. CGE's requested remedy is not to block the rule but to require the Department to withdraw and reissue the Notice with sufficient detail to allow a genuine 60-day comment period, arguing the current process is procedurally inadequate as a matter of law.
FAO Response
The Department of State has reviewed the comment submitted by the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Professor Pamela Herd, and Professor Donald Moynihan in response to the 60-Day Notice of Proposed Information Collection: Foreign Assistance Requirements (Public Notice 12977,
91 FR 17322
, April 6, 2026).
The commenters objected to the Notice's application of the segregation requirement to foreign recipients as contradicting the rules. The rules require U.S. NGOs to ensure that any program, project, or activity for which funds are made available under a Department award must be organized so that the program, project, or activity is physically and financially separate from any “prohibited activities” undertaken using other funding sources. However, in accordance with
2 CFR 200.334
, all recipients need to preserve records. The Department recognizes that the terminology utilized in the Notice generated confusion due to the separation requirement for U.S. NGOs under the rules and will clarify the terminology in the 30 day notice. Regarding the concern on information collection, Appendix A to Part 602 I outlines relevant terms and conditions in alignment with
Part 200 of Title 2 of the CFR
.
Additionally, the Department's operating expectation is that grantees will be required to maintain records that track expenses attributable to U.S. funded activities separate from expenses attributable to other activities. A single record or records system may include both U.S. funded and other expenses but the U.S. funded expenses would need to be demonstrated separately. For U.S. NGOs impacted by the physical separation requirement, the requirement that U.S. NGOs maintain records for U.S. funded activities and that those records are physically separate from the records of other activities, the Department confirms that that requirement applies only to U.S. NGOs and only when there is an activity funded from any other source that would otherwise be prohibited under the rules. Reiterating this point, a U.S. NGO needs to maintain physical and financial separation only if it engages in any of the otherwise “prohibited activities” outlined in the rules—with another source of funds. Certain activities remain prohibited for U.S. NGOs regardless of funding sources.
Regarding concerns that there are calculation discrepancies between the burden figures in the final rules, the Notice, and the Supporting Statement. The final rules address compliance estimates beyond the more narrow scope of the PRA notice which is focused on the information collection. The final rules also include associated training. The Department is aware that burden estimates at the notice stage are preliminary and welcome continued dialogue with implementers as these compliance costs become more apparent.
Regarding the comment's point that the estimate of 2,500 respondents fails to account for subrecipients, the Department's position is that prime recipients have the duty to monitor their subrecipients and the estimate reflects the respondents as the prime recipient. The final rules require prime recipients to ensure that award terms flow down to subrecipients, as applicable, and to monitor subrecipient compliance.
Regarding the issue of the Small Entity Burden, the Department acknowledges that the PRA requires agencies to consider how to minimize burden on small entities, including through exemptions or simplified requirements that account for resource limitations.
Effect on the Proposed Collection
The Department has considered the commenters' submission in full. These actions reflect the Department's standard process for finalizing a PRA submission and are responsive to the requirements of
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)-(C)
.
The Department does not agree that the collection must be withdrawn and reissued. The concerns raised are appropriately addressed through the
(
printed page 67388)
Supporting Statement and supplemental guidance, which are the standard mechanisms for providing the level of detail the commenters seek.
Conclusion
The Department thanks the Council for Global Equality, Professor Herd, and Professor Moynihan.
Ryan H. Leppert,
Chief of Staff, Office of the Under Secretary for Foreign Assistance, Humanitarian Affairs, and Religious Freedom, U.S. Department of State.

Office of the United States Trade Representative
AGENCY:
Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR).
ACTION:
Request for comments.
SUMMARY:
To allow for further negotiation with China regarding the acts, policies, and practices at issue in this investigation, the U.S. Trade Representative (Trade Representative) is proposing to modify the action taken in this investigation to further suspend that action for two months, through January 9, 2027. This notice invites public comment from interested parties on the proposed modification.
DATES:
October 23, 2026, 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time:
Comment period opens.
October 30, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time:
To be assured of consideration, submit written comments regarding the proposed modification of the action by this date.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Philip Butler, Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Monitoring and Enforcement; Thomas Au, Senior Counsel for Industrial Policy; or David Salkeld, Associate General Counsel at (202) 395-5725.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
For background on the proceedings in this investigation, please see the prior notices issued in this investigation, including
89 FR 29424
(April 22, 2024),
90 FR 8089
(January 23, 2025),
90 FR 10843
(February 27, 2025),
90 FR 17114
(April 23, 2025) (April 23, 2025 notice),
90 FR 24856
(June 12, 2025),
90 FR 48320
(October 16, 2025) (October 16, 2025 notice);
90 FR 50762
(November 10, 2025) (November 10, 2025 notice), and
90 FR 50947
(November 13, 2025) (November 13, 2025 notice).
On April 17, 2025, pursuant to sections 301(b), 301(c), and 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 2411(b)
,
2411(c)
, and
2414(a)
), and following consideration of public comments, as well as consultations with advisory committees and the Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative determined to take action in this investigation.
See
April 23, 2025 notice.
On November 1, 2025, the White House announced a historic trade and economic deal reached between President Trump and President Xi Jinping of China.
[
1
]
Pursuant to this deal, the United States would suspend for one year, beginning on November 10, 2025, the responsive actions taken in this investigation. This period would allow the United States to negotiate with China pursuant to Section 301 regarding the issues raised in this investigation as well as to continue U.S. domestic efforts and discussions with key allies and partners on revitalizing American shipbuilding.
On November 6, 2025, pursuant to this deal, the Trade Representative, at the direction of the President, proposed to suspend for one year, beginning on November 10, 2025, the responsive actions taken in this investigation.
See
November 10, 2025 notice.
Following consideration of public comments and advice from the Section 301 Committee, the Trade Representative suspended the actions in this investigation from 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on November 10, 2025, through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on November 9, 2026.
See
November 13, 2025 notice.
II. Request for Comments
The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation. The Trade Representative is therefore proposing to further suspend for two months, through January 9, 2027, the responsive actions taken in this investigation. The Trade Representative is requesting comments from any interested person regarding the proposal to suspend the responsive actions from 12:00 a.m. Eastern Time on November 10, 2026, through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027.
During the suspension period, no party would accrue liability for or be required to pay the fees on maritime transport services under Annexes I, II, or III of the April 23, 2025 notice, as modified by the October 16, 2025 notice. Further, during the suspension period, no party would accrue liability for or be required to pay the duties provided in Annex V.A of the October 16, 2025 notice.
III. Request for Public Comments
In accordance with Section 307(a)(2) of the Trade Act (
19 U.S.C. 2417(a)(2)
), USTR invites comments from interested persons with respect to the proposed modification to further suspend the action as described in Section II above. To be assured of consideration, you must submit written comments on the proposed modification by October 30, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
IV. Procedures for Written Comments
You must submit written comments using docket number USTR-2026-0694 on the electronic portal at
https://comments.ustr.gov/​s/​
.
To submit written comments, use the docket on the portal entitled “Request for Comments on Further Suspension of Section 301 Action: China's Targeting of the Maritime, Logistics, and Shipbuilding Sectors for Dominance.”
You do not need to establish an account to submit comments. The first screen of each docket allows you to enter identification and contact information. Third party organizations such as law firms, trade associations, or customs brokers, should identify the full legal name of the organization they represent, and identify the primary point of contact for the submission. Information fields are optional; however, your comment or request may not be considered if insufficient information is provided. Fields with a gray Business Confidential Information (BCI) notation are for BCI information which will not be made publicly available. Fields with a green (Public) notation will be viewable by the public.
After entering the identification and contact information, you can complete the remainder of the comment, or any portion of it by clicking `Next.' You may upload documents at the end of the form and indicate whether USTR should treat the documents as business confidential or public information.
Any page containing BCI must be clearly marked `BUSINESS CONFIDENTIAL' on the top of that page and the submission should clearly indicate, via brackets, highlighting, or
(
printed page 67389)
other means, the specific information that is BCI. If you request business confidential treatment, you must certify in writing that disclosure of the information would endanger trade secrets or profitability, and that the information would not customarily be released to the public.
Parties uploading attachments containing BCI also must submit a public version of their comments. If these procedures are not sufficient to protect BCI or otherwise protect business interests, please contact the USTR Section 301 support line at (202) 395-5725 to discuss whether alternative arrangements are possible.
USTR will post attachments uploaded to the docket for public inspection, except for properly designated BCI. You can view submissions on USTR's electronic portal at
https://comments.ustr.gov/​s/​
by entering docket number USTR-2026-0694 in the search field on the home page.
Jennifer Thornton,
General Counsel, Office of the United States Trade Representative.

[Investigation Nos. 701-TA-787-788 and 731-TA-1775-1776 (Final)]
AGENCY:
United States International Trade Commission.
(
printed page 67329)
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice of the scheduling of the final phase of antidumping and countervailing duty investigation Nos. 701-TA-787-788 and 731-TA-1775-1776 (Final) pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 to determine whether an industry in the United States is materially injured or threatened with material injury, or the establishment of an industry in the United States is materially retarded, by reason of imports of large diameter graphite electrodes from China and India, provided for in subheadings 8545.11.00, 3801.10.50, and 3801.90.00 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, preliminarily determined by the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) to be subsidized and sold at less-than-fair-value.
DATES:
September 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Camille Bryan ((202) 205-2811), Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov
). The public record for these investigations may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Scope
.—For purposes of these investigations, Commerce has defined the subject merchandise as all large diameter graphite electrodes of any length, whether or not finished, of a kind used in furnaces, with a nominal or actual diameter exceeding 425 millimeters (16.7 inches), and whether or not attached to a graphite pin joining system or any other type of joining system or hardware. The merchandise covered by the investigation also includes graphite pin joining systems (commonly referred to as pins or nipples) for large diameter graphite electrodes, of any length, and with a minimum diameter of 228.6 mm (9 inches) at its widest transverse cross-section, whether or not finished, of a kind used in furnaces, and whether or not the graphite pin joining system is attached to, sold with, or sold separately from, the large diameter graphite electrode. Unfinished large diameter graphite electrodes are graphitized electrodes that have not undergone final machining. For purposes of the investigation, the country of origin is determined by the country of graphitization.
Excluded from the scope of the investigation are large diameter graphite electrodes that are subject to the existing antidumping duty order on Small Diameter Graphite Electrodes from the People's Republic of China. See Antidumping Duty Order: Small Diameter Graphite Electrodes from the People's Republic of China,
74 FR 8775
(February 26, 2009) (SDGE China AD Order) due to an affirmative determination of circumvention that imports of graphite electrodes from the People's Republic of China, produced and/or exported by Sinosteel Jilin Carbon Co., Ltd. and Jilin Carbon Import & Export Company (collectively, Jilin Carbon), with an actual or nominal diameter of 17 inches and otherwise meeting the description of the scope of the SDGE China AD Order constitute merchandise subject to the SDGE China AD Order. See Small Diameter Graphite Electrodes from the People's Republic of China: Affirmative Final Determination of Circumvention of the Antidumping Duty Order and Rescission of Later-Developed Merchandise Anticircumvention Inquiry,
78 FR 56864
(September 16, 2013). In the case of graphite electrodes entering the United States determined to be subject to the SDGE China AD Order, such order controls. In the case of graphite electrodes entering the United States meeting the scope definition of the investigation and not covered by the scope of the SDGE China AD Order, the scope of the investigation controls.
Excluded from the scope of the investigation are certain thermal energy storage (TES) graphite blocks. The excluded TES graphite blocks are machine-milled, non-cylindrical graphite blocks, which have: a coefficient of thermal expansion of 1.5 µm/(m·K) or greater, and an apparent (also known as bulk) density below 1.74 g/cm3, and which have an actual length of between 228.6 mm (9.0 inches) and 3010 mm (118.5 inches), an actual width between 228.6 mm (9.0 inches) and 560 mm (22.0 inches), an actual height between 228.6 mm (9.0 inches) and 560 mm (22.0 inches), and which have been machined to include two or more holes of at least 150 mm (5.9 inches) in depth and at least 35 mm (1.4 inches) in diameter.
The two or more 150 mm deep holes must be located: (i) along the longest centerline of the longest side of the block, each located on the same side of the block, (ii) spaced at intervals of no greater than 1000 mm (39.4 inches) apart as measured from the outer edge of the holes, and (iii) with the hole closest to each end of the longest centerline located within 1000 mm of the corresponding end of the block. Blocks may contain any number of additional holes, channels, or grooves in any configuration or location, provided that at least two or more holes of at least 150 mm depth are present as described above.
Further excluded from the scope of the investigation are certain TES graphite blocks, anchors, and pins, regardless of shape, which have a coefficient of thermal expansion of 1.5 µm/(m·K) or greater, and an apparent (also known as bulk) density below 1.74 g/cm3, with actual dimensions such that any one or more of the length, width, or height is less than 228.6 mm (9.0 inches).
Background
.—The final phase of these investigations is being scheduled pursuant to sections 705(b) and 731(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930 (
19 U.S.C. 1671d(b)
and
1673d(b)
), as a result of affirmative preliminary determinations by Commerce that certain benefits which constitute subsidies within the meaning of § 703 of the Act (
19 U.S.C. 1671b
) are being provided to manufacturers, producers, or exporters in China and India of large diameter graphite electrodes, and that such products are being sold in the United States at less than fair value within the meaning of § 733 of the Act (
19 U.S.C. 1673b
). The investigations were requested in petitions filed on February 24, 2026, by Resonac Graphite America Inc., Ridgeville, South Carolina; and Tokai Carbon GE LLC, Charlotte, North Carolina.
For further information concerning the conduct of this phase of the investigations, hearing procedures, and rules of general application, consult the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, part 201, subparts A and B (
19 CFR part 201
), and part 207, subparts A and C (
19 CFR part 207
).
Participation in the investigations and public service list
.—Persons, including industrial users of the subject merchandise and, if the merchandise is sold at the retail level, representative consumer organizations, wishing to participate in the final phase of these investigations as parties must file an entry of appearance with the Secretary to the Commission, as provided in § 201.11 of the Commission's rules, no later than 21 days prior to the hearing date specified in this notice. A party that filed a notice of appearance during
(
printed page 67330)
the preliminary phase of the investigations need not file an additional notice of appearance during this final phase. The Secretary will maintain a public service list containing the names and addresses of all persons, or their representatives, who are parties to the investigations.
Please note the Secretary's Office will accept only electronic filings during this time. Filings must be made through the Commission's Electronic Document Information System (EDIS,
https://edis.usitc.gov
). No in-person paper-based filings or paper copies of any electronic filings will be accepted until further notice.
Limited disclosure of business proprietary information (BPI) under an administrative protective order (APO) and BPI service list
.—Pursuant to § 207.7(a) of the Commission's rules, the Secretary will make BPI gathered in the final phase of these investigations available to authorized applicants under the APO issued in the investigations, provided that the application is made no later than 21 days prior to the hearing date specified in this notice. Authorized applicants must represent interested parties, as defined by
19 U.S.C. 1677(9)
, who are parties to the investigations. A party granted access to BPI in the preliminary phase of the investigations need not reapply for such access. A separate service list will be maintained by the Secretary for those parties authorized to receive BPI under the APO.
Staff report
.—The prehearing staff report in the final phase of these investigations will be placed in the nonpublic record on January 26, 2027, and a public version will be issued thereafter, pursuant to § 207.22 of the Commission's rules.
Hearing
.—The Commission will hold a hearing in connection with the final phase of these investigations beginning at 9:30 a.m. on February 9, 2027. Requests to appear at the hearing should be filed in writing with the Secretary to the Commission on or before February 3, 2027. Any requests to appear as a witness via videoconference must be included with your request to appear. Requests to appear via videoconference must include a statement explaining why the witness cannot appear in person; the Chairman, or other person designated to conduct the investigations, may in their discretion for good cause shown, grant such a request. Requests to appear as remote witness due to illness or a positive COVID-19 test result may be submitted by 3:00 p.m. the business day prior to the hearing. Further information about participation in the hearing will be posted on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/​calendarpad/​calendar.html
.
A nonparty who has testimony that may aid the Commission's deliberations may request permission to present a short statement at the hearing. All parties and nonparties desiring to appear at the hearing and make oral presentations should attend a prehearing conference, if deemed necessary, to be held at 9:30 a.m. on February 8, 2027. Parties shall file and serve written testimony and presentation slides in connection with their presentation at the hearing by no later than noon on February 8, 2027. Oral testimony and written materials to be submitted at the public hearing are governed by sections 201.6(b)(2), 201.13(f), and 207.24 of the Commission's rules. Parties must submit any request to present a portion of their hearing testimony in camera no later than 7 business days prior to the date of the hearing.
Written submissions
.—Each party who is an interested party shall submit a prehearing brief to the Commission. Prehearing briefs must conform with the provisions of § 207.23 of the Commission's rules; the deadline for filing is 5:15 p.m. on February 2, 2027. Parties shall also file written testimony in connection with their presentation at the hearing, and posthearing briefs, which must conform with the provisions of § 207.25 of the Commission's rules. The deadline for filing posthearing briefs is 5:15 p.m. on February 17, 2027. In addition, any person who has not entered an appearance as a party to the investigations may submit a written statement of information pertinent to the subject of the investigations, including statements of support or opposition to the petition, on or before 5:15 p.m. on February 17, 2027. On March 8, 2027, the Commission will make available to parties all information on which they have not had an opportunity to comment. Parties may submit final comments on this information on or before 5:15 p.m. on March 10, 2027, but such final comments must not contain new factual information and must otherwise comply with § 207.30 of the Commission's rules. All written submissions must conform with the provisions of § 201.8 of the Commission's rules; any submissions that contain BPI must also conform with the requirements of §§ 201.6, 207.3, and 207.7 of the Commission's rules. The Commission's
Handbook on Filing Procedures,
available on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/​documents/​handbook_​on_​filing_​procedures.pdf
,
elaborates upon the Commission's procedures with respect to filings.
Additional written submissions to the Commission, including requests pursuant to § 201.12 of the Commission's rules, shall not be accepted unless good cause is shown for accepting such submissions, or unless the submission is pursuant to a specific request by a Commissioner or Commission staff.
In accordance with §§ 201.16(c) and 207.3 of the Commission's rules, each document filed by a party to the investigations must be served on all other parties to the investigations (as identified by either the public or BPI service list), and a certificate of service must be timely filed. The Secretary will not accept a document for filing without a certificate of service.
Authority:
These investigations are being conducted under authority of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930; this notice is published pursuant to § 207.21 of the Commission's rules.
By order of the Commission.
Issued: October 21, 2026.
Sharon Bellamy,
Supervisory Hearings and Information Officer.

Department of Homeland Security
AGENCY:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”), Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Ratification.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”), through the Secretary of Homeland Security, ratifies all final civil penalties that had been assessed in accordance with interim regulations. These interim regulations were later adopted as final with only slight modification so retained substantially the same procedures by which the civil penalties are assessed. This notification ratifies all civil penalties assessed in accordance with the interim regulations prior to the final adoption.
DATES:
This ratification is issued on October 26, 2026 and relates back to the original date of each civil penalty assessed in accordance with the interim regulations.
All claims submitted pursuant to this notice must be received by ICE on or before November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of the General Counsel, DHS, Washington, DC 20528, (202) 282-9822.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background and Purpose
On June 27, 2025, DHS and EOIR published a joint interim final rule (“IFR”) titled “Imposition and Collection of Civil Penalties for Certain Immigration-Related Violations.”
90 FR 27439
. This IFR modified the procedures by which civil monetary penalties issued under three statutory provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”)—
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
,
1229c(d)
, and
1325(b)
—are assessed. Whereas civil penalties issued under these provisions were previously assessed pursuant to the procedures codified at
8 CFR part 280
, the IFR announced a new procedure, codified at
8 CFR part 281
, effective immediately on the date of publication of the IFR.
Although it was unnecessary because the IFR was subject to two exceptions to the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act regarding notice and comment, DHS and EOIR opened the IFR for public comments through July 28, 2025. The public submitted 28 comments. After considering the comments received, DHS and EOIR published a Final Rule on October 14, 2026.
91 FR 65390
. The Final Rule has no material difference from the IFR for the purposes of the civil penalties that had already been assessed prior to the publication of the Final Rule. Thus, under the Final Rule, just as under the IFR, the procedure outlined at
8 CFR part 281
remains the procedure by which civil penalties issued under
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
,
1229c(d)
, and
1325(b)
are assessed. The only change the Final Rule makes as compared to the IFR is that the Final Rule permits acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documentary evidence demonstrating a mail delivery delay that ICE finds was beyond an alien's control.
II. Overview of Ratification
To resolve any uncertainty, the Secretary of Homeland Security has decided to ratify all civil penalties issued under the interim adoption of 8 CFR part 281 from June 27, 2025, through October 13, 2026. Under established case law, any agency may, through ratification, “purge[ ] any residual taint or prejudice left over from” a potential defect in a prior
(
printed page 67326)
governmental action.
[
1
]
The Department of Homeland Security is issuing this ratification out of an abundance of caution, and this ratification is not a statement that the fines covered by this ratification would have been invalid absent this ratification.
III. Ratification
The Secretary of Homeland Security hereby ratifies all final civil penalty decisions, as defined in
8 CFR 281.1(f)(3)
, issued pursuant to the procedures codified at 8 CFR part 281 from June 27, 2025, through October 13, 2026, except for those that have been reversed on appeal, are currently pending appeal, or have otherwise been reopened and rescinded pursuant to
8 CFR 281.1(f)(1)
. Any respondent alien who asserts that he or she has been prejudiced by the interim regulations may raise that claim to ICE to evaluate whether such prejudice has been shown and what remedy, if any, is appropriate. This process is not an additional appeal mechanism; rather, it is limited to claims of prejudice for civil penalties issued under the interim regulations.
To raise a claim, please email
IFRCivilFinesReview@ice.dhs.gov
. In the subject line of the email, please provide the respondent alien's full name, date of birth, and alien registration number. This claim must also contain the respondent alien's current address and current phone number, the penalty tracking number of the respondent alien's applicable civil penalty, and an invoice number (if applicable). ICE will not review claims that fail to include the above-listed required information. All claims must be received by ICE on or before November 16, 2026.
Markwayne Mullin,
Secretary, U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

1.
Guedes

Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives
, 920 F.3d 1, 13 (D.C. Cir. 2019).

Unless otherwise noted herein, the meetings will be open to public observation via LSC's YouTube channel:

, (7), (9) and (10), will not be available for public inspection. A copy of the General Counsel's certification that, in his opinion, the closing is authorized by law will be available upon request.

notice is hereby given that, on October 14, 2026, NYSE American LLC (“NYSE American” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to modify the NYSE American Options Fee Schedule (“Fee Schedule”) regarding fees and rebates applicable to Manual transactions. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to modify the Fee Schedule to adjust the fees and rebates applicable to Manual transactions. Specifically, the Exchange proposes to (1) amend the fees applicable to Manual transactions in non-Penny issues executed by e-Specialists, Market Makers, and Specialists (collectively, “Market Makers”), and (2) establish a rebate payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with a Market Maker order on the Trading Floor (“Trading Floor” or “Floor”). The Exchange proposes that these changes become effective October 14, 2026.
[
4
]
With respect to the first proposed change, the Exchange proposes to amend Section I.A. of the Fee Schedule, which sets forth rates for Electronic and Manual transactions in both Penny and non-Penny issues. Currently, a $0.50 per contract fee applies to Market Makers' Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, except for those in MXEA, MXEF, MXUSA, MXWLD, and MXACW. The Exchange proposes to increase this fee to $0.90 per contract and then, effective November 1, 2026, increase the fee to $1.00 per contract. The increase to $1.00 per contract would align the Exchange's fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues consistent with similar fees adopted and proposed by other exchanges.
[
5
]
The two-tiered increase is necessary to simplify the Exchange's billing process during the transition and to allow market participants sufficient time to adapt.
The Exchange also proposes to establish a rebate of $0.20 per contract payable to Floor Broker orders that trade with Market Maker orders on the Trading Floor. For Floor Brokers that participate in the FB Prepay Program, the proposed rebate would apply in lieu of any rebates earned through the Manual Billable Rebate Program as provided in Section III.E. of the Fee Schedule. The Exchange proposes to add new text to Section III.E. of the Fee Schedule describing the proposed rebate.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rebate for Penny and non-Penny issues would strengthen the Exchange's competitive position for order flow by incentivizing Floor Brokers to participate on the Trading Floor, including when the counterparty to such trading is a Market Maker, rather than routing such orders to other exchanges' trading floors. The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market for order flow, and Floor Brokers may readily direct their order flow to competing exchanges that offer more favorable pricing. Accordingly, the Exchange believes the proposed rebate is a reasonable means of remaining competitive and attracting order flow to its Trading Floor. The Exchange notes that, in August 2026, executions in non-Penny issues represented only 12% of executed Manual volume, underscoring that the proposed fee increase is much smaller in scope than the proposed Floor Broker rebate, which is applicable to executions in both Penny and non-Penny issues.
Taken together with the proposed rebate payable to Floor Broker orders, the Exchange believes that the proposed increase in the Market Maker fee for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues from $0.50 to $0.90 per contract and then to $1.00 per contract beginning on November 1, 2026 would, on balance, not discourage Market Makers from continuing to participate in transactions on the Trading Floor, thereby promoting trading opportunities and competition on the Trading Floor to the benefit of all market participants. Specifically, the Exchange notes that Market Maker participation in non-Penny issues on the Trading Floor has continued to grow since the Exchange's initial fee increase on January 2, 2026. For example, in December 2025, prior to the Exchange's initial filing, Market Makers paid $0.50 per contract for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues and were involved in only 12% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. However, in August 2026,
(
printed page 67357)
after the fee was raised to $1.00 per contract for Manual executions in non-Penny issues and, subsequently, to $0.90 per contract, Market Makers were involved in 20% of executed Manual volume in non-Penny issues. Despite higher Market Maker fees for Manual transactions, the Exchange has continued to observe elevated Market Maker interest on the Trading Floor, even in non-Penny issues where the fee was specifically increased, demonstrating that this fee has not deterred, and will not deter Market Maker participation.
The Exchange further notes that the amount of the proposed fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is within the range of fees currently in place for responses by Market Makers (and other market participants) in non-Penny issues in various electronic paired-order auction mechanisms on other options exchanges, which is largely analogous to the Manual transactions impacted by the proposed fee increase on the Trading Floor. For example, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“EDGX”) imposes a $1.05 per contract fee on all market participants (including Market Makers) responding to Automated Improvement Mechanism Auctions (“AIM Auctions”), while charging the paired contra order only $0.02 per contract in non-Penny issues.
[
6
]
In this example, the large disparity in fees between the auction responder and the paired contra order demonstrates the unique position of the responder to evaluate the full terms of a transaction immediately prior to execution, including size, pricing, and counterparty interest. This position enables responders to EDGX AIM Auctions to exercise discretion in determining whether to engage in a trade under informed conditions. In addition, the responder has a guaranteed participation entitlement of up to 60% of the trade under the relevant rules, even in the absence of price improvement. This allocation represents a meaningful structural advantage, as it ensures a substantial share of order flow once a responder elects to participate. The Exchange believes that Market Makers hold a similar advantageous position in choosing to participate in Manual transactions on the Trading Floor and, therefore, believes that the difference in fees between Market Makers and other market participants for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is justified.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
7
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and (5) of the Act,
[
8
]
in particular, because it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its members, issuers and other persons using its facilities and does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers or dealers.
The Proposed Rule Change Is Reasonable
The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market. The Commission has repeatedly expressed its preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
9
]
There are currently 20 registered options exchanges competing for order flow. Based on publicly-available information, and excluding index-based options, no single exchange has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
10
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in August 2026, the Exchange had 11.30% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
11
]
In such a low-concentrated and highly competitive market, no single options exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of options order flow. Within this environment, market participants can freely and often do shift their order flow among the Exchange and competing venues in response to changes in their respective pricing schedules.
The Exchange believes that the ever-shifting market share among the exchanges from month to month demonstrates that market participants can shift order flow or discontinue or reduce use of certain categories of products in response to fee changes. Accordingly, competitive forces constrain options exchange transaction fees. Specifically, as it relates to Manual executions, Market Makers, like other market participants, retain the ability to adjust their trading behavior, reduce participation, or reallocate order flow and liquidity-provision activity across competing exchanges in response to fee changes.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rebate is reasonable because, in a highly competitive market where Floor Brokers may readily direct order flow to other exchanges' trading floors, the rebate would strengthen the Exchange's competitive position by incentivizing Floor Brokers to continue directing Manual orders to the Trading Floor, including orders that trade against Market Makers, thereby promoting trading opportunities and competition on the Floor for the benefit of all market participants. The Exchange also believes that the amount of the proposed fee for Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is reasonable, as it is (i) narrow in scope, applying only to non-Penny Manual transactions, which represent just 12% of executed Manual volume; (ii) unlikely to discourage Market Maker participation, which has continued to grow after the implementation of the increase; and (iii) consistent with, and more moderate than, comparable fee disparities imposed by another options exchange on responders in analogous electronic paired-order auctions (
e.g.,
EDGX's AIM Auction).
Furthermore, the Exchange believes that assessing a higher fee for Manual transactions on the Trading Floor is reasonable considering the distinct advantages afforded to Floor-based Market Makers. Floor-based Market Makers who, by virtue of their physical presence and participation model, are uniquely positioned to evaluate the full terms of a transaction, including size, pricing, and counterparty interest, immediately prior to execution. This capability enables Floor-based Market Makers to exercise discretion in determining whether to engage in a
(
printed page 67358)
trade under informed conditions that are not available to off-floor or fully electronic participants. In addition, the Exchange's rules provide Floor-based Market Makers with a guaranteed participation entitlement of up to 60% of the trade for both Solicitation and Facilitation Cross Transactions,
[
12
]
even in the absence of price improvement. This allocation represents a meaningful structural advantage, as it ensures a substantial share of order flow if a Floor-based Market Maker elects to participate.
[
13
]
Together, these features—the ability to assess trading opportunities in real time before committing capital and the certainty of receiving a guaranteed, significant allocation—enhance the likelihood of favorable execution outcomes and revenue opportunities for Floor-based Market Makers.
Accordingly, the Exchange believes it is reasonable to assess higher fees on Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues. This fee differential is consistent with the fee structure of another options exchange's offerings in its electronic paired-order auction, which similarly differentiate fees based on the trading privileges and informational advantages available to certain participants. For example, EDGX's AIM Auction charges all market participants responding to an auction (including Market Makers) $1.05 per contract, while charging the paired contra order only $0.02 per contract in non-Penny issues—in each case reflecting a substantial fee differential tied to the distinct informational and structural advantages afforded to the responder, largely similar to the advantages afforded to Floor-based Market Makers here. The differential between the fee charged to Market Makers and the fee charged to other participants in non-Penny Manual transactions reflects the enhanced trading privileges, informational advantages, and allocation guarantees uniquely available to Trading Floor-based participants and appropriately aligns fees with the relative value of these benefits as compared to other market participants operating without such advantages.
The Exchange believes that the proposed changes are reasonably designed to incent Floor Brokers to increase the number of Manual orders directed to the Trading Floor, including orders that trade with Market Maker orders. Any increase in trading volume would create more trading opportunities for all market participants and would in turn attract additional order flow to the Exchange, further contributing to a deeper, more liquid market to the benefit of all market participants. The Exchange also notes that the proposed rebate is similar in structure to incentive programs for Floor Brokers offered by competing options exchanges.
[
14
]
The Exchange further believes the proposed fee increase is reasonable because it is designed to offset the costs associated with the proposed Floor Broker rebate, which, as noted above, is intended to create more trading opportunities on the Trading Floor for all market participants, including Market Makers. As discussed above, Market Maker participation on the Trading Floor has continued to grow even as Market Maker fees for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues have increased, and the Exchange believes the increased order flow generated by the proposed rebate would similarly provide Market Makers with additional trading opportunities that offset the impact of the higher fee. In addition, the Exchange notes that market participants remain free to direct their order flow to competing venues if they believe other markets offer more favorable fees and rebates. Specifically, Market Makers, like other market participants, retain the ability to adjust their trading behavior, reduce participation, or reallocate order flow and liquidity-provision activity across competing exchanges in response to fee changes.
To the extent the proposed rule change attracts greater volume and liquidity by encouraging Floor Brokers to increase their options volume on the Exchange in an effort to earn the proposed rebate, the Exchange believes the proposed changes would improve the Exchange's overall competitiveness and strengthen its market quality for all market participants. Against the backdrop of the competitive environment in which the Exchange operates, the proposed rule change is a reasonable attempt by the Exchange to increase the depth of its market and improve its market share relative to its competitors.
The Proposed Rule Change Is an Equitable Allocation of Credits and Fees
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is an equitable allocation of its fees and credits. With respect to the proposed rebate, the Exchange believes it is equitable because it is based on the type of business transacted on the Exchange, and Floor Brokers may choose whether or not to seek to earn the rebate based on their own order-routing decisions. The Exchange also believes the rebate is equitable because it is intended to support Floor Brokers' role in facilitating the execution of Manual orders, a function that benefits all market participants on the Trading Floor, including Market Makers.
With respect to the proposed fee applicable to Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, the Exchange believes it is equitable for several reasons. First, the fee is designed to offset the costs associated with the proposed rebate while encouraging increased execution opportunities in Manual transactions on the Trading Floor, and an increase in such orders would, in turn, enhance trading opportunities for all market participants. The fee is also consistent with fees charged, and differences allowed, by EDGX, for analogous transactions (
e.g.,
AIM Auction fees). Assessing Market Makers a higher fee for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is equitable because Floor-based Market Makers, who account for the majority of Market Maker Manual transaction volume in non-Penny issues, occupy a uniquely advantaged position relative to other market participants—specifically, the exclusive ability to evaluate the terms of a transaction immediately prior to execution, as well as a guaranteed participation allocation of up to 60% of the trade under the Exchange's rules.
[
15
]
Moreover, the proposal is designed to incent participation on the Trading Floor in an effort to make the Exchange a primary execution venue and to attract more Manual transactions to the Exchange. To the extent that the proposed change attracts more Floor Broker orders to the Exchange, this increased order flow would continue to make the Exchange a more competitive venue for, among other things, order execution. Thus, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change would
(
printed page 67359)
improve market quality for all market participants on the Exchange and, as a consequence, attract more order flow to the Exchange thereby improving market-wide quality and price discovery.
The Proposed Rule Change Is Not Unfairly Discriminatory
The Exchange believes it is not unfairly discriminatory to modify the fee applicable to Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues because the proposed change would apply to all similarly situated Market Maker orders equally, regardless of the identity of the Market Maker responding to such orders. The Exchange notes that any participant can become a Floor-based Market Maker on the Exchange and avail themselves equally to all the benefits and obligations that such role entails. As discussed above, the Exchange believes it is not unfairly discriminatory to incent order flow to the Exchange through the proposed rebate, which would enhance liquidity on the Exchange to the benefit of all market participants. The Exchange also believes that the proposed rebate payable to Floor Brokers for a Manual order that trades with a Market Maker order on the Trading Floor is not unfairly discriminatory because it would be available to all similarly situated Floor Brokers on an equal and non-discriminatory basis, based solely on their order flow and trading activity on the Trading Floor.
The Exchange further believes that the proposed rebate is not unfairly discriminatory to other market participants because it is intended to encourage the role performed by Floor Brokers in facilitating the execution of orders via open outcry, a function which the Exchange wishes to support for the benefit of all market participants, including Market Makers, who would benefit from the additional execution opportunities generated by increased Floor Broker participation. In addition, although the proposed change would increase the fee applicable to Market Maker Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, the proposed fee is consistent with fees charged, and differences allowed, by another options exchange for analogous transactions. For example, EDGX's AIM Auction, which charges responders (including Market Makers) $1.05 per contract while charging the paired contra order only $0.02 per contract in non-Penny issues.
The Exchange further believes that Market Makers would not be discouraged from continuing to participate actively on the Trading Floor and would benefit from increased Manual order flow, including from Floor Brokers seeking to earn the proposed rebate. Indeed, as discussed above, Market Maker participation in non-Penny Manual transactions on the Trading Floor grew from 12% in December 2025 to 20% in August 2026, notwithstanding higher Market Maker fees already in effect for much of that period, demonstrating that a fee differential of this magnitude has not discouraged, and is not expected to discourage, Market Maker participation.
The Exchange also believes that the higher fee assessed to Market Makers for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues is not unfairly discriminatory because it reasonably reflects the uniquely advantaged position of Trading Floor-based Market Makers, who account for approximately 95% of such volume, relative to other market participants. In particular, these Trading Floor-based Market Makers possess the exclusive ability to evaluate the full terms of a transaction immediately prior to execution and benefit from a guaranteed participation allocation of up to 60% of the trade under the Exchange's rules.
[
16
]
These features provide Floor-based Market Makers with meaningful informational and allocation advantages that are not available to off-floor or purely electronic participants. The Exchange notes that any participant can become a Floor-based Market Maker on the Exchange and avail themselves equally to all the benefits and obligations that such role entails. Accordingly, the Exchange believes that the differential in fees, which is similar in kind to the differential EDGX charges between AIM Auction responders and the paired contra orders is appropriately calibrated to the distinct structural benefits available to Trading Floor-based Market Makers and therefore does not constitute unfair discrimination. Rather, the higher fee reflects a rational alignment between pricing and the value of the enhanced trading opportunities and execution certainty afforded to these participants. Moreover, to the extent that the exercise of these advantages contributes to increased Trading Floor activity and attracts additional order flow, the proposed fee would enhance overall market quality, deepen liquidity, and promote additional trading opportunities for all market participants on the Exchange.
Finally, the Exchange believes that it is subject to significant competitive forces, as described below in the Exchange's statement regarding the burden on competition.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
In accordance with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change would impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. Instead, the Exchange believes that the proposed changes would encourage the submission of additional liquidity to a public exchange, thereby promoting market depth, price discovery and transparency and enhancing order execution opportunities for all market participants. As a result, the Exchange believes that the proposed change furthers the Commission's goal in adopting Regulation NMS of fostering integrated competition among orders, which promotes “more efficient pricing of individual stocks for all types of orders, large and small.”
[
17
]
Intramarket Competition.
The proposed change is designed to attract additional order flow to the Exchange. The Exchange notes that any participant can become a Floor-based Market Maker on the Exchange and avail themselves equally to all the benefits and obligations that such role entails. The Exchange believes that the proposed change to Market Maker fees for Manual transactions in non-Penny issues, and the proposed rebate payable to the Floor Broker orders that trade against Market Maker orders on the Trading Floor would encourage Floor Broker Manual order flow and would not disincentivize Market Maker activity on the Trading Floor. Greater liquidity benefits all market participants on the Exchange and increased order flow would increase opportunities for execution of other trading interest. The proposed changes would apply and be available to all similarly situated market participants that execute Manual transactions on the Trading Floor, and, accordingly, the proposed changes would not impose a disparate burden on competition among market participants on the Exchange.
Intermarket Competition.
The Exchange operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor one of the other 19 competing options exchanges if they deem the Exchange's fee levels to be excessive. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges and to attract order flow to the Exchange. Based on publicly available information, and excluding index-based options, no single exchange
(
printed page 67360)
has more than 16% of the market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
18
]
Therefore, currently no exchange possesses significant pricing power in the execution of multiply-listed equity and ETF options order flow. More specifically, in August 2026, the Exchange had 11.30% market share of executed volume of multiply-listed equity and ETF options trades.
[
19
]
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change reflects this competitive environment because it modifies the Exchange's fees in a manner designed to continue to incent participants on the Trading Floor to direct trading interest to the Exchange, to provide liquidity and to attract additional order flow. To the extent that Floor Brokers are encouraged to utilize the Exchange as a primary trading venue for all transactions, all Exchange market participants stand to benefit from the improved market quality and increased opportunities for price improvement. The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually review, and consider adjusting, its fees and credits to remain competitive with other exchanges. For the reasons described above, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change reflects this competitive environment.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change is effective upon filing pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
20
]
of the Act and subparagraph (f)(2) of Rule 19b-4
[
21
]
thereunder, because it establishes a due, fee, or other charge imposed by the Exchange.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
22
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-93 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-93. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSEAMER-2026-93 and should be submitted on or before November 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
23
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

full_text:
