Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106712; File No. SR-CboeBYX-2026-040]
October 21, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 19, 2026, Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “BYX”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe BYX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “BYX”) proposes to amend its Fee Schedule to update the definition of “Trading Platform.” The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​byx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend the definition of “Trading Platform” set forth in the Definitions section of its Fee Schedule.
[
3
]
The existing definition enumerates three categories of execution venue—a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, and an Electronic Communications Network. The Exchange now seeks to amend this definition to add a functional, use-based category—namely, any other system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity—so that the term also captures other systems that perform a functionally equivalent execution function. The amended definition identifies, as non-exhaustive examples, a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment.
[
4
]
The current
(
printed page 67374)
and proposed amended definitions are set forth below.
Current Definition:
“A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), or an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS).”
Proposed Amended Definition:
“A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS), or any other system, facility, or platform (including but not limited to a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, or a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment) through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity.”
The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, including the increasing use of functionally equivalent execution systems that operate outside the three enumerated categories. For example, under the current definition, a platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, or an Electronic Communications Network plainly constitutes a Trading Platform and is thus subject to the applicable fees associated with a Trading Platform.
[
5
]
However, a functionally equivalent system that performs the same execution function—such as a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow, or a decentralized or tokenized execution venue—is not expressly named in the current enumerated categories, despite performing the same execution function as the enumerated venues. To facilitate more consistent and equitable outcomes across functionally equivalent venues, the Exchange proposes to add this language so that “Trading Platform” better covers the intended scope of execution venues.
The new framework operates as a functional, use-based standard. It reaches any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of the execution model employed. The definition expressly covers both (i) systems that match third-party orders against one another and (ii) systems in which the operator or its affiliate executes third-party orders in a principal trading capacity. Accordingly, a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow falls within the definition on its face. The parenthetical examples—a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment—are illustrative only and the amended definition is not intended to limit the scope of the broader category. The requirement that orders be “systematically executed by electronic means” distinguishes covered systems from manual, negotiated, or voice-brokered bilateral trading.
The amended definition is intended to capture emerging technologies and execution venues that are functionally analogous to venues with established regulatory definitions—including tokenized order books or decentralized execution protocols, to the extent they perform or support an execution function, and other novel platforms. These venues operate in a manner similar to defined legacy execution platforms and should be treated as such. The examples set out in the definition—broker crossing systems not filed as ATSs, systematic internalization systems, and decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environments—as well as the references to single-dealer platforms in this filing, are illustrative of this approach, not an exhaustive list, and the definition applies to any system through which third-party orders are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of label.
The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity as to the scope of “Trading Platform,” with new and emerging execution technologies in mind. The Exchange notes that this update better aligns itself with the ongoing evolution of market structure and industry practice.
[
6
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”) and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
7
]
Specifically, the Exchange also believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
8
]
which requires that Exchange rules provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Members and other persons using its facilities. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
9
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
In particular, the proposed definition change is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Members and other persons using its facilities. The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, and to ensure that the term “Trading Platform” is applied consistently and comprehensively to functionally equivalent execution systems, regardless of the underlying technology or business model. As noted above, the amended definition is intended to reach any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching or by principal execution by the operator or its affiliate—including, for example, a single-dealer platform that internalizes order flow, as well as decentralized or tokenized execution venues. A definition that excluded single-dealer platforms on the basis of their bilateral structure would draw an arbitrary line between venues that use market data in the same way. Applying the definition on a consistent, function-based basis to all functionally analogous venues, legacy and emerging alike, ensures equal treatment and avoids selective application. By ensuring that similar venues are treated alike, the proposed definition supports the equitable allocation of fees and avoids disparate treatment of functionally equivalent venues that do not meet an existing
(
printed page 67375)
definition. The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity on the platforms that should be covered under the definition, with new and emerging trading technologies in mind.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is grounded in the Exchange's efforts to compete more effectively (
e.g.,
by updating its definition of Trading Platform to conform with changes in the industry).
[
10
]
As a result, the Exchange believes this proposed rule change permits fair competition among national securities exchanges.
Further, the Exchange believes that these changes will not cause any unnecessary or inappropriate burden on intramarket competition, as the revised definition applies uniformly to all market participants that meet the definition of Trading Platform, regardless of their specific business model or the technology employed by the execution venue.
Further, the proposed change to update the Trading Platform definition does not create an unnecessary or inappropriate inter-market burden on competition because it merely updates the Exchange's definitions to ensure consistency with the evolving technological landscape. Indeed, this proposal ensures that the Exchange's Fee Schedule accurately reflects the current scope of execution venues. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will relieve any burden on, or otherwise promote, competition.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
11
]
and paragraph (f) of Rule 19b-4
[
12
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.

Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:

All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeBYX-2026-040. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (

Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. (

AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Notice of Availability.
SUMMARY:
We are advising the public that we are making available for review and comment a revised version of the Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) Herd Certification Program Standards. The CWD Program Standards provide guidance on how to meet CWD Herd Certification Program and interstate movement requirements. We are taking this action to address concerns of State and industry participants regarding the existing standards.
DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before November 25, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov
.
Enter APHIS-2026-0563 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.
Postal Mail/Commercial Delivery:
Send your comment to Docket No. APHIS-2026-0563, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., #AP760, Beltsville, MD 20705.
Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
www.regulations.gov
or in our reading room, which is located in room 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dr. Tracy Nichols, Molecular Biologist, Cervid Health Staff, Strategy and Policy, Veterinary Services, APHIS; 2150 Centre Ave, Bldg. B, Fort Collins, CO 80526; (970) 494-7380;
Tracy.A.Nichols@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Chronic wasting disease (CWD) is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy of cervids (members of Cervidae, the deer family). Species currently known to be susceptible to CWD include elk, mule deer, moose, white-tail deer, sika deer, muntjac, axis, reindeer, and black-tail deer.
In 2014, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) implemented the National CWD Herd Certification Program (HCP), a voluntary Federal-State-industry cooperative program administered by APHIS and implemented by participating States. States and herd owners choosing to participate must comply with the provisions of
9 CFR part 55
and all producers must comply with part 81 (referred to below as the regulations), which include requirements for animal identification, interstate movement, fencing, recordkeeping, herd inspections and inventories, animal mortality testing, and response to any findings of CWD-exposed, -suspect, or -positive herds. APHIS monitors the approved State HCPs to ensure consistency with Federal standards by means of annual State reporting and state reviews. With each year of successful compliance with the requirements, participating herds will advance in status. After 5 years of compliance with no evidence of CWD, the State or APHIS will certify the herd as being low risk for CWD. Farmed cervids may only move interstate from enrolled herds certified as low risk for CWD.
The CWD Program Standards, last revised in 2019, provide detailed guidance on how to meet the regulatory requirements referred to above. The Program Standards are reviewed on an ongoing basis by APHIS in collaboration with State agencies and industry representatives.
We are advising the public that we have prepared revisions of the CWD Program Standards. The proposed revisions include the following:
Reducing the trace and quarantine period for white-tail and mule deer, and maintaining it for elk and other species.
Updating indemnity prioritization to include reducing CWD transmission risk, strategically removing high risk animals, and encouraging HCP participation and genetic strategies to lower herd susceptibility.
Making science-based updates and clarifications in areas that were open to interpretation.
Including guidelines for use of predictive genetics to reduce herd CWD susceptibility and increase CWD prevention.
Adding a section on the indemnity appeal process and revising the prioritization guidelines for indemnity funds to include predictive genetics.
Allowance for moving cervids from a CWD positive herd to a terminal positive quarantined hunt facility in a wildlife endemic area in another State with concurrence of the State Animal Health Authorities in the origin and receiving States.
The revised Program Standards may be viewed on the
Regulations.gov
website or in our reading room. (Instructions for accessing
Regulations.gov
and information on the location and hours of the reading room are provided under the heading
ADDRESSES
at the beginning of this notice.) The documents are also available by contacting the person listed under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
.
We welcome public comment on this notice and the proposed revisions to the CWD Program Standards. Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106719; File No. SR-CboeEDGX-2026-068]
October 21, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 9, 2026, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“EDGX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to: (1) amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rules 3.7 and 3.21; (2) delete current Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety, thereby removing the requirement that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP
(
printed page 67344)
Derivative Security
[
3
]
that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular approved by the listing exchange; (3) amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities; (4) renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively; and (5) make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2). The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​edgx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to: (1) amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rules 3.7 and 3.21; (2) eliminate the requirement that the Exchange distribute an information circular to Members prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Derivative Security that generally includes the same information as contained in the information circular provided by the listing exchange as provided in current Rule 14.1(c)(1) by deleting Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety; (3) amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities;
[
4
]
(4) renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively; and (5) make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2). The proposal is based on Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (“BZX”) Rule 14.11(j).
[
5
]
Rule 14.1(c) governs the trading of UTP Derivative Securities on the Exchange—securities listed on another national securities exchange that trade on the Exchange pursuant to unlisted trading privileges (“UTP”). Under current Rule 14.1(c)(1), the Exchange must distribute an information circular prior to the commencement of trading in each UTP Derivative Security that generally mirrors the information circular issued by the primary listing exchange, including: (a) the special risks of trading the Derivative Security; (b) the Exchange Rules that will apply to the Derivative Security, including Rule 3.7; (c) information about the dissemination of the value of the underlying assets or indexes; and (d) the risk of trading during the Early Trading Session (7:00 a.m.—8:00 a.m. Eastern Time), Pre-Opening Session (8:00 a.m.—9:30 a.m. Eastern Time) and the Post-Closing Session (4:00 p.m.—8:00 p.m. Eastern Time) due to the lack of calculation or dissemination of the intra-day indicative value or a similar value. The Exchange proposes to delete Rule 14.1(c)(1) in its entirety.
The information circular requirement is unnecessary because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce. Members have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes.
[
6
]
The Exchange's issuance of a separate, duplicative circular therefore serves no independent investor protection function. The existing Member-level suitability and customer disclosure obligations under Rules 3.7 and 3.21 continue to apply independently of the information circular requirement.
The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 14.1(a) to add express cross-references to Rule 3.7 (Recommendations to Customers) and Rule 3.21 (Customer Disclosures). The Exchange is adding express cross-references to those rules in Rule 14.1(a) to enhance their visibility in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. These rules already apply to Members by operation of the Exchange's rulebook. The cross-references are intended to make the applicable framework explicit in the context of UTP Derivative Securities. Rule 3.7 independently requires Members to ensure that any recommendation of a UTP Derivative Security is suitable for the customer based on the customer's investment profile, a standing obligation that applies regardless of whether the Exchange has issued a product-specific information circular. Similarly, Rule 3.21 independently requires Members, before accepting an order from a customer for execution in the Early Trading, Pre-Opening or Post-Closing Trading Session, to disclose to such customer that extended hours trading involves material trading risks, including the possibility of lower liquidity, high volatility, changing prices, unlinked markets, an exaggerated effect from news announcements, wider spreads and any other relevant risk, and this obligation is not contingent on the Exchange's issuance of a product-specific information circular.
Because current Rule 14.1(c)(1) has historically served as the mechanism through which the Exchange satisfies the notification obligation under current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B), deletion of Rule 14.1(c)(1) necessitates a conforming amendment to current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B). The Exchange proposes to amend current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) to require that the written description referenced therein be provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities. The Exchange will notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange. This amendment is consistent with the broader purpose of the proposed rule change: where the listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the information necessary to assess a UTP Derivative Security, a duplicative written description obligation serves no independent investor protection function. Members may rely on the
(
printed page 67345)
listing exchange's information circular in the same manner and to the same effect.
Finally, the Exchange proposes to renumber current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), respectively, and to make a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2).
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
7
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
8
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
9
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes the proposed deletion of current Rule 14.1(c)(1) is consistent with the Act because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures that the Exchange's information circular would contain. The investor protection functions historically served by the information circular requirement are independently addressed through the primary listing exchange's information circular and the Member-level obligations imposed by Rules 3.7 and 3.21, to which the Exchange proposes to add express cross-references in Rule 14.1(a). The proposed amendment to current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) ensures that where a written description is required, it is provided in a form approved by the listing exchange or prepared by the open-ended management company issuing such securities, thereby aligning the Exchange's requirements with those of the primary listing market. The Exchange will further notify Members by information circular that such written description will only be required when mandated by the listing exchange, ensuring that no duplicative obligation is imposed where the listing exchange has not determined one to be warranted. The renumbering of current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4), and the conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 updating the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2), are ministerial. Additionally, as discussed above, the proposal does not raise any novel issues not previously considered by the Commission. For these reasons, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change: (1) adds express cross-references to Rules 3.7 and 3.21 in Rule 14.1(a), which does not impose any new obligations on Members; (2) eliminates duplicative procedural obligations applicable to the Exchange in its capacity as a UTP trading venue by deleting current Rule 14.1(c)(1); (3) aligns the written description obligation under current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) with the primary listing market's requirements; (4) renumbers current Rules 14.1(c)(2) through (5) as Rules 14.1(c)(1) through (4); and (5) makes a conforming amendment to Interpretations and Policies .01 to update the cross-reference from Rule 14.1(c)(3) to Rule 14.1(c)(2), which is ministerial. The proposed rule change does not alter the terms or conditions under which UTP Derivative Securities may be traded on the Exchange, impose any new requirements on Members, or affect the ability of any market participant to access the Exchange's markets. Members will continue to have access to the primary listing exchange's information circular prior to the commencement of UTP trading and may rely upon it for the same purposes as the Exchange's information circular. The proposed amendment to current Rule 14.1(c)(2)(B) aligns the written description obligation with the primary listing market's requirements and does not impose any burden on Members beyond what the primary listing market itself requires. Accordingly, the Exchange does not believe the proposed rule change imposes any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
10
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
11
]
thereunder. Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; or (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
12
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
13
]
thereunder.
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
14
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b4(f)(6)(iii),
[
15
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposed rule change may become operative immediately upon filing. The Exchange states that the proposed rule change eliminates duplicative procedural obligations applicable to the Exchange in its capacity as a UTP trading venue because the primary listing exchange's information circular already provides Members with the same disclosures the Exchange would otherwise be required to produce.
[
16
]
The Exchange also notes that the proposed rule change does not alter the terms or conditions under which UTP Derivative
(
printed page 67346)
Securities may be traded on the Exchange. For these reasons, the Commission finds that waiver of the 30-day operative delay is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. Therefore, the Commission hereby waives the 30-day operative delay and designates the proposed rule change to be operative upon filing.
[
17
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-068 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-068. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-068 and should be submitted on or before November 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
18
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106710; File No. SR-NYSETEX-2026-37]
October 21, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that, on October 7, 2026, the NYSE Texas, Inc. (“NYSE Texas” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.18 (“Trading Halts”) regarding Initial Listing Regulatory Halts, Rule 7.35(a)(8)(A) regarding the definition of “Auction Reference Price” for a Trading Halt Auction, and Rule 7.35(f) regarding IPO Auctions. The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
NYSE Texas, Inc. (“NYSE Texas” or the “Exchange”) proposes to amend Rule 7.18 (“Trading Halts”) regarding Initial Listing Regulatory Halts, Rule 7.35(a)(8)(A) regarding the definition of “Auction Reference Price” for a Trading Halt Auction, and Rule 7.35(f) regarding IPO Auctions.
Background
Rule 7.18(b)(1)(B) lists the types of discretionary regulatory halts the Exchange may declare, including, at subparagraph (i), an “Initial Listing Regulatory Halt.”
The Initial Listing Regulatory Halt was first adopted in 2018 on the Exchange's affiliate exchange, the New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE”), as NYSE Rule 123D(d).
[
4
]
The text of that rule stated, in pertinent part, that the Exchange “may declare a regulatory halt in a security that is the subject of an initial pricing on the Exchange of a security that has not been listed on a national securities exchange . . . immediately prior to the initial pricing.”
[
5
]
NYSE's Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the rule specified that the purpose of the rule change was to “provide authority to declare a regulatory halt for a new listing that is not the subject of an IPO.”
[
6
]
In its order granting approval of the rule, the Commission noted that the rule “should facilitate the initial opening . . . of certain securities not listed in connection with an underwritten IPO . . . .”
[
7
]
(
printed page 67347)
The Exchange adopted the Initial Listing Regulatory Halt as part of a reorganization of Rule 7.18 (“Trading Halts”) in August 2026.
[
8
]
Rule 7.18 (b)(1)(B)(1) defines the Initial Listing Regulatory Halt as “of a security that is the subject of an initial pricing on the Exchange that has not been listed on a national securities exchange immediately prior to initial pricing.”
[
9
]
Proposed Change to Rule 7.18(b)(1)(B)(i)
The Exchange proposes to amend the text of Rule 7.18(b)(1)(B)(i) to explicitly specify that the Initial Listing Regulatory Halt does not apply to corporate securities that are subject to an IPO. The Exchange believes that the transparency and clarity of the rule would be enhanced by specifying that the Exchange may declare an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt if a security is the subject of an initial pricing on the Exchange, “except for (a) IPOs in equity securities that are not derivative security products, or (b) securities that are listed on a national securities exchange immediately prior to initial pricing.” Because both these exceptions are covered by the existing rule, the proposed change is not substantive, but rather clarifying in nature.
Proposed Changes to Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v), Rule 7.35(a)(8)(A), and Rule 7.35(f)
Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) describes how the Exchange will resume trading after an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt. The current rule text provides that the Exchange “will resume trading after an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt when the security is open for trading,” but does not specify the mechanism by which the security will reopen.
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) to provide that “[t]he Exchange will resume trading after an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt with a Trading Halt Auction, except that an ETP New Issue as defined in Rule 7.35(f) will (a) reopen after 9:30 a.m. ET with an IPO Auction, or (b) if the issuer elects, at or after 7:00 a.m. ET with a Trading Halt Auction.”
The proposed change to the first clause is not substantive. Currently, trading after an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt generally reopens with a Trading Halt Auction,
[
10
]
which is the default process described in Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B).
[
11
]
Adding reference to a Trading Halt Auction in the base clause of Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) would add specificity without making any substantive change.
Similarly, proposed clause (v)(a) is also a non-substantive change, because it is already provided for in the Exchange's rules. Rule 7.35(f) currently provides that an “ETP IPO Security” will participate in an IPO Auction during the Core Trading Session (
i.e.,
after 9:30 a.m. ET) on its first day of trading. The Exchange proposes to reference that rule in Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) to enhance the transparency and specificity of the rule. Concurrently with this change, the Exchange proposes to replace the term “ETP IPO Security” in current Rule 7.35(f) with “ETP New Issue,” which more accurately describes the initial listing of an ETP security on the Exchange. The term “ETP New Issue” would also be used in the proposed revision of Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v), as indicated above.
Regarding proposed clause (v)(b), the Exchange recently amended Rule 7.35(f) to add that the issuer of an ETP IPO Security (
i.e.,
ETP New Issue) may elect to commence trading in the Early Trading Session (which commences at 7:00 a.m. ET) with an Early Open Auction.
[
12
]
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.35(f) to conduct a Trading Halt Auction to open an ETP New Issue in the Early Trading Session and to reflect that change in the proposed clause (v)(b) of Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B).
This change is necessary in connection with the implementation of 23/5 Trading, under which trading on the Exchange will commence each day at 9:00 p.m. ET. Under that model, the Exchange could not conduct a 7:00 a.m. ET auction to open an ETP New Issue without first issuing a regulatory halt to prevent the security from trading beginning at 9:00 p.m. ET. The Exchange, however, cannot operationally support commencement of trading in a security subject to a regulatory halt through an Early Open Auction and instead must use a Trading Halt Auction. Accordingly, the Exchange proposes to replace the reference in Rule 7.35(f) to “Early Open Auction” with “Trading Halt Auction” and include the reference to “Trading Halt Auction” in Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v).
Substantively, a Trading Halt Auction differs from an Early Open Auction because it is conducted following a regulatory halt and is therefore subject to auction protections and pricing parameters, including, where applicable, auction collars. Pursuant to Rule 7.35(e)(5) and (6), if, at 7:00 a.m. ET, the Indicative Match Price is below (above) the Lower (Upper) Auction Collar, the Exchange will not conduct the Trading Halt Auction but will instead extend the time of the auction in increments of five minutes until the Trading Halt Auction can occur at the Indicative Match Price. As a result, as proposed, the timing of the Trading Halt Auction for an ETP New Issue may be at or slightly after 7:00 a.m. ET.
As part of this change, the Exchange proposes to amend the definition of “Auction Reference Price” for Trading Halt Auctions in Rule 7.35(a)(8)(A). The rule currently provides that the Auction Reference Price for a Trading Halt Auction will be “[t]he price of the last consolidated trade of at least one round lot of that trading day and, if none, the prior trading day's Official Closing Price (except as provided for in Rule 7.35-E(e)(7)(A)).”
[
13
]
An ETP New Issue would not have traded the prior day and would not have a prior trading day's Official Closing Price, but it is customary for ETP issuers to provide exchanges with a value to use in place of that Official Closing Price (sometimes referred to as a “Seeding NAV”). Accordingly, to account for the opening of an ETP New Issue using a Trading Halt Auction, the Exchange proposes to add the following to the provision above: “or, in the case of an ETP New Issue, a value provided to the Exchange by the issuer.”
[
14
]
The Exchange believes that this proposed change will not negatively impact issuers or market participants. ETP issuers have expressed a preference to retain the option to open ETP New Issues with an auction at or after 7:00 a.m. ET, notwithstanding that such trading would begin through a Trading Halt Auction instead of an Early Open
(
printed page 67348)
Auction. While a Trading Halt Auction is subject to auction collars and extensions that do not apply to an Early Open Auction, the Exchange believes those features are designed to promote fair and orderly price discovery and reduce the likelihood of executions at prices that are not reasonably related to the value of the underlying ETP. Accordingly, the proposed change preserves issuers' ability to launch ETP New Issues during the Early Trading Session while providing market participants with the additional pricing protections associated with a Trading Halt Auction.
Implementation
The Exchange proposes that this rule change would become operative at the commencement of 23/5 Trading, which is scheduled to commence industry-wide on December 6, 2026.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder that are applicable to a national securities exchange, and, in particular, with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
15
]
Specifically, the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act
[
16
]
because it would promote just and equitable principles of trade, remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would protect investors and the public interest and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system by adding transparency and specificity to the rule.
Regarding the proposed change to Rule 7.18(b)(1)(B)(i), the existing text and the history of the rule are clear that an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt will not be used in the case of an IPO of a corporate security. The Exchange believes that stating that exception explicitly in the rule text will enhance the transparency of the rule and benefit the public interest.
Similarly, the current text of Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) does not specify the mechanism for reopening trading after an Initial Listing Regulatory Halt, and the Exchange believes that explicitly specifying those mechanisms in the rule text will enhance the transparency of the rule and benefit the public interest. Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B) already states that a Trading Halt Auction is the default method of reopening after a Regulatory Halt other than a SIP Halt, and Rule 7.35(f) already provides that an ETP IPO Security (
i.e.,
ETP New Issue) generally opens with an IPO Auction. The proposed rule change would make those rules explicit in the text of Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v), thereby adding further specificity and transparency to the Exchange's rules.
Finally, the proposal to amend Rule 7.35(f), to make a supporting change to Rule 7.35(a)(8)(A), and to reflect such changes in Rule 7.18(b)(5)(B)(v) to provide that the Exchange would use a Trading Halt Auction to open the security if the issuer of an ETP New Issue elects to commence trading in the Early Trading Session would remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system, and protect investors and the public interest. The proposed change preserves the issuer's ability to choose that an ETP New Issue start trading in the Early Trading Session in the 23/5 Trading environment, while providing market participants with the additional pricing protections associated with a Trading Halt Auction.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange believes the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act
[
17
]
in that it does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act as explained below. The majority of the proposed changes are non-substantive and, rather than impacting competition, would simply enhance the specificity and transparency of the rule. As for the proposed change to use a Trading Halt Auction to open trading in an ETP New Issue where the issuer elects to start trading in the Early Trading Session, the Exchange understands that other listing exchanges are making similar changes to their rules in light of 23/5 Trading, and as such, the proposed change would enhance, rather than burden, competition.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days after the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
18
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
19
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
20
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSETEX-2026-37  on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSETEX-2026-37. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your
(
printed page 67349)
comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSETEX-2026-37 and should be submitted on or before November 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

]

AGENCY:
Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS).
ACTION:
Notice; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Office of the Chairman of ACUS is requesting public input on federal agency approaches and processes for receiving, publicizing, and responding to comments related to rulemaking proceedings. ACUS is accepting written comments. Responses to this request may inform an ongoing ACUS project,
Processing Public Comments in Agency Rulemaking,
which, if warranted, may recommend best practices for agencies to use.
DATES:
Written comments must be received no later than 10:00 a.m. (ET) December 28, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit written comments by email to
info@acus.gov
(with “Processing Public Comments in Agency Rulemaking” in the subject line of the message), or by U.S. Mail addressed to Processing Public Comments in Agency Rulemaking, Administrative Conference of the United States, Suite 706 South, 1120 20th Street NW, Washington, DC 20036. ACUS will ordinarily post comments on the project web page (
https://www.acus.gov/​projects/​processing-public-comments-agency-rulemaking
) as they are received. Commenters should not include information, such as personal information or confidential business information, that they do not wish to appear on the ACUS website. For the full ACUS public comment policy, please visit
https://www.acus.gov/​policy/​public-comment-policy
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Becaja Caldwell, Attorney Advisor, Administrative Conference of the United States, 1120 20th Street NW, Suite 706 South, Washington, DC 20036; Telephone (202) 480-2080; email
bcaldwell@acus.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Administrative Conference Act,
5 U.S.C. 591-596
, established the Administrative Conference of the United States. The Conference studies the efficiency, adequacy, and fairness of the administrative procedures used by federal agencies and makes recommendations to agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States for procedural improvements (
5 U.S.C. 594(1)
). For further information about the Conference and its activities, see
www.acus.gov
.
Processing Public Comments in Agency Rulemaking
The public notice-and-comment process is an integral part of federal agency rulemaking. It provides an important opportunity for interested persons to share their perspectives, expertise, and experiences relevant to an agency's proposed action. Public comments can help inform an agency's decision making, for example by identifying potential local impacts, implementation challenges, and alternative approaches to regulatory action. Addressing public comments adequately is essential to ensure that final agency actions are based on the best available information, are perceived as legitimate by the public, and are not subsequently set aside on judicial review.
[
1
]
While most proposed rules receive few or no public comments, many receive hundreds or thousands of them. Processing voluminous comments requires significant agency resources, but even small numbers of comments may raise complex questions of law and policy that require substantial time and effort to address. Accordingly, agencies must ensure they employ robust procedures for processing comments from intake and analysis to response and resolution of comments.
ACUS is undertaking a project to examine how agencies receive public comments related to rulemaking proceedings; make those comments available to agency staff, contractors, and the public; analyze the content of the comments; and develop responses to them. The project includes consideration of the organizational practices agencies use to process comments; how agencies use contractors in comment processing; and how agencies procure and use various technological tools (including algorithmic tools) in receiving, analyzing, and responding to comments.
General Topics for Public Comment
ACUS welcomes views, information, and data on all aspects of federal agencies' process for receiving, reviewing, analyzing, and responding to comments in connection with rulemaking proceedings. ACUS invites interested persons to share their experiences with submitting comments on proposed rules or other rulemaking-related requests for information. For example:
A. What has been your experience submitting comments to federal agencies on proposed rules or in response to advance notices of proposed rulemaking or other rulemaking-related requests for information?
B. If you have submitted comments via both
Regulations.gov
and another agency platform, such as the Federal Communications Commission Electronic Comment Filing System, in what ways were the experiences similar? In what ways were they different?
Specific questions that ACUS is examining as part of this study include:
1. Which agencies conduct rulemakings that commonly receive public comments? What are the notable variations in the kinds of rules that receive comments and the quantity and quality of those comments?
2. How do agencies use
Regulations.gov
and the Federal Docket Management System (FDMS) to solicit, organize, store, and publish public comments? What agency officials (or contractors) are involved in these processes?
3. Which agencies have developed their own electronic systems to solicit, organize, and store public comments? How do these systems compare to
Regulations.gov
and FDMS?
4. How do agencies conduct comment analysis? What are the primary elements of the agency's comment analysis process? Who is involved in it? What
(
printed page 67263)
technologies, if any, do agencies use to analyze comments? How formal or informal is the process?
5. How do agencies develop responses to public comments? How does this stage of the process relate to prior stages? How does the development of comment responses relate to other aspects of developing the final rule? How do public comments affect the substance of final rules?
6. What aspects of agency comment processing procedures seem to be working well and why? For areas where things are not working well, what seem to be the sources of the problems and what are the potential solutions?
(Authority:
5 U.S.C. 595
.)
Dated: October 21, 2026.
Shawne C. McGibbon,
General Counsel.

The OMB approves these ICs through OMB No. 3064-0204 and last approved the ICR on December 18, 2023 (2023 ICR). OMB No. 3064-0204 is set to expire on December 31, 2026. There is no change in the substance or methodology of this information collection. The burden has increased by 125 hours, from 505 hours in 2023 to 630 hours. The increase is attributable to the inclusion of previously unaccounted for recordkeeping burden under
12 CFR 349.11(a)(1)
. All other burden estimates remain unchanged from the 2023 approval.
Request for Comment

All comments will become a matter of public record.

October 21, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”),
[
1

[

notice is hereby given that on October 8, 2026, Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “BZX”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (“BZX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend the annual listing fees applicable to exchange-traded products listed on the Exchange, which are set forth in BZX Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E), to eliminate the annual listing fee applicable to Legacy Listings. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
(
printed page 67342)
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​bzx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
On August 30, 2011, the Exchange received approval of rules applicable to the qualification, listing and delisting of companies on the Exchange,
[
3
]
which it modified on February 8, 2012 in order to adopt pricing for the listing of exchange-traded products (“ETPs”)
[
4
]
on the Exchange.
[
5
]
Effective January 1, 2019, the Exchange amended Rule 14.13 to adopt annual listing fees for ETPs, including a reduced annual listing fee of $4,000 for ETPs listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 (a “Legacy Listing”).
[
6
]
Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) now sets forth the annual listing fee structure for ETPs, which distinguishes among ETPs based on, among other things, the date on which an ETP first listed on the Exchange. The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) to eliminate the $4,000 annual listing fee currently applicable to Legacy Listings.
Currently, Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) provides that the issuer of each class of securities (not otherwise identified in Rule 14.13) that is a domestic or foreign issue listed on the Exchange as an ETP shall pay an annual listing fee to the Exchange, and that an issuer will be charged the lowest applicable fee among the categories set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i) through (vi). Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i) currently provides: “[w]here an ETP was listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 (a “Legacy Listing”) or is a Transfer Listing, such ETP will have an annual listing fee of $4,000.” Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) also provides for an annual listing fee of $4,500 for a New Listing; a collective maximum annual listing fee of $16,000 for a series of Outcome Strategy ETPs or a series of Defined Distribution Strategy ETPs; and an annual listing fee of $9,000 for an ADR Hedge.
[
7
]
Under Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi), an ETP that is not a Legacy Listing, a New Listing, an Outcome Strategy ETP, a Defined Distribution Strategy ETP, an ADR Hedge, or a Transfer Listing is subject to an annual listing fee based on the consolidated average daily volume (“CADV”) of the ETP in the fourth quarter of the preceding calendar year, ranging from $5,000 for an ETP with CADV greater than 1,000,000 shares to $7,000 for an ETP with CADV of 0-10,000 shares.
The Exchange proposes to delete the Legacy Listing category from Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(i), such that the $4,000 annual listing fee would apply only to Transfer Listings. The Exchange also proposes to make a conforming change to Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi) to delete the reference to a Legacy Listing. As a result, an ETP listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 would no longer qualify for the $4,000 annual listing fee by virtue of its initial listing date, and would instead be charged the lowest applicable annual listing fee for which it otherwise qualifies under Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E), including the CADV-based fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi). The proposed rule change does not amend the annual listing fees applicable to Transfer Listings, New Listings, Outcome Strategy ETPs, Defined Distribution Strategy ETPs, or ADR Hedges, or the CADV-based fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(vi).
The Legacy Listing category was designed to preserve a reduced annual listing fee for ETPs that were already listed on the Exchange when the Exchange adopted its current annual listing fee structure. More than seven years have passed since January 1, 2019, and the Exchange believes that it is no longer appropriate to differentiate the annual listing fee applicable to an ETP based solely on whether the ETP first listed on the Exchange before or after that date. Rather, the Exchange believes that all ETPs listed on the Exchange should be subject to the same objective criteria in determining the applicable annual listing fee, namely the characteristics of the product and its trading activity, as reflected in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E)(ii) through (vi). Transfer Listings would continue to be eligible for the $4,000 annual listing fee, as the Exchange continues to believe that such fee is an appropriate incentive for issuers to transfer the listing of existing ETPs to the Exchange.
The Exchange will implement the proposed change beginning with the annual listing fees assessed for calendar year 2027. Unless otherwise specified, the Exchange assesses all annual fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2) upon initial listing and in the first quarter of the calendar year.
[
8
]
Accordingly, the proposed change will not affect any annual listing fee already assessed for calendar year 2026, and affected issuers will have notice of the proposed change in advance of the assessment of annual listing fees for calendar year 2027.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule changes are consistent with the objectives of Section 6 of the Act,
[
9
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5),
[
10
]
in particular, as it is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among its issuers, and it does not unfairly discriminate between customers, issuers, brokers or dealers.
The Exchange believes that the proposed elimination of the Legacy Listing category from Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E) is reasonable because it will subject all ETPs listed on the Exchange to the same objective criteria for determining the applicable annual listing fee, based on the characteristics of the product and its trading activity, rather than on the date on which the ETP first listed on the Exchange. The Exchange believes that a distinction based solely on whether an ETP listed on the Exchange prior to January 1, 2019 is no longer warranted given the passage of time since the Exchange adopted its current annual listing fee structure. Further, the annual listing fees that will apply to former Legacy Listings are the same fees that currently apply to all other ETPs listed on the Exchange that are not Transfer
(
printed page 67343)
Listings, which the Exchange believes remain reasonable.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because it will apply uniformly to all issuers of ETPs listed on the Exchange. Upon implementation, each ETP listed on the Exchange, regardless of its initial listing date, will be charged the lowest applicable annual listing fee for which it qualifies under Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E). The Exchange believes that continuing to provide the $4,000 annual listing fee to Transfer Listings is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because the Transfer Listing fee is available to any issuer that transfers the listing of an ETP from another national securities exchange to the Exchange, and is designed to attract additional listings to the Exchange, which the Exchange believes will enhance competition among listing venues.
Furthermore, the marketplace for listings is extremely competitive and there are several other national securities exchanges that offer ETP listings. Transfers between listing venues occur frequently for numerous reasons, including listing fees. Issuers of ETPs, including issuers of ETPs that are currently Legacy Listings, may transfer their listings to another venue if they deem the Exchange's listing fees excessive. The proposed rule change reflects a competitive pricing structure, which the Exchange believes will enhance competition both among ETP issuers and listing venues, to the benefit of investors.
Based on the foregoing, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule changes are consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will burden intramarket competition because the annual listing fees set forth in Rule 14.13(b)(2)(E), as amended, will apply uniformly to all issuers of ETPs listed on the Exchange, without regard to the date on which an ETP first listed on the Exchange. The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will burden intermarket competition because the market for ETP listings is highly competitive, and issuers may transfer the listing of an ETP to another national securities exchange if they deem the Exchange's listing fees excessive. The proposed rule change is a competitive pricing decision that reflects the Exchange's determination to apply consistent, objective criteria to all ETPs listed on the Exchange.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
11
]
and paragraph (f) of Rule 19b-4
[
12
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-CboeBZX-2026-085 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeBZX-2026-085. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeBZX-2026-085 and should be submitted on or before November 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
13
