Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106706; File No. SR-OCC-2026-009]
October 21, 2026.
I. Introduction
On August 19, 2026, the Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”) filed with the Securities and Exchange
(
printed page 67363)
Commission (“Commission”), pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
a proposed rule change to amend OCC's requirements and procedures for membership as well as protective measures and sanctions including, but not limited to, the suspension of members (hereinafter “Proposed Rule Change”). The Proposed Rule Change was published for comment in the
Federal Register
on September 8, 2026.
[
3
]
The Commission received comments from interested persons.
[
4
]
For the reasons discussed below, the Commission is approving the Proposed Rule Change.
II. Background
OCC is a central counterparty (“CCP”), which means that, as part of its function as a clearing agency, it interposes itself as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer for financial transactions. As the CCP for the listed options markets in the United States,
[
5
]
as well as for certain futures and stock loans, OCC is exposed to various risks arising from providing clearance and settlement services to its Clearing Members because OCC is obligated to perform on the contracts it clears.
[
6
]
OCC mitigates such risks, in part, by setting requirements for its members (and applicants to become members), the protective measures OCC may impose to manage specific risks, and the sanctions OCC may impose where members do not comply with the requirements of membership.
Generally, the proposed changes affect OCC's requirements and procedures for membership as well as protective measures and sanctions including, but not limited to, the suspension of members. The proposed changes related to membership include conditions for admission of clearing member applicants as well as standards for existing Clearing Members. The proposed changes also include the adoption of several new definitions, technical, clarifying changes, amendments to OCC's governance standards, and, generally, the adoption of new rules relating to risk mitigation practices.
A. Clearing Membership
As noted above, OCC proposes changes to its membership rules. The proposed changes would address the conditions for admission of clearing member applicants as well as the who are authorized to approve or deny such applications. The proposed changes also would address the ongoing requirements for Clearing Members.
1. Confidentiality Standards
OCC's proposed confidentiality standards apply generally to its membership rules. Proposed Rule 207(d) sets forth the standards Clearing Members must observe when maintaining or exchanging “OCC Confidential Information”
[
7
]
—the proposed rule demands that members exercise a standard of care that it would employ to protect its own confidential information, but not less than a reasonable standard of care. The proposed rule further acknowledges that breach of confidentiality may result in OCC seeking injunction or other equitable relief against the breaching party and states that the rule does not preclude or otherwise prohibit OCC from providing confidential information to the government or other regulatory authority.
2. Conditions for Admission
OCC proposes several changes to its Clearing Membership eligibility and admission standards, which are generally set forth in Chapter II of its rules. First, proposed rule 201(b) requires Clearing Members or applicants to maintain an operating history of at least one year in the same or substantially same business activities the member or applicant applies for. Alternatively, the member or applicant can maintain senior personnel with sufficient background or experience in such business activities.
Rule 204 sets forth OCC's Conditions to Admission. OCC proposes to amend its rules with regard to who is authorized to approve or deny applications for Clearing Membership. In 2016, OCC vested authority to approve or disapprove new membership applications in the risk committee of its board of directors (the “Risk Committee”) and delegated authority to approve certain applications to specific members of OCC management.
[
8
]
Now, OCC proposes to allow the Risk Committee to delegate, to its designated delegates or agents, the ability to approve or deny new applications or reapplications. Specifically, OCC proposes amending Rules 203(b) through (e), Rule 204(a), (c) through (e), and (l) to include the phrase “or its designated delegates or agents,” which would vest in OCC's management the Risk Committee's authority to approve or deny certain applications and reapplications for Clearing Membership and requests for business expansion. OCC states that the purpose of permitting such delegation is streamline and accelerate the decision-making process and approval, while continuing to utilize a risk-based decision-making approach.
[
9
]
OCC states further that the change would eliminate the need to wait until scheduled quarterly Risk Committee meetings to determine whether it will approve such applications or business expansion requests.
[
10
]
The proposed changes would also amend an applicant's obligations to notify OCC regarding Statutory Disqualification. Specifically, OCC proposes to require that such notifications be provided not only where an applicant or Key Person
[
11
]
is subject to a Statutory Disqualification, but also where the applicant or person is subject to formal investigation by a regulatory organization. OCC proposes to require that such notice be provided within two business days.
OCC next proposes amending Chapter II to include new Rules 204(e), (f) and (g). Rule 204(e) would set forth the standards by which OCC may disapprove an application or reapplication for membership or otherwise restrict denied applicants from reapplying upon becoming aware of any facts or circumstances about said applicant or reapplicant that poses
(
printed page 67364)
elevated risk to OCC or otherwise impacts the suitability of the applicant as a Clearing Member. Such revisions would include allowing denial of an application where a Key Person becomes an elevated risk to OCC or impacts the suitability of the applicant as a Clearing Member.
[
12
]
Rule 204(f) would require a denied applicant to address the specific grounds for denial prior to reapplying for membership. Rule 204(g) would require an applicant to maintain physical office space unless OCC determines that the applicant's use of a remote office remote model does not present a heightened risk to OCC. Lastly, proposed Rule 204(g) would make an applicant subject to OCC's procedure for conducting on-site visits to an applicant's facility as part of OCC's onboarding process. OCC believes the use of a fully remote, non-hybrid, office model may introduce challenges for OCC to communicate with the applicant and perform an onsite examination of the applicant, therefore posing heightened risk to OCC.
[
13
]
OCC is also amending Rule 204(h) (which concerns conditional approval of an application) to explicitly state that approval of an application may be conditioned on Clearing Fund deposits and operational testing requirements. OCC's changes to Rule 204 also include an amendment to Rule 204(l), which states that any imposed conditions will remain in effect until OCC judges that the heightened risks presented by the member are sufficiently reduced. Other changes to the rules governing conditions to admission include (i) empowering OCC to deny an application for failure to respond to requests for information under proposed Rule 204(j); (ii) stating explicitly that OCC may share information provided by an applicant with designated examining authorities under proposed Rule 204(k); and (iii) requiring that an applicant provide to OCC its business plan, supported by financial projections and assumptions under proposed Rule 204(m). Additional changes to Rule 204 would authorize OCC to impose risk-based limitations, restrictions and contingencies on applicants under proposed Rule 204(n)
[
14
]
and to request that an applicant provide the annual audited financial statements from its parent or affiliate under proposed Rule 204(p).
3. Ongoing Membership Standards
In addition to the conditions and requirements for applicants, OCC proposes to amend the standards to which current Clearing Members must adhere. For example, OCC proposes amendments to Rule 301(b), which would permit OCC to establish discretionary, risk-based minimum capital levels higher than those specified in current Rule 301. The proposed change aims to strengthen financial responsibility obligations for existing Clearing Members.
[
15
]
OCC's amendments to Rule 301(d) would require that every Clearing Member furnish copies of its contingency planning procedures upon OCC's request.
Likewise, OCC proposes substantive amendments and clarifying changes to Rules 302(b), 302(c), and 302(f). Consistent with the proposed changes to Rule 204(g) described above, proposed Rule 302(b) would require Clearing Members to maintain a physical office unless OCC deems the member's fully remote office model does not present a heightened risk to OCC. Moreover, Rule 302(b) would subject Clearing Members' physical offices to on-site visits from OCC with no more than 24-hours' notice. Similarly, OCC proposes amending Rule 302(c) to clarify that a member must make its books and records available for inspection by OCC upon request.
Next, OCC proposes to update Rule 303(a) to require Clearing Members to employ individuals with relevant industry experience in senior management roles or equivalent positions (
e.g.,
President of Chief Executive Officer). In addition, OCC proposes amending Rule 305, which concerns Clearing Member Risk Management, to explicitly state that following periodic review(s) of a Clearing Member's risk management framework, any of OCC's actions or subsequent imposition of protective measures will be based on its review of a Clearing Member's written risk management policies, practices, and procedures.
OCC proposes various changes to Rule 306A, which sets forth the standards for event-based reporting. Under the rule, Clearing Members must notify an officer of OCC prior to 3:00 p.m. Central Time on the next business day if certain, triggering events occur—OCC's proposed rule changes clarify under what circumstances a Clearing Member must report. To clarify Rule 306A's meaning, OCC proposes amending the entirety of the rule to reference Rule 101 definitions, where applicable. OCC also proposes changing Rule 306A(1)(a) clarify that OCC's reporting requirements do not supersede laws applicable to the member that might prevent disclosure of such notice to OCC; OCC adopted the same requirement for eligible bank Clearing Members in Rule 306A(a)(5)(D). In addition, OCC proposes changing Rule 306A(a)(2)(A)(i) to require that a Clearing Member report to OCC when its net capital is less than the greater of 20% above the applicable member's minimum capital requirement. Rule 306(a)(4)(B)(i) sets forth the same requirement for non-U.S. securities firms.
OCC's proposed change to Rule 306B(b) would require Clearing Members to provide OCC with a complete copy of the annual audited financial statements of the Clearing Member's parent or affiliate; if such statements are not available, the member must provide unaudited financial statements, or applicable financial information, upon OCC's request. In addition, OCC proposes adding Rule 306B(f), which would explicitly require Clearing Members to provide accurate, complete and timely responses to its annual and periodic due diligence information requests.
Lastly, OCC proposes amending Rule 2212 to require all clearing members that are participants of the Stock Loan/Hedge program to register their existing Master Securities Loan Agreement relationship within OCC's clearing system.
[
16
]
OCC's proposed changes to
(
printed page 67365)
Rule 2212 also include removing the modifying term “Hedge” from Rule 2212's text and removing the phrase “within the Stock Loan/Hedge Program” from Rule 2212(a).
B. Admission and Disciplinary Proceedings
1. Membership Applications
OCC proposes changes to its rules regarding the process provided both to applicants for membership as well as to members subject to disciplinary sanctions. OCC proposes adopting rules setting forth in expanded detail the processes and procedures for review of an application or reapplication by the Risk Committee or its delegates, which include: (i) the procedures to request a hearing following denial of an application or reapplication; (ii) procedure for submitting, precedent to a hearing, a concise statement setting for a member's objection to the denial; and (iii) the specific procedures for conducting a hearing before the risk committee, including, but not limited to, procedures for proffering documents and presenting testimony.
[
17
]
In addition, OCC proposes adopting a rule explicitly stating that any decision by the Risk Committee or its delegate to deny an application or reapplication must be written and noticed to the applicant—the proposed changes go on to state that a decision rendered by OCC is final upon the date an applicant receives notice of said decision. Lastly, OCC's proposed changes to Rule 203 include clarifying that any final decision to deny a reapplication pursuant to OCC Rule 309 constitutes grounds for summary suspension under OCC Rule 1102.
OCC's rules currently require a Clearing Member to notify OCC of material changes (
e.g.,
merger, sale, name change).
[
18
]
OCC proposes to amend its rules to empower OCC to require a Clearing Member to reapply for membership following notice of such a change. OCC proposes adopting Rule 309 in connection with Rule 306A(b)(1)—Rule 309 sets forth the processes and procedures for reapplying for membership. Rule 309(a) would authorize OCC to require a Clearing Member to reapply for membership if OCC determines, in its sole discretion, that the financial or operational condition of a Clearing Member has materially changed or materially changes the business strategy of the member in a manner that might adversely affect OCC. As proposed, Rule 309(b) would permit a Clearing Member to conditionally maintain its membership during the application period, notwithstanding any protective measures implemented pursuant to Rules 307 through 307C. Lastly, proposed Rule 309(c) would require that the denial of Clearing Membership following reapplication is subject to the process provided under Rule 203, as described above. Other proposed changes include amending rules 306A(a)(5)(C) and (D) to clarify that reporting obligations are triggered by the receipt of notice of any violation delineated in Rule 306A, amending Rule 306A(b)(1) to require that members provide notice of any material changes in its form of organization or ownership structure, and updating Rule 306A(c) to reference the newly adopted term “Key Person.”
2. Disciplinary Proceedings
OCC also proposes changes to Chapter XII, including amendments and clarifying additions to Rule 1201, which concerns sanctions. OCC proposes including among the sanctions available under Rule 1201(a) fines. OCC also proposes amending Rule 1201 to explicitly state that a Clearing Member may be sanctioned for violating statutory rules of OCC (
i.e.,
in addition to violating the By-Law and Rules). To clarify what conduct might constitute a sanction under the rule, OCC proposes adding Rules 1201(a)(1)-(5), which set forth examples of conduct that may warrant sanctions, including: (i) failure by a member to provide adequate personnel or facilities; (ii) failure by a member to comply with a protective measure proscribed under Rules 307 or 307C; (iii) exhibiting a pattern of tardily providing financial information; (iv) providing false financial information, or (iv) exhibiting a pattern of regulatory or legal infractions.
3. Suspension of a Clearing Member
Further, OCC proposes to Chapter XI of its Rules modify the procedures for summary suspension of a Clearing Member. OCC proposes adding Rule 1101(b), which would require any non-U.S. Clearing Member subject to expulsion or suspension by a non-U.S. regulatory agency or securities exchange to immediately notify OCC of any such occurrence. OCC also proposes amending Rule 1102(b)(5) to include examples of when a member is in such financial or operating difficulty that OCC may exercise its discretion to suspend the member (
e.g.,
the member loses access to sufficient financial resources or the ability to participate in default management activities). Under the proposed changes to Chapter XI, a Clearing Member could also be subject to suspension if it is in default in the payment of funds or other obligations in respect of Rule 707 X-M accounts or if it does not meet OCC's membership standards following reapplication under Rule 309. Lastly, OCC proposes an amendment clarifying that any event described in Rule 1102(a) constitutes a “default” and any default under any part of the rules must be noticed to OCC's Board if the suspension determination is made by any agent of OCC other than the Board itself.
C. Clearing Member Risk Criteria
OCC proposes to expand Rule 307(a) to include in the universe of risks factors that may precipitate the imposition of protective measures “market risk” and “regulatory or compliance risks.” In addition, OCC proposes amending Rule 307 to state that new Clearing Members may be subject to enhanced monitoring and surveillance. OCC also proposes adding Rules 307(b) and (c), which empower OCC to impose protective measures on any Clearing Member or applicant at their discretion, on a case-by-case basis depending on factors which include, but are not limited to, the member or applicant's financial or operational risk profile.
OCC proposes amending Rule 307B(b) to include new procedures relating the imposition of restrictions on certain transactions, positions and activities, which include: (i) requiring a Clearing Member to notice in writing its objections to any imposed restrictions and its intent to retain counsel; (ii) specifying OCC's notice of hearing obligations and stating that any hearing will proceed pursuant to Rule 203(b)(6); and (iii) setting forth the procedure and requirements by which OCC will provide a member a notice of its final decision.
OCC also proposes amending Rule 307C, which delineates additional operational, personnel, financial, and risk management requirements, to empower OCC to require a financial guaranty from a Clearing Member's parent company or affiliate, to impose limitations on a member's financial leverage, to require a member to fill a key risk management or operational role created by the loss of a Key Person, or to require that members implement or enhance certain internal controls, procedures or systems.
(
printed page 67366)
III. Discussion and Commission Findings
Section 19(b)(2)(C) of the Exchange Act requires the Commission to approve a proposed rule change of a self-regulatory organization if it finds that the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the organization.
[
19
]
Under the Commission's Rules of Practice, the “burden to demonstrate that a proposed rule change is consistent with the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations issued thereunder . . . is on the self-regulatory organization [`SRO'] that proposed the rule change.”
[
20
]
Based on a review of the Proposed Rule Change, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to OCC. The Proposed Rule Change is consistent with Sections 17A(b)(3)(F),
[
21
]
17A(b)(3)(H),
[
22
]
17A(b)(4)(B),
[
23
]
17A(b)(5)
[
24
]
of the Exchange Act, and Rules 17ad-22(e)(18)
[
25
]
thereunder.
A. Consistency With Sections 17A(b)(3)(F) and 17A(b)(4)(B) of the Exchange Act
Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Exchange Act requires that the rules of a clearing agency are designed, in general, to protect investors and the public interest while not being designed to permit unfair discrimination in the admission of participants or among participants in the use of the clearing agency.
[
26
]
Relatedly, Section 17A(b)(4)(B) of the Exchange Act provides that a clearing agency may deny participation to, or condition the participation of, any person if such person does not meet such standards of financial responsibility, operational capability, experience, and competence as are prescribed by the rules of the clearing agency.
[
27
]
Section 17A(b)(4)(B) of the Exchange Act also provides that a registered clearing agency may examine and verify the qualifications of an applicant to be a participant in accordance with procedures established by the rules of the clearing agency.
[
28
]
As described in Section II.A.2, OCC proposes to authorize the Risk Committee to continue to approve or deny applications and to delegate such authority to streamline the process. The proposed change would continue to rely on the current risk-based decision-making approach to reviewing applications without requiring an applicant to wait for a quarterly meeting of the Risk Committee for final determination. Although the initial decision could be made by a delegee, an applicant would continue to have the right to challenge a denial before the Risk Committee, preserving Board-level oversight of the process.
Further, OCC proposes changes to the substantive requirements both for applicants and members addressing various concerns. As described above, OCC proposes changes related to financial responsibility, including the change to OCC Rule 301(a) that would authorize OCC in to increase a Clearing Member's minimum capital requirement to mitigate various risks (
e.g.,
an inadequate liquidity profile)
[
29
]
and the proposed new section (p) of OCC Rule 204 that would authorize OCC to require an applicant to produce the financial statements of its parent or affiliate. Other proposed changes pertain to an applicant's or member's operations, such as compliance with the confidentiality requirements of proposed OCC Rule 207(d), the physical office requirements of proposed Rules 204(g) and 302(b), and the books and records requirements of proposed Rule 302. The proposal also includes changes related to experience and competence, such as the requirement for a viable business plan under proposed OCC Rule 204(m), an operating history of one year or for an applicant or Clearing Member to employ sufficiently experienced senior personnel in the relevant area of business activity under proposed OCC Rule 201(b), and responsibilities for employing risk management personnel under proposed Rule 303. OCC also proposes replacing a reference in the definition of the term “Office” to Rule 201 with a reference to Rule 302 to comport with proposed rule changes to Chapter II Clearing Membership and Chapter III Membership Standards.
One commenter took issue with the addition of certain requirements for applicants and members stating that the proposal erects nearly insurmountable barriers for anyone trying to enter the market.
[
30
]
Specifically, the commenter states that requiring an established operating history penalizes lean startups and that “[m]andating traditional physical office facilities disregards modern, secure remote infrastructure, forcing early-stage teams to absorb unnecessary real estate expenses before generating revenue.”
[
31
]
With regard to the year of operating history, OCC states that this proposed requirement would provide OCC with additional data or information (
e.g.,
an applicant or Clearing Member's operating history and its senior management's employment history) to determine whether they meet OCC's membership standards.
[
32
]
With regard to the requirement for a physical office, OCC explains that the purpose of the proposed requirement is to address issues of communication and transparency.
[
33
]
Based on the information provided, the proposed requirements around operations, experience, and competence are consistent with the Exchange Act. The Exchange Act does not permit unfair discrimination, but it does acknowledge the potential need to deny participation based on specific criteria. The commenter's concern regarding a one-year operating history ignores the alternative that OCC offers in its proposed rules (
e.g.,
employing sufficiently experienced personnel). Similarly, the proposed rules allow for a scenario in which an applicant or member may operate in a fully remote business model but allow OCC to assess the potential risks of such an operating model. OCC is permitted to adopt rules that limit participation to the extent such rules are consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act, such as not discriminating unfairly and not imposing a burden on competition that is not unnecessary or inappropriate.
Accordingly, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Sections 17A(b)(3)(F) and 17A(b)(4)(B) of the Exchange Act.
[
34
]
B. Consistency With Sections 17A(b)(3)(H) and 17A(b)(5)(B) of the Exchange Act
Section 17A(b)(3)(H) of the Exchange Act requires that the rules of a clearing agency are in accordance with the
(
printed page 67367)
provisions of Section 17A(b)(5) of the Exchange Act, and, in general, provide a fair procedure with respect to the disciplining of participants, the denial of participation to any person seeking participation therein, and the prohibition or limitation by the clearing agency of any person with respect to access to services offered by the clearing agency.
[
35
]
Section 17A(b)(5)(B) of the Exchange Act provides for the requirements related to any proceeding by a clearing agency to determine whether a person shall be denied participation or prohibited or limited with respect to access to services offered by the clearing agency.
[
36
]
As described in Section II.B.2, OCC proposes changes to the procedures around the denial of participation whether through the review of a membership application or disciplinary proceedings. Regarding the review of applications, the proposed changes explicitly provide procedures for the request a hearing following denial of an application as well as how such a hearing would proceed. For example, the proposed rules require that such a hearing proceed before the Risk Committee. OCC's proposed changes also include amending Rules 203 and 309 (
i.e.,
OCC's admissions procedures), to cover and encompass reapplications for Clearing Membership. In addition, the proposed changes to Rule 203 include amendments that specify in detail the processes and procedures for requesting a hearing contesting the denial of a Clearing Membership application or reapplication. The proposed amendments to the admission procedures serve to provide applicants and reapplicants an opportunity to be heard upon and explicitly provides for OCC to keep a record of any such hearing. After a hearing, the proposed rules would require that OCC produce a written statement setting forth specific grounds underlying the risk committee's disapproval decision. More specifically, proposed Rule 203(b)(8) mirrors proposed Rule 1201(b), which provides the same with respect to a suspension or expulsion following disciplinary proceedings undertaken pursuant to Chapter XII.
Likewise, Rule 309(c), as described in Section II.B.1., is consistent with Section 17A(b)(5)(B) of the Exchange Act. Proposed Rule 309(c) provides that any decision to deny Clearing Membership following reapplication will be made pursuant to Rule 203. The admission procedures described in Rule 203 already provide for the requirements outlined in Section 17A(b)(5)(B) of the Exchange Act, specifically in proposed Rules 203(b)(3) and (4). OCC's proposed changes to Rule 1201, which governs sanctions and is described above in Section II.B.2., describes, defines and explicitly delineates the universe of sanctions that OCC may impose on a Clearing Member.
Accordingly, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Sections 17A(b)(3)(H) and 17A(b)(5)(B) of the Exchange Act.
[
37
]
C. Consistency With Section 17A(b)(5)(C) Under the Exchange Act
Section 17A(b)(5)(C) of the Exchange Act authorizes a registered clearing agency to summarily suspend a participant who: (i) has been and is expelled or suspended from any SRO; (ii) is in default of any delivery of funds or securities to the clearing agency; or (iii) is in such financial or operating difficulty that the clearing agency determines that suspension of the participant is necessary for the protection of the clearing agency, its participants, creditors, or investors.
[
38
]
Section 17A(b)(5)(C) also provides that a summarily suspended participant shall be promptly afforded an opportunity for a hearing by the clearing agency in accordance with 17A(b)(5)(A) of the Exchange Act.
[
39
]
As described above, OCC proposes to reorganize and amend its rules pertaining to summary suspension of a Clearing Member. Specifically, the changes to Rule 1102(a) clarify upon what grounds OCC may summarily suspend a Clearing Member, by adding a nonexclusive list of scenarios involving financial or operating difficulty that may serve as grounds for suspension. The proposed changes would further clarify the current grounds for suspension related to OCC Rule 707 (
i.e.,
failure to meet an obligation in respect to cross-margin accounts). The proposed changes would also add a potential ground for suspension and proposed Rule 309 (
i.e.,
for Clearing Member who do not meet OCC's membership standards following reapplication). Further, the proposed changes would clarify that a summary suspension constitutes a default, following which OCC would cease to act for the suspended Clearing Member.
Accordingly, the proposed changes to Chapter XI of OCC's Rules are consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(5)(C) of the Exchange Act.
[
40
]
D. Consistency With Rule 17ad-22(e)(18) Under the Exchange Act
Rule 17ad-22(e)(18) under the Exchange Act requires a clearing agency, in part, to “[e]stablish objective, risk-based, and publicly disclosed criteria for participation” that “require participants to have sufficient financial resources and robust operational capacity to meet obligations arising from participation in the clearing agency” and “monitor compliance with such participation requirements on an ongoing basis.”
[
41
]
As discussed above, Section 17A(b)(4)(B) of the Exchange Act, the Proposed Rule Change would expand OCC's existing financial and operational membership standards to address specific risks such as allowing OCC to set higher capital requirements where a member has an inadequate liquidity profile. The proposed changes to Rules 204(g) and 302(b) allowing for on-site visits by OCC would facilitate OCC's ability to monitor for compliance with its participation requirements. Similarly, the proposed changes to Rules 306B, 307, 307B and 307C provide for additional notification and reporting requirements that support OCC's monitoring of its members as well as protective measures OCC may impose. Protective measures such as restricting transactions that pose additional risk or increasing operation, personnel, financial resource and risk management requirements would support OCC's ability to set membership requirements aimed to ensure that participants to have sufficient financial resources and robust operational capacity to meet obligations arising out of clearing transactions with OCC.
Accordingly, the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(18).
[
42
]
IV. Conclusion
On the basis of the foregoing, the Commission finds that the Proposed Rule Change is consistent with the requirements of the Exchange Act, and in particular, with the requirements of Sections 17A(b)(3)(F),
[
43
]
17A(b)(3)(H),
[
44
]
17A(b)(4)(B),
[
45
]
and 17A(b)(5)(B)
[
46
]
of the
(
printed page 67368)
Exchange Act, and Rule 17ad-22(e)(18)
[
47
]
thereunder.
It is therefore ordered
pursuant to Section 19(b)(2) of the Exchange Act
[
48
]
that the proposed rule change (SR-OCC-2026-009) be, and hereby is, approved.
[
49
]
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
50
]

Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106715; File No. SR-CboeEDGX-2026-072]
October 21, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 19, 2026, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “EDGX”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange” or “EDGX”) proposes to amend its Fee Schedule to update the definition of “Trading Platform.” The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
The text of the proposed rule change is also available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
), the Exchange's website (
https://www.cboe.com/​us/​equities/​regulation/​rule_​filings/​edgx/​
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these
(
printed page 67361)
statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend the definition of “Trading Platform” set forth in the Definitions section of its Fee Schedule.
[
3
]
The existing definition enumerates three categories of execution venue—registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, and an Electronic Communications Network. The Exchange now seeks to amend this definition to add a functional, use-based category—namely, any other system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity—so that the term also captures other systems that perform a functionally equivalent execution function. The amended definition identifies, as non-exhaustive examples, a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment.
[
4
]
The current and proposed amended definitions are set forth below.
Current Definition:
“A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), or an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS).”
Proposed Amended Definition: “A Trading Platform is any execution platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange (as defined in Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act), an Alternative Trading System (as defined in Rule 300(a) of Regulation ATS), an Electronic Communications Network (as defined in Rule 600(b)(23) of Regulation NMS), or any other system, facility, or platform (including but not limited to a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, or a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment) through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching such orders against one another or by the operator or its affiliate acting in a principal trading capacity.”
The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, including the increasing use of functionally equivalent execution systems that operate outside the three enumerated categories. For example, under the current definition, a platform operated as or by a registered National Securities Exchange, an Alternative Trading System, or an Electronic Communications Network plainly constitutes a Trading Platform and is thus subject to the applicable fees associated with a Trading Platform.
[
5
]
However, a functionally equivalent system that performs the same execution function—such as a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow, or a decentralized or tokenized execution venue—is not expressly named in the current enumerated categories, despite performing the same execution function as the enumerated venues. To facilitate more consistent and equitable outcomes across functionally equivalent venues, the Exchange proposes to add this language so that “Trading Platform” better covers the intended scope of execution venues.
The new framework operates as a functional, use-based standard. It reaches any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of the execution model employed. The definition expressly covers both (i) systems that match third-party orders against one another and (ii) systems in which the operator or its affiliate executes third-party orders in a principal trading capacity. Accordingly, a single-dealer platform that internalizes and/or facilitates execution of client order flow falls within the definition on its face. The parenthetical examples—a broker crossing system not filed as an ATS, a systematic internalization system, and a decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environment—are illustrative only and the amended definition is not intended to limit the scope of the broader category. The requirement that orders be “systematically executed by electronic means” distinguishes covered systems from manual, negotiated, or voice-brokered bilateral trading.
The amended definition is intended to capture emerging technologies and execution venues that are functionally analogous to venues with established regulatory definitions—including tokenized order books or decentralized execution protocols, to the extent they perform or support an execution function, and other novel platforms. These venues operate in a manner similar to defined legacy execution platforms and should be treated as such. The examples set out in the definition—broker crossing systems not filed as ATSs, systematic internalization systems, and decentralized blockchain-based or tokenized environments—as well as the references to single-dealer platforms in this filing, are illustrative of this approach, not an exhaustive list, and the definition applies to any system through which third-party orders are systematically executed by electronic means, regardless of label.
The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity as to the scope of “Trading Platform,” with new and emerging execution technologies in mind. The Exchange notes that this update better aligns itself with the ongoing evolution of market structure and industry practice.
[
6
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”) and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
7
]
Specifically, the Exchange also believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b)(4) of the Act,
[
8
]
which requires that Exchange rules provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Members and other persons using its facilities.
(
printed page 67362)
Additionally, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
9
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
In particular, the proposed definition change is designed to provide for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among its Members and other persons using its facilities. The change is intended to capture changes in the evolving landscape of market structure and trading technology, and to ensure that the term “Trading Platform” is applied consistently and comprehensively to functionally equivalent execution systems, regardless of the underlying technology or business model. As noted above, the amended definition is intended to reach any system, facility, or platform through which orders of persons other than the operator are systematically executed by electronic means, whether by matching or by principal execution by the operator or its affiliate—including, for example, a single-dealer platform that internalizes order flow, as well as decentralized or tokenized execution venues. A definition that excluded single-dealer platforms on the basis of their bilateral structure would draw an arbitrary line between venues that use market data in the same way. Applying the definition on a consistent, function-based basis to all functionally analogous venues, legacy and emerging alike, ensures equal treatment and avoids selective application. By ensuring that similar venues are treated alike, the proposed definition supports the equitable allocation of fees and avoids disparate treatment of functionally equivalent venues that do not meet an existing definition. The intent of this revised definition is not to introduce a new or novel concept; it is instead intended to provide further clarity on the platforms that should be covered under the definition, with new and emerging trading technologies in mind.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed rule change is grounded in the Exchange's efforts to compete more effectively (
e.g.,
by updating its definition of Trading Platform to conform with changes in the industry).
[
10
]
As a result, the Exchange believes this proposed rule change permits fair competition among national securities exchanges.
Further, the Exchange believes that these changes will not cause any unnecessary or inappropriate burden on intramarket competition, as the revised definition applies uniformly to all market participants that meet the definition of Trading Platform, regardless of their specific business model or the technology employed by the execution venue.
Further, the proposed change to update the Trading Platform definition does not create an unnecessary or inappropriate inter-market burden on competition because it merely updates the Exchange's definitions to ensure consistency with the evolving technological landscape. Indeed, this proposal ensures that the Exchange's Fee Schedule accurately reflects the current scope of execution venues. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will relieve any burden on, or otherwise promote, competition.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
11
]
and paragraph (f) of Rule 19b-4
[
12
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-072 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-072. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-CboeEDGX-2026-072 and should be submitted on or before November 16, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
13
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

SUMMARY:
In this document, the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau (Bureau) announces that it has received detailed selection criteria and related submission instructions for proposals for the position of Upper C-band Clearinghouse. In
Upper C-band (3.98-4.2 GHz); Expanding Flexible Use of the 3.7 to 4.2 GHz Band,
GN Docket Nos. 25-59 and 18-122, Report and Order, Order of Proposed Modification, and Order on Reconsideration, FCC 26-46 (July 24, 2026) (
Upper C-band R&O
), the Commission provided for the creation of an independent, third-party Upper C-band Clearinghouse to oversee the cost-related aspects of the Upper C-band transition, including the receipt, review, and disposition of all actual cost and lump sum reimbursement claims. The Upper C-band Clearinghouse will also administer the rebates for adjacent band radio altimeter retrofits.
DATES:
Potential clearinghouse candidates must email the selection committee with any questions about the selection criteria or submission requirements no later than October 23, 2026. Potential clearinghouse candidates must submit proposals according to the filing instructions contained in the selection committee's notification no later than November 9, 2026.

.

.

), in GN Docket No. 25-59, DA 26-1099, released on October 9, 2026. The

,

,

This proceeding shall be treated as a “permit-but-disclose” proceeding in accordance with the Commission's
ex parte
rules. Persons making
ex parte
presentations must file a copy of any written presentation or a memorandum summarizing any oral presentation within two business days after the presentation (unless a different deadline applicable to the Sunshine period applies). Persons making oral

If the presentation consisted in whole or in part of the presentation of data or arguments already reflected in the presenter's written comments, memoranda or other filings in the proceeding, the presenter may provide citations to such data or arguments in his or her prior comments, memoranda, or other filings (specifying the relevant page and/or paragraph numbers where such data or arguments can be found) in lieu of summarizing them in the memorandum. meetings are deemed to be written

e.g.,
.doc, .xml, .ppt, searchable .pdf). Participants in this proceeding should familiarize themselves with the Commission's
ex parte
rules.
Synopsis
With this Public Notice, the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau (Bureau) announces that it has received detailed selection criteria and related submission instructions for proposals for the position of Upper C-band Clearinghouse.
On July 24, 2026, the Commission released the
Upper C-band R&O,
91 FR 48700
, which adopted rules to make 160 megahertz of mid-band spectrum available for flexible use throughout the contiguous United States by transitioning incumbent Fixed Satellite Service (FSS) operations out of 4.0-4.16 GHz. The
Upper C-band R&O
provided for the creation of an independent, third-party Upper C-band Clearinghouse to oversee the cost-related aspects of the transition, including the receipt, review, and disposition of all actual cost and lump sum reimbursement claims. The Upper C-band Clearinghouse will also administer the rebates for adjacent band radio altimeter retrofits.
The
Upper C-band R&O
required a selection committee of stakeholders to establish detailed selection criteria based upon the Upper C-band Clearinghouse's duties set forth in section 27.1414(c) of the Commission's rules and to notify the Bureau of such criteria within 30 days of its initial meeting. The Commission directed the Bureau to issue a public notice that: (1) notifies the public of the detailed selection criteria; (2) outlines the submission requirements; and (3) provides the closing dates for candidate submissions. The selection committee timely notified the Bureau of its updated selection criteria and proposal submission instructions on October 7, 2026.
The selection committee's notification, attached to the October 9, 2026, Public Notice, specifies its detailed selection criteria and instructions for filing proposals for the clearinghouse position. The selection committee requests that potential clearinghouse candidates with any questions about the selection criteria or submission requirements may email the selection committee no later than October 23, 2026, at
RPCSelectionCommittee@gmail.com
.
Potential clearinghouse candidates must submit proposals according to the filing instructions contained in the selection committee's notification no later than November 9, 2026.
The selection committee and potential clearinghouse candidates are reminded that the selection process must comply
(
printed page 67314)
with all requirements of the
Upper C-band R&O
and the Commission's rules. The selection committee shall inform the Commission of its choice no later than December 15, 2026, after which the Bureau will release a public notice seeking comment on whether that entity meets the selection criteria. The Bureau will then issue a final order announcing whether the selection criteria has been satisfied. After release of a decision finding that the clearinghouse selectee meets the relevant criteria, the selection committee will be dissolved without further action by the Commission.
Federal Communications Commission.
Amy Brett,
Chief of Staff, Wireless Telecommunications Bureau.

AGENCY:
Office of the Secretary, USDA.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) is issuing this notice to announce that civil monetary penalty (CMP) amounts assessed or enforced will not increase for calendar year 2026. USDA is generally required by statute to amend its regulations annually to adjust for inflation the civil monetary penalties assessed or enforced by its components. However, in accordance with guidance from the Office of Management and Budget (“OMB”), USDA will continue to use the 2025 civil monetary penalty levels because there will be no cost-of-living adjustment for 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mr. Michael Poe, Office of the General Counsel, USDA, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20250-1400, (202) 769-8247.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Statutory Process for Implementing Annual Inflation Adjustments
In accordance with the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act of 1990 (
28 U.S.C. 2461 note
), USDA is required to adjust civil monetary penalties periodically for inflation. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (
Pub. L. 114-74
) revised the methodology, requiring agencies to adjust penalties annually based on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) for the month of October of the preceding year. USDA has issued annual inflation adjustments pursuant to this authority, most recently in its final rule on May 29, 2025 (
90 FR 22607
).
II. No Adjustments for 2026
The annual inflation adjustment is based on October CPI-U data. Due to the October-November 2025 lapse in appropriations, the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not produce October 2025 CPI-U data. The statute provides no alternative method for calculating the adjustment. On April 17, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget issued Memorandum M-26-11, instructing all Federal agencies to retain 2025 civil monetary penalty amounts for calendar year 2026. Accordingly, USDA will not make inflation adjustments for 2026.
Consistent with the guidance provided in M-26-11, USDA is not making any adjustments to civil money penalties under the Inflation Adjustment Act in 2026.

full_text:

Department of Justice
Drug Enforcement Administration
On April 7, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Barry Backiewicz, D.D.S., of Gahanna, Ohio (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 2, at 1, 3. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. BB2606436, alleging that Registrant's registration should be revoked because Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Ohio, the state in which [he is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2. (citing
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
).
[
1
]
The OSC notified Registrant of his right to file a written request for hearing, and that if he failed to file such a request, he would be deemed to have waived his right to a hearing and be in default.
Id.
(citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds him to be in default. RFAA, at 2.
[
2
]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
at 1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to
21 CFR 1301.43(c)
,
(f)
,
1301.46
. RFAA, at 3;
see also
21 CFR 1316.67
.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. According to the OSC, on December 31, 2023, Registrant's Ohio dental license expired by its own terms. RFAAX 2, at 2. According to Ohio online records, of which the Agency takes official notice,
[
3
]
Registrant's Ohio dental license is expired. eLicense Ohio Professional Licensure License Lookup,
https://elicense.ohio.gov/​oh_​verifylicense
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice dentistry in Ohio, the state in which he is registered with DEA.
[
4
]
Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. 802(21).”). The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g.,
Lawrence Rudolph, D.M.D.,
89 FR 79310
(2024);
Henry-Norbert O. Ndekwe, M.D.,
90 FR 15990
(2025);
Benson Sergiles, P.A.,
90 FR 32016
(2025).
[
5
]
According to Ohio statute, “[n]o person shall knowingly obtain, possess, or use a controlled substance or a controlled substance analog,” except pursuant to a “prescription issued by a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs if the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose.” Ohio Rev. Code §  2925.11(A), (B)(1)(d) (2025). Further, a “ `[l]icensed
(
printed page 67334)
health professional authorized to prescribe drugs' or `prescriber' means an individual who is authorized by law to prescribe drugs or dangerous drugs or drug therapy related devices in the course of the individual's professional practice.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I). Ohio statute further defines an authorized prescriber as “[a] dentist licensed under Chapter 4715. of the [Ohio] Revised Code.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I)(1). Additionally, Ohio law permits “[a] licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs, if acting in the course of professional practice, in accordance with the laws regulating the professional's practice” to prescribe or administer schedule II, III, IV, and V controlled substances to patients.
Id.
§ 3719.06(A)(1)(a)-(b).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to practice dentistry in Ohio. As discussed above, an individual must be a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in order to handle controlled substances in Ohio. Thus, because Registrant is not a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in Ohio, and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Ohio, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 824(a)
, I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. BB2606436 issued to Barry Backiewicz, D.D.S. Further, pursuant to
28 CFR 0.100(b)
and the authority vested in me by
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
, I hereby deny any pending applications of Barry Backiewicz, D.D.S., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Barry Backiewicz, D.D.S., for additional registration in Ohio. This Order is effective November 25, 2026.
Signing Authority
This document of the Drug Enforcement Administration was signed on October 19, 2026, by DEA Administrator Terrance C. Cole. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DEA. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of DEA. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
Heather Achbach,
Federal Register Liaison Officer, Drug Enforcement Administration.
Footnotes
1.
    
                         According to Agency records, Registrant's registration expired on July 31, 2026. The fact that a registrant allows his registration to expire during the pendency of an OSC does not impact the Agency's jurisdiction or prerogative under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) to adjudicate the OSC to finality.
Jeffrey D. Olsen, M.D.,
84 FR 68474
,
68476-79
(2019).
Back to Citation
2.
    
                         Based on the Government's submissions in its RFAA dated July 21, 2026, the Agency finds that service of the OSC on Registrant was adequate. The RFAA's included Declaration from a DEA Diversion Investigator (DI) indicates that on or about April 9, 2026, the DI along with a second DI traveled to Registrant's registered address to attempt personal service of the OSC, which was unsuccessful. RFAAX 3, at 2. On the same date, the DI mailed a copy of the OSC to Registrant's registered address and emailed a copy of the OSC to Registrant's registered email address, which received successful delivery confirmation.
Id.
at 2-3;
see also id.,
Attachments B-D. Here, the Agency finds that Registrant was successfully served the OSC by email and that the DI's efforts to serve Registrant by other means were “ `reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise [Registrant] of the pendency of the action.' ”
Jones
v.
Flowers,
547 U.S. 220, 226 (2006) (quoting
Mullane
v.
Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.,
339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950)). Therefore, due process notice requirements have been satisfied.
See Mohammed S. Aljanaby, M.D.,
82 FR 34552
,
34552
(2017) (finding that service by email satisfies due process where the email is not returned as undeliverable and other methods have been unsuccessful);
Emilio Luna, M.D.,
77 FR 4829
,
4830
(2012) (same).
Back to Citation
3.
    
                         Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency “may take official notice of facts at any stage in a proceeding—even in the final decision.” United States Department of Justice, Attorney General's Manual on the Administrative Procedure Act 80 (1947) (Wm. W. Gaunt & Sons, Inc., Reprint 1979).
Back to Citation
4.
    
                         Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 556(e)
, “[w]hen an agency decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the evidence in the record, a party is entitled, on timely request, to an opportunity to show the contrary.” The material fact here is that Registrant, as of the date of this Order, is not licensed to practice dentistry in Ohio. Accordingly, Registrant may dispute the Agency's finding by filing a properly supported motion for reconsideration of findings of fact within fifteen calendar days of the date of this Order. Any such motion and response shall be filed and served by email to the other party and to the Office of the Administrator, Drug Enforcement Administration, at
dea.addo.attorneys@dea.gov
.
Back to Citation
5.
    
                         This rule derives from the text of two provisions of the CSA. First, Congress defined the term “practitioner” to mean “a physician . . . or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by . . . the jurisdiction in which he practices . . ., to distribute, dispense, . . . [or] administer . . . a controlled substance in the course of professional practice.”
21 U.S.C. 802(21)
. Second, in setting the requirements for obtaining a practitioner's registration, Congress directed that “[t]he Attorney General shall register practitioners . . . if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.”
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)
. Because Congress has clearly mandated that a practitioner possess state authority in order to be deemed a practitioner under the CSA, DEA has held repeatedly that revocation of a practitioner's registration is the appropriate sanction whenever he is no longer authorized to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which he practices.
See, e.g., Elias Garcia Garcia, P.A.,
90 FR 31242
(2025);
Jason Weakley, R.N., A.P.R.N.,
90 FR 10085
(2025);
Khursheed Haider, M.D.,
90 FR 21950
(2025).
Back to Citation

Abstract:
Funding for the Children, Youth, and Families at Risk (CYFAR) community project grants is authorized under section 3(d) of the Smith-Lever Act (
7 U.S.C. 341
et seq.
), as amended, and other relevant authorizing legislation, which provide jurisdictional basis for the establishment and operation of Extension educational work for benefit of youth and families in communities.
CYFAR funding supports community programs serving children, youth, and families in environments needing support.
CYFAR funds are intended to support the development of high quality, effective programs based on research and to document the impact of programs on intended audiences. The CYFAR Year End Report collects demographic and impact data from each community site to conduct impact evaluations of the programs on its intended audience. The collection of information serves several purposes. It allows NIFA staff to gauge if the program is reaching the audience, and make programmatic improvements. This collection also allows program staff to demonstrate the impacts and capacity that is developed in the locales where federal assistance is provided.
The evaluation processes of CYFAR are consistent with the requirements of Congressional legislation and OMB. The Government Performance and Results Act (GPRA) of 1993 (Pub. L. 103-62), the Federal Activities Inventory Reform Act (FAIR) (
Pub. L. 105-270
), and the Agricultural, Research, Extension and Education Reform Act (AREERA) of 1998 (
Pub. L. 105-185
), together with OMB requirements, support the reporting requirements requested in this information collection. The immediate need of this information collection is to provide a means for satisfying accountability requirements. The long-term objective is to provide a means to enable the evaluation and assessment of the effectiveness of programs receiving federal funds and to fully satisfy requirements of performance and accountability legislation in GPRA, the FAIR Act, and AREERA.

SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard announces its intent to enter a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with LOOKOUT to assess Super Intelligence for automated target detection and establish a reliable coverage-factor value supporting data-driven Lateral Range Curve (LRC) results for Search and Rescue (SAR) operations. Proposed tools must be high technology-readiness-level, commercially available, self-contained, portable, capable of edge computing, and compatible with video-feed-agnostic sensors. While considering LOOKOUT, the Coast Guard seeks public comment on the proposed CRADA and potential participation by other parties. Interested Federal entities with relevant capabilities may submit proposals for similar CRADAs for agency consideration and future collaboration.
DATES:
Your comments and related material must reach the Coast Guard on or before November 25, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by docket number USCG-2026-0374 at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
See the “Public Participation and Request for Comments” portion of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for further instructions on submitting comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this notice of intent, call or email Mr. Sean Lester, Connectivity Branch, U.S. Coast Guard Research and Development Center; telephone 860-271-2600, email
RDC-info@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CG U.S. Coast Guard
DHS Department of Homeland Security
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Purpose
The CG is evaluating the operational impact and technical integration of Super Intelligence (SI) situational awareness tools to perform benchmarking, evaluate system interoperability, and propose data handling best practices. The CG currently leverages a variety of sensor inputs and processes across multiple units and operational assets to complete SAR operations. The incorporation of SI tools may allow the CG to automatically detect, classify, and track targets while addressing variables, such as low light, fog, precipitation, and rough sea states. By implementing these tools and analyzing system performance, the Coast Guard will improve critical decision-making during SAR mission execution when the necessity for rapid data aggregation and continuous analysis is critical.
By examining LOOKOUT's situational awareness tools, the CG has an opportunity to streamline, simplify or augment the existing SAR process workflows and generate performance data relevant to future operations. An additional possible goal is to characterize SI system confidence and operational performance, to build a measurable evaluation tool that could reduce the CG's barrier to integrate SI tools.
III. Public Participation and Request for Comments
We request public comments on this notice. Although we do not plan to respond to comments in the
Federal Register
, we will respond directly to commenters and may modify our proposal in light of comments.
We encourage you to submit comments in response to this notice of inquiry at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
To do so, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
,
type USCG-2026-0374 in the search box and click “Search.” Next, look for this document in the Search Results column, and click on it. Then click on the Comment option. In your submission, please include the docket number for this notice of inquiry and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation. If your material cannot be submitted using
https://www.regulations.gov
,
contact the person in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this document for alternate instructions. To view documents mentioned in this notice of inquiry as being available in the docket, find the docket as described in the previous paragraph, and then select “Supporting & Related Material” in the Document Type column. Public comments will also be placed in our online docket and can be viewed by following instructions on the
https://www.regulations.gov
Frequently Asked Questions webpage.
We accept anonymous comments. Comments we post to
https://www.regulations.gov
will include any personal information you have provided. For more information about privacy and submissions in response to this document, see DHS's eRulemaking System of Records notice (
85 FR 14226
, March 11, 2020).
IV. Discussion
CRADAs are authorized under
15 U.S.C. 3710a
.
[
1
]
A CRADA promotes the transfer of technology to the private sector for commercial use, as well as specified research or development efforts that are consistent with the
(
printed page 67325)
mission of the Federal parties to the CRADA. The Federal party or parties agree with one or more non-Federal parties to share research resources, but the Federal party does not contribute funding.
CRADAs are not procurement contracts. Care is taken to ensure that CRADAs are not used to circumvent the contracting process. CRADAs have a specific purpose and should not be confused with procurement contracts, grants, and other types of agreements.
Under the proposed CRADA, the U. S. Coast Guard Research and Development Center (R&D Center) will collaborate with one non-Federal participant. Together, the R&D Center and the non-Federal participant will conduct testing, development and evaluation of artificial intelligence enabled situational awareness tools designed to augment existing SAR workflows and generate critical performance data to inform future operational adoption.
We anticipate that the Coast Guard's contributions under the proposed CRADA will include the following:
1. Provide appropriate staff with pertinent expertise to take the lead in accomplishing the agreed tasks.
2. Provide all support resources, including travel for Coast Guard staff that support this CRADA.
3. Provide data feeds as required to support test objectives.
We anticipate that the non-Federal participants' contributions under the proposed CRADA will include the following:
1. Provide appropriate staff with pertinent expertise to support the agreed upon tasks in Statement of Work.
2. Provide all support resources, including travel for staff that support this CRADA.
3. Assist with installation of system equipment and software for evaluation.
4. Provide technical support, as needed.
5. Draft summary report in collaboration with all participants.
The Coast Guard reserves the right to select for CRADA participants all, some, or no proposals submitted for this CRADA. The Coast Guard will provide no funding for reimbursement of proposal development costs. Proposals and any other material submitted in response to this notice will not be returned. Proposals submitted are expected to be unclassified and consist of not more than five single-sided pages (excluding cover page, DD 1494, JF-12). The Coast Guard will select proposals at sole discretion on the basis of:
1. How well they communicate an understanding, of and ability to meet, the proposed CRADA's goal; and
2. How well they address the following criteria:
a. Technical capability to support the non-Federal party contributions described, and
b. Resources available for supporting the non-Federal party contributions described.
Currently, the Coast Guard is considering LOOKOUT for participation in this CRADA. This consideration is based on the fact that LOOKOUT has demonstrated its technical ability and availability of SI tools that are ready to be deployed, evaluated and operated in a CG test environment with CG sensor feeds. However, we do not wish to exclude other viable participants from this or similar CRADAs in the future.
This is a technology assessment effort. The goal of the Coast Guard for this CRADA is to establish a framework to determine SI's effectiveness in automating target detection, which will be used to establish a reliable coverage factor value to enable data-driven Lateral Range Curve (LRC) results for Search and Rescue (SAR) operations. Special consideration will be given to small business firms and consortia, and preference will be given to business units located in the United States. This notice is issued under the authority of
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
.
P.J. Granati,
Captain, Commanding Officer, U.S. Coast Guard Research and Development Center.

AGENCY:
